title: Raster Operations
text:
Overview
This notebook uses geolattice.raster.basic_raster_operation: high-level helpers that mirror the GDAL gdal raster CLI while staying compatible with classic GDAL Python bindings (Translate, Warp, FillNodata, Polygonize, ComputeProximity, ContourGenerate, BuildVRT, DEMProcessing).
The exercises follow the R notes in R_Code/working-with-raster-data-r.qmd and R_Code/working-with-raster-data.Rmd: clip, reclassify, focal statistics, raster algebra, aggregation / disaggregation, resample, mosaic, stack, and zonal statistics, using Bangladesh and USA DEM data.








Part
Input
Typical outputs




1 Bangladesh
hilly_DEM_UTM.tif, hilly_dem_BTM.tiff, HILLY_DEM/*.tiff
clip, reclass, focal, algebra, aggregate, mosaic


2 USA
Onondaga_DEM.tif, DEM_TILES/*_PROJ.tif, CO_ELEV.tif, CO_COUNTY_PROJ.shp
mosaic, stack, zonal stats, proximity, contour



Written files land under Data/00_shared/raster_data/output_folder/bangladesh and .../usa.

title: Raster Operations
text:
API overview (basic_raster_operation)
Public helpers and private utilities documented at the top of geolattice/raster/basic_raster_operation.py:
- create: Create a new raster dataset
- edit: Edit raster metadata without changing pixel dimensions
- convert: Convert a raster dataset
- resize: Resize a raster without changing georeferenced extents
- unscale: Convert scaled values into unscaled values using band scale/offset
- fill_nodata: Fill nodata regions by interpolation from edges
- neighbors: Compute each pixel from its neighbors / focal statistics
- focal_statistics: Moving-window focal statistics over a single raster band
- calc: Perform raster algebra
- raster_algebra: Evaluate a NumPy-backed raster algebra expression and write the result
- blend: Blend two rasters
- compare: Compare two rasters
- clip: Clip a raster to a bounding box
- reclassify: Reclassify a raster
- resample: Resample a raster to a new resolution
- aggregate: Aggregate a raster by a factor
- disaggregate: Disaggregate a raster by a factor
- mosaic: Mosaic multiple rasters
- stack: Stack multiple rasters
- summarize_raster: Summarize a raster
- zonal_stats: Calculate zonal statistics
- rasterize / polygonize: Polygonize a raster
- proximity: Calculate proximity
- color_map: Create a color map
- contour: Create a contour
- _gdal: Get the GDAL library
- _gdal_ogr: Get the GDAL OGR library
- _band_nodata: Get the nodata value for a band
- _normalize_dtype: Normalize a dtype
- _gdal_dtype: Normalize a GDAL dtype
- _normalize_resample: Normalize a resample method
- _creation_options: Normalize creation options
- _format_from_path: Get the format from a path
- _vector_driver_from_path: Get the vector driver from a path
- _prepare_destination: Prepare a destination
- _broadcast_band_values: Broadcast band values
- _bounds_to_proj_win: Convert bounds to projection window
- _translate: Translate a raster
- _focal_kernel: Get the focal kernel
- _apply_focal: Apply a focal statistic
- _eval_expression: Evaluate an expression
- _eval_node: Evaluate a node
- _zone_summary: Calculate zone summary
- _read_band_array: Read a band array
- _polygonize: Polygonize a raster
- _proximity: Calculate proximity
Names starting with _ are internal helpers. Prefer the public functions imported below.

title: Raster Operations
text:
Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, points at the Bangladesh and USA raster folders, creates output directories, and imports the operation helpers.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup and package reloads.
import sys  # mutate sys.path so geolattice can be imported from the repo root
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for locating sample rasters

# Third-party numeric / plotting stack used throughout the notebook.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for custom maps
import numpy as np  # array ops for holes, masks, and block aggregates
import pandas as pd  # tabular display of summarize / zonal results
from IPython.display import display  # rich table previews in the notebook

# ===================================================================
# Setup and helpers for basic raster operations and maps.
# Walk up from the working directory to the repo root, reload geolattice.raster,
# import operation helpers, point BD/USA/OUTPUT at sample folders, and
# define show_raster() for quick GeoTIFF summaries.
# ===================================================================

# Resolve the current working directory to an absolute Path.
# Resolve the current working directory as a starting point for the root search.
ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve()
while not (ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "raster_data").is_dir():
    if ROOT.parent == ROOT:
        raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find Data/00_shared/vector_data from the working directory.")
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

# Reload so a long-lived Jupyter kernel picks up package edits.
import importlib  # force-reload modules after editing the package source
import geolattice.raster.basic_raster_operation as _bro  # operation helpers module
import geolattice.raster as _raster  # public raster package that re-exports helpers
importlib.reload(_bro)  # refresh basic_raster_operation in this kernel
importlib.reload(_raster)  # refresh the geolattice.raster package exports

# Public raster operation helpers used in the Bangladesh and USA demos.
from geolattice.raster import (
    aggregate,  # coarsen a raster by an integer factor
    blend,  # opacity blend of two aligned rasters
    calc,  # evaluate a short algebra expression on one source
    class_intervals,  # compute quantile / jenks / equal breaks
    clip,  # crop (and optionally mask) a raster to bounds or a cutline
    color_map,  # GDAL color-relief style RGB from a color text file
    compare,  # pixel-wise equality / diff stats between two rasters
    contour,  # vector contour lines at a fixed interval
    convert,  # copy / reformat a raster (dtype, driver, etc.)
    create,  # write a new empty raster with given size / CRS / geotransform
    disaggregate,  # refine a raster by an integer factor
    edit,  # attach metadata (description, scale, offset) without changing pixels
    fill_nodata,  # interpolate into nodata holes from valid edges
    focal_statistics,  # moving-window statistic (mean, sum, ...)
    mosaic,  # merge several rasters into one continuous surface
    neighbors,  # alias for focal_statistics-style neighborhood ops
    open_raster_data,  # open a GeoTIFF (or other GDAL raster) as a dataset
    polygonize,  # convert raster classes to vector polygons
    proximity,  # distance to target pixel values
    raster_algebra,  # NumPy-backed algebra expression written to a new file
    reclassify,  # map value ranges to new integer classes
    rasterize,  # burn vector attributes onto a regular grid
    reclassify_by,  # reclassify using class_intervals styles (quantile, jenks)
    resample,  # match a target resolution with bilinear / nearest
    resize,  # change pixel dimensions while keeping geographic extent
    stack,  # combine rasters into a multi-band GeoTIFF
    summarize_raster,  # count / min / max / mean / percentiles summary
    unscale,  # apply band scale/offset into pixel values
    write_raster_data,  # write a NumPy array as a georeferenced GeoTIFF
    zonal_stats,  # summarize raster values inside polygon zones
)
# Shared map styling helpers from geolattice.viz.
from geolattice.viz import apply_map_style, plot_raster, plot_raster_histogram, plot_rasters

# Sample raster folders and shared output destinations for this tutorial.
BD = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "raster_data" / "Bangladesh"  # Bangladesh DEM inputs
USA = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "raster_data" / "USA"  # USA DEM and county inputs
OUTPUT = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "raster_data" / "output_folder"  # parent for written results
BD_OUT = OUTPUT / "bangladesh" / "ops"  # Bangladesh operation outputs
USA_OUT = OUTPUT / "usa" / "ops"  # USA operation outputs
# Ensure both output folders exist before any write.
for folder in (BD_OUT, USA_OUT):
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create nested dirs as needed

# Apply the shared GeoLattice map style (fonts, colors, spines).
apply_map_style()


# helper: print size, resolution, bounds, CRS, and nodata for a raster path
def show_raster(path, title=None):
    """Print size, resolution, bounds, CRS, and nodata for a raster path."""
    # Normalize the path argument to a Path object.
    path = Path(path)
    # Open the dataset and print a short metadata summary.
    with open_raster_data(path) as ds:
        gt = ds.geotransform  # affine geotransform (origin, pixel size, rotation)
        print(f"path:    {path.name}")  # file name only for readability
        print(f"size:    {ds.width} x {ds.height}  bands={ds.band_count}")  # pixel grid
        print(f"res:     {abs(gt[1]):.4f} x {abs(gt[5]):.4f}")  # absolute pixel size
        print(f"bounds:  {ds.bounds}")  # geographic extent
        print(f"crs:     {ds.crs}")  # coordinate reference system
        print(f"nodata:  {ds.get_band(1).nodata}")  # band-1 nodata flag
        # Optional extra label when the caller passes a title.
        if title:
            print(f"title:   {title}")


# Confirm which folders the notebook will read from and write to.
print(f"Bangladesh: {BD}")
print(f"USA:        {USA}")
print(f"BD output:  {BD_OUT}")
print(f"USA output: {USA_OUT}")

Part 1: Bangladesh

Inspect the hilly DEM
hilly_DEM_UTM.tif is a 250 m SRTM elevation mosaic for the hilly districts of Bangladesh (same dataset as the R terra::rast(...) example). hilly_dem_BTM.tiff is the Bangladesh Transverse Mercator version used for many of the R processing steps.


Code
# Paths to the UTM and BTM versions of the hilly Bangladesh DEM.
dem_utm = BD / "hilly_DEM_UTM.tif"  # 250 m SRTM mosaic in UTM
dem_btm = BD / "hilly_dem_BTM.tiff"  # same surface in Bangladesh Transverse Mercator
# Confirm both input files are present on disk.
print(f"UTM exists: {dem_utm.exists()}")
print(f"BTM exists: {dem_btm.exists()}")
print()  # blank line between existence checks and metadata
# Print metadata for the UTM DEM.
show_raster(dem_utm, "hilly DEM (UTM)")
print()  # blank line between the two summaries
# Print metadata for the BTM DEM (used by most Bangladesh steps below).
show_raster(dem_btm, "hilly DEM (BTM)")

Summarize and plot
summarize_raster reports count / min / max / mean / std and selected percentiles (similar to R summary(dem)).


Code
# Compute count / min / max / mean / std and selected percentiles for the BTM DEM.
stats = summarize_raster(dem_btm, percentiles=(2, 25, 50, 75, 98))
# Show the summary dict as a one-column table in the notebook.
display(pd.Series(stats).to_frame("value"))

# Draw a terrain-colored map of the BTM DEM (robust stretch hides outliers).
ax = plot_raster(
    dem_btm,  # path to the elevation GeoTIFF
    title="DEM of hilly districts of Bangladesh (BTM)",  # map title
    cmap="terrain",  # elevation-friendly colormap
    kind="general",  # single-band continuous display
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch for contrast
    show=False,  # defer display so we can call plt.show() ourselves

Create / convert / resize / edit / unscale
These match the GDAL-style create / convert / resize / edit / unscale helpers.


Code
# Create: empty float32 template with the DEM geotransform / CRS and visualize it.
# Open the BTM DEM to copy its CRS, geotransform, and size into the template.
with open_raster_data(dem_btm) as ds:
    template_crs = ds.crs  # coordinate reference system for the new file
    template_gt = ds.geotransform  # affine transform (origin + pixel size)
    w, h = ds.width, ds.height  # full DEM width and height in pixels

# Destination path for a small empty template GeoTIFF.
empty_path = BD_OUT / "empty_template.tif"
# Write a small float32 raster filled with nodata (-9999).
create(
    empty_path,  # output path
    width=min(w, 64),  # cap width at 64 pixels for a lightweight demo
    height=min(h, 64),  # cap height at 64 pixels
    bands=1,  # single-band template
    dtype="float32",  # floating-point pixels
    crs=template_crs,  # same CRS as the DEM
    geotransform=template_gt,  # same origin / pixel size as the DEM
    nodata=-9999,  # nodata flag written to the band
    fill=-9999,  # fill every pixel with nodata
    overwrite=True,  # replace any previous demo file
)

# Visualize the created empty raster metadata.
show_raster(empty_path, title="Empty Raster Template (float32)")

# Convert: GeoTIFF copy (optionally change dtype / format).
converted = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_BTM_copy.tif"  # output path for the converted copy
convert(dem_btm, converted, overwrite=True)  # copy dem_btm to a new GeoTIFF
print(f"\nconverted -> {converted.name}")  # confirm the written file name

# Visualize the converted raster metadata.
show_raster(converted, title="Converted DEM (copy)")

# Resize: change pixel dimensions, keep geographic extent, then visualize.
resized = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_BTM_half_px.tif"  # output path for the half-resolution grid
# Shrink width and height to 50% with bilinear resampling (extent unchanged).
resize(dem_btm, resized, width_pct=50, height_pct=50, resample="bilinear", overwrite=True)
show_raster(resized, title="Resized DEM (50% px)")  # print resized metadata

# Edit: attach description / scale / offset metadata without changing pixels.
scaled_meta = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_scaled_meta.tif"  # output path for metadata edit
edit(
    dem_btm,  # source DEM
    scaled_meta,  # destination with updated metadata
    description="Elevation (m) with demo scale/offset",  # band description string
    scale=1.0,  # demo scale factor (identity)
    offset=0.0,  # demo offset (identity)
    overwrite=True,  # replace any previous demo file
)
print(f"edit -> {scaled_meta.name}")  # confirm the written file name
show_raster(scaled_meta, title="Edited DEM (added scale/offset meta)")  # print metadata
# Plot the edited DEM (pixels unchanged; only metadata differs).
ax = plot_raster(
    scaled_meta,
    title="Edited DEM (added scale/offset meta)",
    cmap="terrain",
    kind="general",
    robust=True,
    show=False,
)
plt.show()  # render the edited DEM map

# Unscale: apply band scale/offset into pixel values (here scale=1, offset=0).
unscaled = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_unscaled.tif"  # output path for unscaled values
unscale(scaled_meta, unscaled, dtype="float32", overwrite=True)  # bake scale/offset into pixels
print(f"unscale -> {unscaled.name}")  # confirm the written file name
show_raster(unscaled, title="Unscaled DEM")  # print unscaled metadata
# Plot the unscaled DEM.
ax = plot_raster(
    unscaled,
    title="Unscaled DEM",
    cmap="terrain",
    kind="general",
    robust=True,
    show=False,
)
plt.show()  # render the unscaled DEM map

# Compare a DEM against itself to demonstrate compare() equality stats.
cmp = compare(dem_utm, dem_utm)  # self-compare should report equal=True
print(
    "compare(self): equal={equal} max_abs_diff={max_abs_diff}".format(**cmp)
)  # print key equality fields

Clip
Raster clipping refers to the process of extracting a portion of a raster dataset based on a specified spatial extent or boundary. This is a common operation in geospatial analysis when you need to focus on a specific area of interest within a larger raster dataset. Raster clipping can help reduce the dataset’s size, improve processing efficiency, and facilitate analysis that’s relevant to a particular region.
Clip by projected bounds (same idea as R crop() / extent). Bounds are (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in the raster CRS. Here we take a window over the southern hills (Bandarban / Cox’s Bazar region in BTM meters).


Code
# Open the BTM DEM and build a southern window from its projected bounds.
with open_raster_data(dem_btm) as ds:
    # Unpack full extent as (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in the raster CRS.
    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = ds.bounds.to_tuple()
    # Southern window ~ lower third of the mosaic (Bandarban / Cox's Bazar region).
    clip_bounds = (
        minx + 0.15 * (maxx - minx),  # inset 15% from the west
        miny,  # keep the southern edge
        maxx - 0.15 * (maxx - minx),  # inset 15% from the east
        miny + 0.35 * (maxy - miny),  # take the lower ~35% of the height
    )
    print("full bounds:", ds.bounds)  # print the full DEM extent
    print("clip bounds:", clip_bounds)  # print the crop window

# Destination path for the clipped GeoTIFF.
clipped = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_BTM_clipped.tif"
# Crop the DEM to the projected bounds window.
clip(dem_btm, clipped, bounds=clip_bounds, overwrite=True)
# Print metadata for the clipped result.
show_raster(clipped)

# Side-by-side map: full DEM vs clipped southern window.
fig, axes = plot_rasters(
    [dem_btm, clipped],  # input paths for the two panels

Fill nodata
fill_nodata interpolates from valid edges into nodata regions (gdal.FillNodata). We introduce a small hole in the clip, then fill it.

# Read the clipped DEM into a NumPy array and capture georeferencing for rewrite.
with open_raster_data(clipped) as ds:
    arr = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float32)  # band-1 elevation array
    crs = ds.crs  # coordinate reference system to preserve on write
    gt = ds.geotransform  # affine transform to preserve on write
    nodata = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # existing nodata flag (may be None)
    # Fall back to -9999 when the source has no nodata or uses NaN.
    if nodata is None or (isinstance(nodata, float) and np.isnan(nodata)):
        nodata = -9999.0  # synthetic nodata used for the punched hole

# Punch a slightly smaller rectangular hole near the center.
h, w = arr.shape  # array height and width in pixels
hole_half_size = 16  # half-width of the hole (32x32 pixels total)
r0, r1 = h // 2 - hole_half_size, h // 2 + hole_half_size  # row slice of the hole
c0, c1 = w // 2 - hole_half_size, w // 2 + hole_half_size  # column slice of the hole
holed = arr.copy()  # copy so the original clipped array stays intact
holed[r0:r1, c0:c1] = nodata  # set the center window to nodata
holed_path = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_with_hole.tif"  # path for the holed GeoTIFF

Focal statistics / neighbors
Focal statistics, also known as neighborhood or moving window statistics, involve performing calculations on a raster dataset using a moving window that slides over each cell. This window defines a local area around each cell, and calculations are carried out based on the values within that window. This technique is commonly used for various geospatial analysis tasks, such as smoothing, edge detection, and texture analysis.
In R, you can perform focal statistics using packages like raster and terra.
To illustrate the neighborhood processing for Focal Statistics calculating a Sum statistic, consider the processing cell with a value of 5 in the following diagram. A rectangular 3 by 3 cell neighborhood shape is specified. The sum of the values of the neighboring cells (3 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 19) plus the value of the processing cell (5) equals 24 (19 + 5 = 24). So a value of 24 is given to the cell in the output raster in the same location as the processing cell in the input raster.
Moving-window stats (focal_statistics / alias neighbors) correspond to R terra::focal(). Window size must be an odd integer.

Aggregate / disaggregate / resample
Raster aggregation involves converting a high-resolution raster dataset into a lower-resolution raster dataset by grouping or summarizing cells into larger cells. This process reduces the level of detail in the data and can help improve processing efficiency and visualization for large datasets. Aggregation is often used when working with raster data at different scales, or when matching the resolution of one raster to another for analysis or visualization purposes.

aggregate(factor=2) -> ~500 m cells from 250 m (R aggregate(..., fact=2))
disaggregate(factor=5) -> ~50 m cells (R disagg(..., fact=5))
resample matches a target resolution with bilinear (or nearest) interpolation



Code
# Re-import write_raster_data for the block mean / SD / SE GeoTIFF writes below.
from geolattice.raster import write_raster_data

# Use Hilly DEM (mosaic) for aggregation, disaggregation, and resampling.
hilly_dem_path = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_mosaic.tif"  # mosaic written in the mosaic cells

# Output paths for coarsened, refined, and resampled products.
agg_500 = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_500m.tif"  # factor-2 aggregate (~500 m)
disagg_50 = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_50m.tif"  # factor-5 disaggregate (~50 m)
resamp_250 = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_resampled_250m.tif"  # resample 500 m back to 250 m

# Aggregate by 2 (average), disaggregate by 5 (bilinear), then resample to original res.
aggregate(hilly_dem_path, agg_500, factor=2, method="average", overwrite=True)
disaggregate(hilly_dem_path, disagg_50, factor=5, method="bilinear", overwrite=True)
# Read the source pixel size so resample can target the original resolution.
with open_raster_data(hilly_dem_path) as ds:
    xres, yres = abs(ds.geotransform[1]), abs(ds.geotransform[5])  # absolute pixel sizes
# Resample the 500 m aggregate back toward the original 250 m grid.
resample(agg_500, resamp_250, resolution=(xres, yres), method="bilinear", overwrite=True)

# Print metadata for each resolution product.
for label, path in [
    ("250 m (source mosaic)", hilly_dem_path),
    ("500 m (aggregate)", agg_500),
    ("50 m (disaggregate)", disagg_50),
    ("250 m (resampled from 500)", resamp_250),
]:

    nodata = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # band nodata flag

# Replace nodata with NaN so nanmean / nanstd ignore those pixels.
if nodata is not None and not (isinstance(nodata, float) and np.isnan(nodata)):
    work = np.where(arr == nodata, np.nan, arr)  # nodata -> NaN
else:
    work = arr.copy()  # no nodata flag: work on a copy of the array

# Trim to even dimensions so 2x2 reshape has no leftover edge.
h, w = work.shape  # full height and width
h2, w2 = h - (h % 2), w - (w % 2)  # even sizes
# Reshape into non-overlapping 2x2 blocks.
blocks = work[:h2, :w2].reshape(h2 // 2, 2, w2 // 2, 2)
mean_500 = np.nanmean(blocks, axis=(1, 3))  # block mean
sd_500 = np.nanstd(blocks, axis=(1, 3))  # block standard deviation
se_500 = sd_500 / np.sqrt(2.0)  # standard error used in this demo (sd / sqrt(2))

# Geotransform with doubled pixel size for the 500 m products.
gt_500 = (gt[0], gt[1] * 2, gt[2], gt[3], gt[4], gt[5] * 2)
mean_path = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_agg_mean_500m.tif"  # mean GeoTIFF path
sd_path = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_agg_sd_500m.tif"  # SD GeoTIFF path
se_path = BD_OUT / "hilly_dem_agg_se_500m.tif"  # SE GeoTIFF path
# Write mean / SD / SE as float32 GeoTIFFs.
write_raster_data(mean_path, mean_500.astype(np.float32), crs=crs, geotransform=gt_500, overwrite=True)
write_raster_data(sd_path, sd_500.astype(np.float32), crs=crs, geotransform=gt_500, overwrite=True)
write_raster_data(se_path, se_500.astype(np.float32), crs=crs, geotransform=gt_500, overwrite=True)

# 1x3 panel: mean / SD / SE (plasma + colorbars).
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 5))  # one row, three columns
panel = [
    (mean_path, "500 m x 500 m of Hilly DEM", (0, 900)),  # mean with fixed stretch
    (sd_path, "SD (m)", (0, 100)),  # SD with fixed stretch
    (se_path, "SE (m)", (0, 70)),  # SE with fixed stretch
]
# Plot each summary raster into its panel with a fixed vmin/vmax.
for ax, (path, title, (vmin, vmax)) in zip(axes, panel):
    plot_raster(
        path,  # summary GeoTIFF
        ax=ax,  # target axes
        title=title,  # panel title
        cmap="plasma",  # shared colormap
        kind="general",  # single-band continuous display
        robust=False,  # use explicit vmin/vmax instead
        vmin=vmin,  # lower color stretch
        vmax=vmax,  # upper color stretch
        add_colorbar=True,  # show a colorbar
        show=False,  # defer display
    )
    ax.set_xticks([])  # hide x ticks
    ax.set_yticks([])  # hide y ticks
    ax.set_xlabel("")  # clear x label
    ax.set_ylabel("")  # clear y label

fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.25)  # space for colorbars
fig.tight_layout()  # final spacing pass
plt.show()  # render the mean / SD / SE figure

Mosaic
Raster mosaicking is the process of combining multiple raster datasets to create a single, continuous raster dataset that covers a larger geographic area. Mosaicking is commonly used when you have multiple raster images that need to be merged into a seamless and complete representation of a larger region. This technique is often employed in remote sensing, geospatial analysis, and cartography.

print(f"counties exist: {counties.exists()}")  # confirm the shapefile is present

# Summarize elevation inside each county polygon (grouped by COUNTY_ID).
rows = zonal_stats(
    co_elev,  # Colorado elevation raster
    counties,  # county polygon zones
    zone_field="COUNTY_ID",  # group zones by county id
    stats=("count", "min", "max", "mean", "sum"),  # requested summary stats
)
# Convert the list of zone dicts into a DataFrame for display and joining.
zonal_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(zonal_df.head(10))  # preview the first 10 zone rows

# GeoPandas is used to join stats back onto county polygons for choropleth maps.
import geopandas as gpd

# Keep county id, name, and geometry for the join / plot.
gdf = gpd.read_file(counties)[["COUNTY_ID", "COUNTY", "geometry"]]
# Align join key dtypes, then keep a GeoDataFrame so .plot() draws polygons.
zonal_df["COUNTY_ID"] = zonal_df["COUNTY_ID"].astype(gdf["COUNTY_ID"].dtype)
merged = gdf.merge(zonal_df, on="COUNTY_ID", how="left")  # left join keeps all counties

# Four choropleth panels for min / max / mean / sum elevation.
statnames = ["min", "max", "mean", "sum"]  # columns to map
titles = [
    "County Min Elevation",
    "County Max Elevation",
    "County Mean Elevation",
    "County Sum Elevation",
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(statnames), figsize=(16, 5))  # one row of panels

# Plot each statistic as a county choropleth.
for ax, stat, title in zip(axes, statnames, titles):
    merged.plot(
        column=stat,  # attribute to color by
        cmap="terrain",  # elevation-friendly colormap
        legend=True,  # show a legend for the color scale
        ax=ax,  # target axes
        edgecolor="black",  # county outlines
        linewidth=0.5,  # thin outlines
        missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"},  # counties with no stats
    )
    ax.set_title(title)  # panel title
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide axes for a clean map

fig.suptitle("Zonal statistics by Colorado county", y=1.02, fontsize=16)  # shared title
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.95])  # leave room for the suptitle
plt.show()  # render the zonal statistics figure

# Open the Onondaga mosaic and build a central window from its projected bounds.
with open_raster_data(usa_mosaic) as ds:

    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = ds.bounds.to_tuple()
    # Central window ~ middle 50% of the mosaic.
    mid_bounds = (
        minx + 0.25 * (maxx - minx),  # inset 25% from the west
        miny + 0.25 * (maxy - miny),  # inset 25% from the south
        maxx - 0.25 * (maxx - minx),  # inset 25% from the east
        maxy - 0.25 * (maxy - miny),  # inset 25% from the north

title: Reading and Writing Raster Data
text:
Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, points SAMPLES at the GDAL rasters, creates OUTPUT, and defines helpers that print metadata and draw a raster.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup.
import sys  # mutate sys.path so geolattice can be imported from the repo root
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for locating sample data

# Third-party GIS / plotting stack used throughout the notebook.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for custom maps
import numpy as np  # array math for RGB scaling and dtype casts
import pandas as pd  # tabular display of supported drivers
from IPython.display import display  # rich table previews in the notebook
from osgeo import gdal  # GDAL version string and quiet error handler


# ===================================================================
# Setup and helpers for reading, plotting, and writing rasters.
# Walk up from the working directory to the repo root, import GeoLattice tools,
# point SAMPLES / OUTPUT at the sample folders, and define plot helpers.
# ===================================================================

# Resolve the current working directory to an absolute Path.
ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve()
# Search this directory and its parents for the GeoLattice repo root.
for candidate in [ROOT, *ROOT.parents]:
    # Require sample data and the geolattice package (src/ layout or a geolattice/ folder).
    if (candidate / "Data").is_dir() and (
        (candidate / "geolattice").is_dir()
        or ((candidate / "src" / "__init__.py").is_file() and (candidate / "pyproject.toml").is_file())
    ):
        # Keep the matching directory as ROOT and stop searching.
        ROOT = candidate
        # Exit the for-loop once the repo root is found.
        break
# for/else: runs only when the loop never hit break.
else:
    # Raise when neither this folder nor any parent looks like the repo.
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find the GeoLattice repository root.")
# Prefer the repo root on sys.path so `import geolattice` resolves locally.
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

# Raster open / write helpers exported from geolattice.raster.
from geolattice.raster import (
    open_raster_data,  # context-managed RasterDataset opener
    read_raster_data,  # open alias used for round-trip checks
    supported_formats,  # list formats open_raster_data knows by extension
    supported_write_formats,  # same list plus writable flags for this GDAL
    write_geotiff,  # write a GeoTIFF with optional creation options
    write_jpeg,  # write a JPEG from a band or RGB stack
    write_png,  # write a PNG from a band or RGB stack
    write_raster_data,  # write any supported format by extension or driver=
)
# Shared map styling and raster plot helpers from geolattice.viz.
from geolattice.viz import apply_map_style, plot_raster, plot_rasters

# Sample GDAL autotest rasters for this tutorial.
SAMPLES = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "raster_data" / "gdal_samples"
# Folder where written demo outputs will be saved.
OUTPUT = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "raster_data" / "output_folder"
# Create the output folder if it does not already exist.
OUTPUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
# Fail early if the sample folder is missing.
assert SAMPLES.is_dir(), SAMPLES

# Suppress noisy GDAL warnings while still raising hard errors.
gdal.PushErrorHandler("CPLQuietErrorHandler")
# Keep printed attribute tables readable in the notebook.
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 12)  # show up to 12 columns
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)  # wider console wrapping for tables
# Apply the shared GeoLattice map style (fonts, colors, spines).
apply_map_style()


# helper: print one line of driver / size / band / CRS metadata
def summarize(path, dataset):
    # short description of what summarize prints
    """Print one-line raster properties."""
    # Format name, driver, dimensions, band count, and CRS on one line.
    print(
        f"{Path(path).name:28}  driver={dataset.driver:8}  "
        f"size={dataset.width}x{dataset.height}  bands={dataset.band_count}  "
        f"crs={dataset.crs}"
    )


# helper: plot a 2-D band or bands-first RGB stack with plot_raster
def display_array(array, *, title=None, cmap="viridis", figsize=(6, 4)):
    # short description of what display_array draws
    """Plot a 2-D band or 3-D RGB stack (bands-first)."""
    # Treat a 3- or 4-band stack as RGB when the first axis is bands.
    if array.ndim == 3 and array.shape[0] in (3, 4):
        # Move bands to the last axis so matplotlib gets HxWx3.
        rgb = np.moveaxis(array[:3], 0, -1)
        # Stretch floating RGB to 0-1 with a robust percentile clip.
        if np.issubdtype(rgb.dtype, np.floating):
            # Compute the 2nd and 98th percentiles as stretch endpoints.
            lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(rgb, (2, 98))
            # Scale into 0-1 and clip outliers outside that range.
            rgb = np.clip((rgb - lo) / max(hi - lo, 1e-9), 0, 1)
        # Scale non-uint8 integer RGB into 0-1 for display.
        elif rgb.dtype != np.uint8:
            # Read the integer type limits for this dtype.
            info = np.iinfo(rgb.dtype)
            # Divide by the max integer value and clip to 0-1.
            rgb = (rgb.astype(np.float32) / max(info.max, 1)).clip(0, 1)
        # Draw RGB without a colorbar.
        return plot_raster(
            rgb, title=title, rgb=True, add_colorbar=False, figsize=figsize  # HxWx3 RGB display
        )
    # For other multiband arrays, show the first band only.
    if array.ndim == 3:
        # Keep band 0 as a 2-D array for a single-band plot.
        array = array[0]
    # Draw a single-band map with a robust stretch.
    return plot_raster(array, title=title, cmap=cmap, figsize=figsize, robust=True)


# helper: open one path, print metadata, plot, and return key fields
def read_and_show(path, *, cmap="viridis", figsize=(6, 4)):
    # short description of what read_and_show returns
    """Open a raster, print metadata, plot pixels, return the array."""
    # Open the raster and release the GDAL handle when the block exits.
    with open_raster_data(path) as dataset:
        # Print driver / size / CRS for this file.
        summarize(path, dataset)
        # Load all bands into a NumPy array (bands-first).
        array = dataset.read()
        # Plot the array (RGB or single band) under the file name.
        display_array(array, title=Path(path).name, cmap=cmap, figsize=figsize)
        # Return fields later cells may reuse for writing.
        return dataset.driver, array, dataset.geotransform, dataset.crs


# Confirm which folders the notebook will read from and write to.
print(f"Samples: {SAMPLES}")
# Print the output folder path used by the write cells.
print(f"Output:  {OUTPUT}")
# Show the linked GDAL build version.
print(f"GDAL:    {gdal.VersionInfo('--version')}")

Drivers known to this package
supported_formats() lists the file-based formats open_raster_data tries by extension. supported_write_formats() adds whether this GDAL build can create them (DCAP_CREATE or DCAP_CREATECOPY).

# Collect one row per format known to open_raster_data.
rows = []
# Walk the list of readable format records.
for record in supported_formats():
    # Find the matching write-capability record by format name, or {}.
    write_info = next(
        (item for item in supported_write_formats() if item["name"] == record["name"]),  # match on name
        {},  # default when this format has no write entry
    )
    # Build a flat dict for the summary table.
    rows.append(
        {
            "format": record["name"],  # human-readable format name
            "extensions": ", ".join(record["extensions"]),  # file suffixes
            "drivers": ", ".join(record["drivers"]),  # GDAL short names
            "readable": record["available"],  # True if this GDAL can open it
            "writable": write_info.get("writable", False),  # True if create/createcopy works
        }
    )
# Show the capability table in the notebook.
display(pd.DataFrame(rows))

title: Reading and Writing Raster Data
text:
GeoTIFF
GeoTIFF is the default exchange format for single-band and multiband grids. These files are the classic GDAL autotest rasters from autotest/gdrivers/data.


Code
# Classic single-band GeoTIFF samples from the GDAL autotest tree.
geotiffs = [
    SAMPLES / "byte.tif",  # 8-bit integer grid
    SAMPLES / "float32.tif",  # 32-bit float grid
    SAMPLES / "int16.tif",  # 16-bit signed integer grid
    SAMPLES / "n43.tif",  # USGS DEM-style GeoTIFF
    SAMPLES / "utm.tif",  # larger UTM-projected grid
]

# Hold pixel arrays for a multi-panel plot.
arrays = []
# Hold panel titles aligned with arrays.
titles = []
# Open each GeoTIFF, print metadata, and collect the pixel array.
for path in geotiffs:
    # Open the raster and release the handle when done.
    with open_raster_data(path) as dataset:
        # Print one-line metadata for this file.
        summarize(path, dataset)
        # Append the full bands-first array.
        arrays.append(dataset.read())
        # Keep the file name as the panel title.
        titles.append(path.name)

# Draw all single-band GeoTIFFs in a shared grid.
plot_rasters(arrays, titles=titles, ncols=3, figsize=(12, 7), cmap="terrain")

section: ESRI ASCII Grid, Erdas Imagine, ENVI, USGS DEM
text:
ESRI ASCII Grid, Erdas Imagine, ENVI, USGS DEM
These are common desktop GIS and remote-sensing formats. Open the data file for ENVI (.img / .dat), not the .hdr header.


Code
# Desktop GIS / remote-sensing formats with a preferred colormap each.
other_paths = [
    (SAMPLES / "aaigrid" / "pixel_per_line.asc", "viridis"),  # ESRI ASCII Grid
    (SAMPLES / "hfa" / "dem10.img", "terrain"),  # Erdas Imagine DEM
    (SAMPLES / "envi" / "envi_rgbsmall_bsq.img", "viridis"),  # ENVI BSQ (data file, not .hdr)
    (SAMPLES / "usgsdem" / "39079G6_truncated.dem", "terrain"),  # USGS DEM
]
# Open, summarize, and plot each format with its colormap.
for path, cmap in other_paths:

title: Reading and Writing Raster Data
text:
Writing rasters
write_raster_data picks the driver from the file extension (or from driver=). write_geotiff, write_png, and write_jpeg fix the driver. Pass overwrite=True to replace an existing file.
The next cells copy the classic byte.tif grid into several formats under Data/00_shared/raster_data/output_folder, then write a compressed tiled GeoTIFF of utm.tif.


Code
# Open the classic byte.tif sample as the write source.
with open_raster_data(SAMPLES / "byte.tif") as src:
    # Load all bands into a NumPy array.
    byte = src.read()
    # Keep the affine geotransform for written copies.
    byte_gt = src.geotransform
    # Keep the CRS string / WKT for written copies.
    byte_crs = src.crs
    # Keep band-1 nodata so GeoTIFF / ASCII preserve it.
    byte_nodata = src.get_band(1).nodata

# Map of output file name -> written path for the verify loop below.
written = {}
# Write a compressed, tiled GeoTIFF copy.
written["byte_copy.tif"] = write_geotiff(
    OUTPUT / "byte_copy.tif",  # destination path
    byte,  # pixel array
    crs=byte_crs,  # CRS from the source
    geotransform=byte_gt,  # geotransform from the source
    nodata=byte_nodata,  # nodata from band 1
    overwrite=True,  # replace an existing file
    creation_options={"COMPRESS": "LZW", "TILED": "YES"},  # LZW + tiles
)
# Write an 8-bit PNG (cast required for PNG).
written["byte.png"] = write_png(OUTPUT / "byte.png", byte.astype(np.uint8), overwrite=True)
# Write an 8-bit JPEG.
written["byte.jpg"] = write_jpeg(OUTPUT / "byte.jpg", byte.astype(np.uint8), overwrite=True)

# Write an ESRI ASCII Grid via the generic writer.
written["byte.asc"] = write_raster_data(
    OUTPUT / "byte.asc",  # destination path
    byte.astype(np.float32),  # AAIGrid expects floating values
    driver="AAIGrid",  # force the ASCII Grid driver
    crs=byte_crs,  # CRS from the source
    geotransform=byte_gt,  # geotransform from the source
    nodata=-9999,  # ASCII nodata sentinel
    overwrite=True,  # replace an existing file
)

# Write an Erdas Imagine .img via the generic writer.
written["byte.img"] = write_raster_data(
    OUTPUT / "byte.img",  # destination path
    byte,  # pixel array
    driver="HFA",  # Erdas Imagine driver
    crs=byte_crs,  # CRS from the source
    geotransform=byte_gt,  # geotransform from the source
    overwrite=True,  # replace an existing file
)

# Re-open each written file and print one-line metadata.
for name, path in written.items():
    # Confirm the file opens and report driver / size / CRS.
    with read_raster_data(path) as dataset:
        # Print driver / size / CRS for this written path.
        summarize(path, dataset)

title: Geometry Operations
text:
Overview
Geometry operations build new features from points, lines, and polygons, and they clean coordinates before area, length, or a map is published.
GeoLattice implements these tools in geolattice.vector.geometry_tools and exports them from geolattice.vector. They use Shapely and return a GeoDataFrame when GeoPandas is installed.
Shapefiles are opened with open_vectors_data(). Maps use plot_layer(), plot_layers(), plot_pair(), and style_axes() from geolattice.viz.
The notebook is organized in three parts:

Load data: US states, counties, Colorado soil samples, Onondaga streets, and Yellowstone.
Construct geometry: bounding boxes, offsets, points along lines, rectangles/ovals/diamonds, transects, transforms, orthogonalize, and snap.
Measure and clean: geometry attributes, collect, centroids, displacement, validity, duplicate vertices, and holes.

Sample files live in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA.

title: Geometry Operations
text:
Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, applies the tutorial map style, and defines read_layer for shapefiles under Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA.
Geometry tools are imported from geolattice.vector. Maps use plot_layer, plot_layers, plot_pair, and style_axes from geolattice.viz.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup.
import sys  # mutate sys.path so geolattice can be imported from the repo root
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for locating sample data

# Third-party GIS / plotting stack used throughout the notebook.
import geopandas as gpd  # GeoDataFrame constructors and CRS handling
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for custom maps
import pandas as pd  # tabular display options
from IPython.display import display  # rich table previews in the notebook
from shapely.geometry import Point, Polygon  # build points and hole rings





Code
# ===================================================================
# Setup and helpers for geometry operations and maps.
# Walk up from the working directory to the repo root, import GeoLattice tools,
# point DATA at the sample folder, and define read_layer().
# ===================================================================

# Resolve the current working directory to an absolute Path.
ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve()
while not (ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data").is_dir():
    if ROOT.parent == ROOT:
        raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find Data/00_shared/vector_data from the working directory.")
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

# Geometry construction / cleanup helpers exported from geolattice.vector.
from geolattice.vector import (
    add_geometry_attributes,  # area, perimeter, length, x/y columns
    affine_transform,  # scale, then rotate, then translate
    build_sections,  # rectangle grid or attribute-based dissolve sections
    centroids,  # center of mass for each feature
    check_validity,  # is_valid flag and reason per feature
    collect_geometries,  # multipart collect without dissolving overlaps
    delete_holes,  # remove interior rings from polygons
    diamonds,  # diamond polygons centered on points
    fix_geometries,  # repair invalid geometries
    offset_lines,  # parallel copies of a line
    open_vectors_data,  # open a shapefile (or other vector source)
    oriented_minimum_bounding_box,  # rotated enclosing rectangle
    orthogonalize,  # square near-right-angle corners
    ovals,  # ellipse polygons centered on points
    point_on_surface,  # guaranteed-interior label point
    points_along_geometry,  # stations spaced along a line
    points_displacement,  # spread stacked points onto a circle
    rectangles,  # axis-aligned then rotated rectangles on points
    remove_duplicate_vertices,  # drop near-duplicate consecutive vertices
    rotate,  # rotate features about a shared or per-feature origin
    snap_geometries_to_layer,  # snap vertices onto a reference layer
    snap_points_to_grid,  # round vertices to a regular grid
    transect,  # cross-path lines at an interval
    translate,  # shift features by a fixed x/y offset
)
# Shared map styling helpers from geolattice.viz.
from geolattice.viz import EDGE, FACE, apply_map_style, plot_layer, plot_layers, plot_pair, style_axes

# Sample vector data for this tutorial.
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA"
assert DATA.is_dir(), DATA  # fail early if the folder is missing

# Keep printed attribute tables readable in the notebook.
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 12)  # show up to 12 columns
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 48)  # truncate long string cells
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)  # wider console wrapping for tables
# Apply the shared GeoLattice map style (fonts, colors, spines).
apply_map_style()


# helper: open one shapefile under DATA as a GeoDataFrame
def read_layer(relative):
    # short description of what read_layer returns
    """Open one shapefile and return a GeoDataFrame without the reader fid."""
    # Build an absolute path under DATA from a relative shapefile path.
    path = DATA / relative
    # Open the vector dataset and convert it to a pandas/GeoPandas table.
    with open_vectors_data(path) as dataset:
        frame = dataset.to_dataframe()  # attribute table plus geometry column
        crs = frame.crs  # coordinate reference system of the layer
    # Drop the driver-added fid column when present so demos stay tidy.
    if "fid" in frame.columns:
        frame = frame.drop(columns="fid")  # remove the driver-added fid column
    # Rebuild an explicit GeoDataFrame with the preserved CRS.
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(frame, geometry="geometry", crs=crs)


# Confirm which folder the notebook will read from.
print(f"Data folder: {DATA}")

title: Geometry Operations
text:
Available operations
Each function below is imported from geolattice.vector.








Operation
Function
What it does




Rectangles
rectangles()
Builds a rectangle centered on each point. width runs east-west and height runs north-south, then angle rotates the polygon. A multipoint becomes one rectangle per part.


Ovals
ovals()
Builds an ellipse centered on each point. width and height are the full axis lengths. quad_segs is the number of segments used for a quarter of the ellipse.


Diamonds
diamonds()
Builds a diamond centered on each point. width is the horizontal diagonal and height is the vertical diagonal before rotation.


Oriented minimum bounding box
oriented_minimum_bounding_box()
Builds the rotated rectangle that encloses the layer, or each feature when per_feature=True. Returns angle, width (longer side), and height (shorter side).


Rotate
rotate()
Rotates features counterclockwise about one origin. "center" uses the middle of the layer bounds, "centroid" uses the combined centroid, "feature" uses each feature’s own centroid, and (x, y) uses that point.


Affine transform
affine_transform()
Scales, then rotates, then translates, in that order, about the same kinds of origin as rotate(). scale is one number or an (x_scale, y_scale) pair. translation is an (x, y) shift applied after rotation.


Translate
translate()
Shifts every feature by the same xoff, yoff, and optional zoff.


Offset lines
offset_lines()
Copies each line into parallel lines. side is "left", "right", or "both". count is the number of copies on each requested side. The result adds offset_index and offset_distance. A polygon is offset along its exterior ring.


Points along a line
points_along_geometry()
Places points along each line at a fixed spacing. start_offset skips the beginning and end_offset leaves the end unused. Each point keeps the source attributes and records distance_along.


Transects
transect()
Draws lines across a path. interval is the spacing along the path; when it is omitted, a transect is drawn at each vertex. angle is measured from the path direction, so 90 is perpendicular and points to the left. length is the full length when side is "both".


Orthogonalize
orthogonalize()
Squares corners that are already within angle_tolerance degrees of 90. Neighboring vertices stay fixed. Line endpoints stay where they are. Rings and holes are squared on their own.


Snap points to a grid
snap_points_to_grid()
Rounds every vertex to the nearest intersection of a regular grid. spacing_y defaults to spacing_x. origin_x and origin_y locate one grid intersection. Z values stay unchanged.


Snap geometries to a layer
snap_geometries_to_layer()
Moves vertices onto a reference layer when they are within tolerance. mode is "vertices", "segments", or "vertices_and_segments". Passing the same layer as both inputs collapses vertices that should share an edge.


Build sections
build_sections()
In grid mode, lays out a rows-by-columns rectangle grid. origin is the southwest corner before angle is applied. Each cell is named R{row}C{column}. In attribute mode, by unions features that share a value and adds n_features.


Geometry attributes
add_geometry_attributes()
Writes polygon area and perimeter, line length, and point x, y, and z when a point has a height. A column is added only for geometry types that are present.


Collect geometries
collect_geometries()
Groups features into one multipart geometry. Overlaps stay as separate parts. Mixed types become a GeometryCollection. n_features counts the features in the part.


Centroids
centroids()
Creates the centroid of each feature. The centroid of a concave polygon can fall outside the polygon.


Point on surface
point_on_surface()
Creates one point that lies inside each feature. For a polygon it is on the surface, for a line it is on the line, and for a point it is the point itself.


Points displacement
points_displacement()
Spreads point features that were recorded at the same location onto a circle of radius distance. proximity is how close points must be to belong to one stack. proximity=0 treats coordinates that match to 8 decimal places as one stack.


Check validity
check_validity()
Adds is_valid and validity_reason. invalid_only=True drops the valid rows.


Fix geometries
fix_geometries()
Repairs invalid geometries. method="make_valid" keeps the original vertex locations. method="buffer" uses a zero-width buffer. Valid geometries are copied through unchanged.


Remove duplicate vertices
remove_duplicate_vertices()
Drops consecutive vertices closer than tolerance. tolerance=0 removes exact duplicates only. A ring that no longer has three distinct corners becomes empty.


Delete holes
delete_holes()
Removes interior rings from polygons. minimum_area=0 deletes every hole. A positive value deletes only holes smaller than that area. Lines and points pass through unchanged.




Shared rules
Angles are degrees counterclockwise from east, the positive X axis. The angle returned by oriented_minimum_bounding_box() can be passed straight to rectangles(), ovals(), diamonds(), rotate(), and affine_transform().
Distances, widths, heights, and tolerances are in the coordinate units of the layer. The layers in this notebook use an Albers projection in metres, so 40 means 40 metres. On a geographic layer those numbers are degrees. The tools warn when that happens. Project the layer to a metre or foot CRS before using a ground distance.
width, height, angle, and distance accept a single number, a sequence with one value per feature, or the name of a numeric attribute.
A function accepts a GeoDataFrame, a GeoSeries, a pandas DataFrame with a geometry column, a Shapely geometry, WKT, a GeoJSON geometry mapping, a sequence of those, a sequence of VectorFeature, or an open vector layer.

title: Geometry Operations
text:
Part 1: Load data

Layers
The shapefiles are in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA:

US state boundaries (US_STATE.shp)
US county boundaries (US_COUNTY.shp)
Colorado soil-sample points (CO_SOC_data.shp)
Onondaga County street centerlines (Ononda_Street_PROJ.shp)
Yellowstone National Park boundary (Yellow_Stone.shp), published by the National Park Service on Data.gov

The state and county layers, the streets, and the park boundary are in a metre-based Albers projection.
The geometry stored in CO_SOC_data.shp keeps the easting in the x field and a shifted northing. The x and y fields are the Albers coordinates that fall inside Colorado. The notebook rebuilds the point geometry from those fields and assigns the CRS of US_STATE.shp.
Line examples use North Road, the longest street segment in the Onondaga layer. Polygon cleanup uses Broomfield County, which has two interior rings. Region examples use the state layer.


Code
# Load the layers used throughout the geometry demos and fix sample coordinates.
states = read_layer("US_STATE.shp")  # US state boundaries
counties = read_layer("US_COUNTY.shp")  # US county boundaries
streets = read_layer("Ononda_Street_PROJ.shp")  # Onondaga street centerlines
park = read_layer("Yellow_Stone.shp")  # Yellowstone park boundary
samples_raw = read_layer("CO_SOC_data.shp")  # Colorado soil samples (raw geometry)

# Median offset between attribute y and stored geometry northing (diagnostic).
northing_shift = float((samples_raw["y"] - samples_raw.geometry.y).median())
# Rebuild point geometry from the Albers x/y attribute fields.
samples = samples_raw.set_geometry(gpd.points_from_xy(samples_raw["x"], samples_raw["y"]))
# Assign the same CRS as the state layer so overlays measure in metres.
samples = samples.set_crs(states.crs)

# Colorado-focused subsets used by later cells.
colorado = states.loc[states["STATE"] == "Colorado"].copy()  # state outline
co_counties = counties.loc[counties["STATE"] == "Colorado"].copy()  # CO counties
broomfield = co_counties.loc[co_counties["COUNTY"] == "Broomfield County"].copy()  # hole demo
# Longest street segment becomes the "North Road" example line.
road = streets.loc[[streets.geometry.length.idxmax()]].copy()

# Count samples that fall inside the Colorado polygon after the rebuild.
inside = int(samples.within(colorado.geometry.iloc[0]).sum())
print(f"Northing shift in CO_SOC_data.shp: {northing_shift:,.1f} m")  # print a short status line
print(f"Soil samples inside Colorado: {inside} of {len(samples)}")  # print a short status line
print(f"Colorado counties: {len(co_counties)}")  # print a short status line
print(f"Street segments: {len(streets)}")  # print a short status line
# Identify the road name and length used in later cells.
print(
    f"Road used below: {road['CompleteSt'].iloc[0]} "  # road name from the CompleteSt field
    f"({road.geometry.length.iloc[0]:,.0f} m)"  # road length in metres, formatted for the print
# close the function call
)
# Preview a few sample attributes.
display(samples[["ID", "COUNTY", "SOC", "Longitude", "Latitude"]].head())

title: Geometry Operations
text:
Part 2: Construct geometry

Oriented minimum bounding box
oriented_minimum_bounding_box() returns the rotated rectangle around the features. width is the longer side and height is the shorter side. angle is the direction of the long side, in degrees counterclockwise from east, folded into the range (-90, 90].
With per_feature=False the box encloses the whole layer and the result has one row. With per_feature=True each feature keeps its attributes and gets its own box.
The park box describes Yellowstone. The road angle is saved for the plot polygons further down, so those polygons follow North Road.


Code
# Oriented minimum bounding boxes for Yellowstone, North Road, and CO counties.
park_box = oriented_minimum_bounding_box(park)  # one box around the whole park
road_box = oriented_minimum_bounding_box(road)  # one box around North Road
# Long-side angle (degrees CCW from east) reused when building plot polygons.
road_angle = float(road_box["angle"].iloc[0])

# Convert park box width/height to kilometres for a compact summary table.
park_summary = park_box[["angle", "width", "height", "n_features"]].copy()
park_summary["width_km"] = park_summary["width"] / 1000  # metres to km
park_summary["height_km"] = park_summary["height"] / 1000
display(park_summary[["angle", "width_km", "height_km", "n_features"]])  # preview the table in the notebook
print(f"North Road long-side angle: {road_angle:.2f} degrees")  # print a short status line

Rectangles, ovals, and diamonds
rectangles(), ovals(), and diamonds() turn each point into a plot polygon of a fixed size. The polygon is built axis-aligned, then rotated by angle. Passing the long-side angle from the bounding box turns the width so it follows the road.
Each plot here is 80 metres along the road and 36 metres across it. A rectangle’s area is width * height. A diamond’s area is half of that. An oval’s area is the ellipse with those full axis lengths. quad_segs controls how smoothly the oval is drawn.

Rotate, translate, and affine transform
translate() shifts every feature by the same easting and northing.
rotate() turns every feature about one shared origin. The default origin is the center of the layer bounds, so a row of plots turns as one piece.
affine_transform() always applies the steps in this order: scale, rotation, then translation. origin="feature" scales and rotates each feature about its own centroid. origin=(x, y) uses one point for the whole layer.
The numeric check uses a point 80 metres east of the midpoint of North Road. Scale 2 moves it to 160 metres east of that midpoint. A rotation of 90 degrees then carries it to 160 metres north. The translation (10, -5) is applied last.


Code
# Numeric affine check on a probe point, then translate / rotate / scale plots.
# Midpoint of North Road used as the transform origin.
anchor = road.geometry.iloc[0].interpolate(0.5, normalized=True)
# Probe point 80 m east of the midpoint.
probe = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"name": ["probe"]},  # one map layer: data plus draw style
    geometry=[Point(anchor.x + 80, anchor.y)],  # active geometry column or list of geometries
    crs=road.crs,  # coordinate reference system
# close the function call
)
# Scale 2, rotate 90 degrees CCW, then translate (10, -5) about the anchor.
ordered = affine_transform(
    probe,  # input point for the ordered affine check
    scale=2,  # double distance from the origin
    angle=90,  # rotate counterclockwise
    translation=(10, -5),  # apply last: +10 east, -5 north
    origin=(anchor.x, anchor.y),  # shared origin for scale and rotate
)
# Print start, transformed, and expected coordinates for the ordered steps.
print(f"Start:    ({probe.geometry.iloc[0].x:,.2f}, {probe.geometry.iloc[0].y:,.2f})")
print(f"Affine:   ({ordered.geometry.iloc[0].x:,.2f}, {ordered.geometry.iloc[0].y:,.2f})")  # print a short status line
print(f"Expected: ({anchor.x + 10:,.2f}, {anchor.y + 160 - 5:,.2f})")  # print a short status line

# Shift every rectangle 25 m east and 15 m north.
shifted = translate(rect_plots, xoff=25, yoff=15)
# Rotate the plot row 25 degrees about the layer center.
turned = rotate(rect_plots, 25)
# Scale each plot 1.5x in X about its own centroid (area should grow).
resized = affine_transform(rect_plots, scale=(1.5, 1), origin="feature")
# print a short status line
print(f"Feature scale changes the area from {rect_plots.geometry.area.iloc[0]:,.0f} to {resized.geometry.area.iloc[0]:,.0f} square metres")

# Three maps: original, translated, and rotated rectangles on the road.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.2))
# (layer, title) pairs for the three transform panels
layers = [
    (rect_plots, "Original rectangles"),  # original plots panel
    (shifted, "Translated 25 m east, 15 m north"),  # translated plots panel
    (turned, "Rotated 25 degrees about the center"),  # rotated plots panel
# close the list of (layer, title) pairs
]
# iterate over panels (or rows) to draw each map
for ax, (layer, title) in zip(axes, layers):
    plot_layer(road, ax=ax, edgecolor="#98A2B3", linewidth=1.1, show=False)
    plot_layer(layer, title, ax=ax, alpha=0.6, linewidth=0.3, show=False)
fig.tight_layout()  # tighten subplot spacing
plt.show()  # render the figure

Orthogonalize
orthogonalize() moves a corner onto a right angle when the corner is already close to 90 degrees. The two neighboring vertices stay fixed, and the corner moves the shortest distance onto that right angle. angle_tolerance is how far from 90 degrees a corner may be and still be squared. max_iterations is the number of passes over the vertices.
Broomfield County is a published boundary, so this is a demonstration of the move. A tolerance of 15 degrees squares the corners that are already near a right angle and changes the county area. On a hand-digitized plot the same call is used with a tolerance that matches the digitizing error.


Code
# Square Broomfield corners that are already within 15 degrees of 90.
squared = orthogonalize(broomfield, angle_tolerance=15)
# Compare area before and after (square kilometres).
print(f"Area before: {broomfield.geometry.area.iloc[0] / 1e6:,.3f} square kilometres")
print(f"Area after:  {squared.geometry.area.iloc[0] / 1e6:,.3f} square kilometres")  # print a short status line
# Overlay the squared outline on the original boundary.
plot_layers(

        {"data": squared, "label": "Squared corners", "facecolor": FACE, "alpha": 0.35, "edgecolor": "#E36414", "linewidth": 1.0},
    ],
    title="Broomfield corners within 15 degrees of 90",  # map title
    figsize=(6, 5),  # figure width and height in inches
# close the function call
)

Snap points to a grid
snap_points_to_grid() rounds every vertex to the nearest grid intersection. The grid size is spacing_x by spacing_y. When spacing_y is omitted the cells are square. Coordinates that land on a cell boundary round half away from zero.
The Colorado samples are rounded onto a 5 kilometre grid. shift_m is how far each sample moved. The map zooms to the county of the sample that moved the farthest.


Code
# Snap Colorado soil samples to a 5 km grid and map the farthest county.
snapped = snap_points_to_grid(samples, 5000)  # 5000 m spacing
# Align indices so shift distances line up row-for-row.
placed = samples.reset_index(drop=True).copy()
# Distance each sample moved when snapped to the grid.
placed["shift_m"] = samples.reset_index(drop=True).geometry.distance(snapped.geometry).to_numpy()
placed["grid_x"] = snapped.geometry.x.to_numpy()  # snapped easting
placed["grid_y"] = snapped.geometry.y.to_numpy()  # snapped northing
# Show the eight samples with the largest shifts.

# close the function call
)

# County containing the sample that moved the farthest.
farthest = placed["shift_m"].idxmax()
county_name = placed.loc[farthest, "COUNTY"]  # county of the sample with the largest shift
county_mask = placed["COUNTY"] == county_name  # boolean mask for that county
county_poly = co_counties.loc[co_counties["COUNTY"] == county_name]
print(f"Largest shift: {placed.loc[farthest, 'shift_m']:,.1f} m in {county_name}")  # print a short status line

# Zoom map: county outline, original samples, and snapped grid points.
plot_layers(
    # each dict is one layer: data plus draw style
    [
        {"data": county_poly, "label": county_name, "facecolor": "#D9E8F2", "edgecolor": EDGE, "linewidth": 0.5},

Snap geometries to a layer
snap_geometries_to_layer() moves vertices of data onto reference when a target is within tolerance.

"vertices" snaps to reference vertices.
"segments" snaps to the nearest location on a reference edge.
"vertices_and_segments" uses a vertex when one is in range, and otherwise uses an edge. This is the default. A vertex inside the tolerance wins over a closer edge.

Passing the same layer as data and reference closes small gaps between features. Vertices within the tolerance collapse to one anchor, the vertex closest to the group centroid.
Colorado counties are snapped to themselves with a 50 metre tolerance. area_change_m2 is the area of the symmetric difference, so it measures how much boundary moved.


Code
# Snap Colorado counties to themselves to close small boundary gaps.
closed = snap_geometries_to_layer(co_counties, co_counties, 50)  # 50 m tolerance
# Align indices with the snapped result for pairwise comparison.
original = co_counties.reset_index(drop=True)
# Area of the symmetric difference measures how much each boundary moved.
change = [
    left.symmetric_difference(right).area  # area where the original and snapped boundaries differ
    for left, right in zip(original.geometry, closed.geometry)  # pair each original geometry with its snapped copy
# close the list of (layer, title) pairs
]
# Attach the change values to county names for ranking.
report = original[["COUNTY"]].copy()
report["area_change_m2"] = change  # store the boundary-change area per county
report = report.sort_values("area_change_m2", ascending=False)  # rank counties by how much the boundary moved
# Count counties whose boundary area change exceeds 1 square metre.
moved = int((report["area_change_m2"] > 1).sum())
print(f"Counties with a boundary change above 1 square metre: {moved} of {len(report)}")  # print a short status line
display(report.head(8))  # preview the table in the notebook

Part 3: Measure and clean

Geometry attributes
add_geometry_attributes() measures each geometry in the units of the layer CRS.
Polygons can receive area and perimeter. Perimeter includes holes, and area excludes holes. Lines can receive length. Points can receive x and y, and z when a point has a Z coordinate. A column is added only when the layer contains that geometry family and the matching flag is True.
The three calls below measure Colorado counties, North Road, and the first soil samples. The sample layer already has x and y fields. Those fields are rewritten from the point coordinates.

# Measure area/perimeter for counties, length for the road, and x/y for samples.

# Five largest counties by area.
display(county_view.sort_values("area", ascending=False).head(5).loc[:, ["COUNTY", "area_km2", "perimeter_km"]])

road_measures = add_geometry_attributes(road)

collect_geometries() groups features into one multipart geometry and does not union the parts. Two overlapping polygons stay two parts of a MultiPolygon, so the collected area can be larger than the dissolved area. build_sections(..., by=) unions each group into one polygon.
States in the same census region share borders and do not overlap, so the areas match. The geometry type shows the difference: collect_geometries() keeps one part per state, and build_sections() dissolves those states into a region polygon. n_features is the number of states in the group.

# Collect states by REGION (multipart) and compare areas to dissolved sections.
collected = collect_geometries(states, by="REGION")  # multipart, no dissolve
collected = collected.copy()
collected["area_km2"] = collected.geometry.area / 1e6  # measured area of the collect
collected["geom_type"] = collected.geometry.geom_type  # MultiPolygon vs Polygon
# Bring in dissolved areas from the earlier build_sections result.
dissolved = regions[["REGION", "area_km2", "n_features"]].rename(columns={"area_km2": "dissolved_km2"})
# Join on region and feature count so rows line up.
comparison = collected[["REGION", "n_features", "geom_type", "area_km2"]].merge(dissolved, on=["REGION", "n_features"])
display(comparison.sort_values("REGION"))  # preview the table in the notebook

Centroids and point on surface
centroids() returns the center of mass. For a concave polygon, or for a multipolygon whose parts are separated, that point can fall outside the feature.
point_on_surface() returns a point that lies in the polygon interior, on the line, or on the point itself.
Island County, Washington, is drawn as more than one island. Its centroid falls in the water between the islands. The point on surface falls on land.


Code
# Compare centroid vs point-on-surface for multipolygon Island County, WA.
island = counties.loc[
    (counties["STATE"] == "Washington") & (counties["COUNTY"] == "Island County")  # Island County is a multipolygon in Washington
].copy()  # copy so later cells can edit safely
center = centroids(island)  # center of mass (can fall in water)
marker = point_on_surface(island)  # guaranteed on land
print(f"Geometry type: {island.geometry.iloc[0].geom_type}")

# print a short status line
print(f"Point on surface inside the county: {bool(marker.geometry.iloc[0].within(island.geometry.iloc[0]))}")
# Map both candidate points on the county outline.
plot_layers(
    # each dict is one layer: data plus draw style
    [
        {"data": island, "label": "Island County", "facecolor": "#D9E8F2", "edgecolor": EDGE, "linewidth": 0.5},
        {"data": center, "label": "Centroid", "facecolor": "#E36414", "markersize": 48},
        {"data": marker, "label": "Point on surface", "facecolor": "#2A9D8F", "markersize": 48},

Points displacement
points_displacement() is for point records that share one coordinate. Points within proximity of each other form one stack. proximity=0 groups coordinates that match to 8 decimal places. A stack is moved onto a circle of radius distance around the stack centroid. The first feature is placed at start_angle degrees counterclockwise from east, and the rest follow counterclockwise. A point that is alone stays where it is. displacement_group identifies the stack. Alone points keep a missing group value.
Street centerlines around North Road reuse the same vertex where segments meet. Those vertices are extracted as points and spread by 12 metres so each copy of a shared node is visible. The map is a 40 metre window around the largest stack.


Code
# Extract shared street vertices near North Road and spread stacked points.
# 250 m buffer around North Road defines the search corridor.
corridor = road.geometry.iloc[0].buffer(250)
# Keep street segments that intersect the corridor.
nearby = streets.loc[streets.geometry.intersects(corridor)].copy()
node_rows = []  # accumulate one point record per vertex
for _, record in nearby.iterrows():
    # Explode every vertex of the segment into its own point feature.
    for coord in record.geometry.coords:
        # append one point feature for this vertex
        node_rows.append({"StreetName": record["StreetName"], "geometry": Point(coord[0], coord[1])})
# Build a GeoDataFrame of all corridor vertices.
nodes = gpd.GeoDataFrame(node_rows, geometry="geometry", crs=streets.crs)
# Spread exact-coordinate stacks onto a 12 m circle, starting at 90 degrees.
spread = points_displacement(nodes, distance=12, proximity=0, start_angle=90)
# Count how many vertices landed in each displacement stack.
counts = spread["displacement_group"].value_counts(dropna=True)
print(f"Segments in the 250 m corridor: {len(nearby)}")  # print a short status line
print(f"Vertices: {len(nodes)}")  # print a short status line
print(f"Stacks: {len(counts)}")  # print a short status line
display(counts.rename("vertices").rename_axis("displacement_group").to_frame())  # preview the table in the notebook

# Zoom to a 40 m window around the largest stack.
group_id = counts.index[0]  # most common displacement group
group = spread.loc[spread["displacement_group"] == group_id]
focus = group.geometry.union_all().centroid  # window center
window = 40  # half-width of the map window in metres
# Clip streets / nodes / spread points to that window with .cx.
local_streets = nearby.cx[focus.x - window : focus.x + window, focus.y - window : focus.y + window]
local_nodes = nodes.cx[focus.x - window : focus.x + window, focus.y - window : focus.y + window]  # same map window for original shared vertices
local_spread = spread.cx[focus.x - window : focus.x + window, focus.y - window : focus.y + window]  # same map window for displaced copies
# compose the map from styled layer dicts
plot_layers(
    # each dict is one layer: data plus draw style
    [
        {"data": local_streets, "label": "Street", "edgecolor": "#98A2B3", "linewidth": 1.2},
        {"data": local_nodes, "label": "Shared vertex", "facecolor": EDGE, "markersize": 36},
        {"data": local_spread, "label": "Displaced", "facecolor": "#E36414", "markersize": 28},
    ],
    title=f"Stack {group_id} spread onto a 12 m circle",  # map title
    figsize=(6, 5),  # figure width and height in inches
# close the function call
)

Check and fix geometry
check_validity() adds is_valid and validity_reason to every feature. invalid_only=True returns only the rows that failed. Run this before publishing an area.
fix_geometries() repairs invalid geometries. method="make_valid" uses the GEOS make-valid operation and keeps the original vertex locations. method="buffer" uses a zero-width buffer. A geometry that is already valid is copied through unchanged.
The Colorado county layer in this dataset is valid, so the repair leaves the geometries in place.

Remove duplicate vertices
remove_duplicate_vertices() drops consecutive vertices that are closer than tolerance. tolerance=0 removes exact duplicates and keeps every distinct corner. A positive tolerance also collapses a short segment. A ring that would lose its shape becomes empty. Points are unchanged.
North Road has no exact duplicate vertices. Its shortest segment is shorter than 40 metres, so a 40 metre tolerance removes that vertex and shortens the line.


Code
# Measure vertex spacing on North Road, then remove near-duplicate vertices.
coords = list(road.geometry.iloc[0].coords)  # ordered (x, y) vertices
# Distance between each consecutive vertex pair.
gaps = [
    Point(start).distance(Point(end))  # length of the segment between consecutive vertices
    for start, end in zip(coords, coords[1:])  # consecutive vertex pairs along the line
# close the list of (layer, title) pairs
]
# tolerance=0 drops exact duplicates only.
exact = remove_duplicate_vertices(road, tolerance=0)
# tolerance=40 also collapses vertices within 40 metres.
collapsed = remove_duplicate_vertices(road, tolerance=40)

print(f"Length before: {road.geometry.length.iloc[0]:,.1f} m")  # print a short status line
print(f"Length after 40 m tolerance: {collapsed.geometry.length.iloc[0]:,.1f} m")  # print a short status line

Delete holes
delete_holes() removes interior rings from polygons. minimum_area=0 deletes every hole. A positive minimum_area deletes only holes smaller than that value. Lines and points are returned unchanged.
Broomfield County contains two holes. The first call removes both. The second call keeps any hole of at least 1 square kilometre and deletes the smaller one. Area goes up by the area of the holes that were removed, because polygon area excludes holes.


Code
# Measure Broomfield holes, then delete all holes vs keep large ones.
polygon = broomfield.geometry.iloc[0]  # county geometry (may have interiors)
# Area of each interior ring treated as its own polygon.
hole_areas = [Polygon(ring).area for ring in polygon.interiors]
print(f"Holes: {len(hole_areas)}")  # print a short status line
# iterate over panels (or rows) to draw each map
for index, area in enumerate(hole_areas, start=1):
    print(f"Hole {index}: {area / 1e6:,.3f} square kilometres")  # print a short status line

# Delete every interior ring.
cleared = delete_holes(broomfield)
# Keep holes whose area is at least 1 square kilometre (1_000_000 m2).
kept = delete_holes(broomfield, minimum_area=1_000_000)
print(f"Holes after deleting all: {len(list(cleared.geometry.iloc[0].interiors))}")  # print a short status line
print(f"Holes at least 1 square kilometre kept: {len(list(kept.geometry.iloc[0].interiors))}")  # print a short status line
print(f"Area with holes: {polygon.area / 1e6:,.3f} square kilometres")  # print a short status line
print(f"Area with holes removed: {cleared.geometry.area.iloc[0] / 1e6:,.3f} square kilometres")  # print a short status line

plot_pair(
