title: Geometry Operations
text:
Summary
Every geometry operation in geolattice.vector.geometry_tools was applied to the US state and county layers, the Colorado soil samples, North Road in Onondaga County, or the Yellowstone boundary.








Operation
What it does
Example in this notebook




Oriented box
Rotated rectangle around a layer or around each feature, with the long-side angle
Yellowstone, and one box per Colorado county


Offset lines
Parallel copies of a line, indexed from the line direction
Three copies on each side of North Road at 40 m


Points along a line
Points at a fixed spacing, with distance_along
Stations every 200 m on North Road


Rectangles, ovals, diamonds
Fixed-size polygons centered on points and rotated by an angle
80 m by 36 m plots turned onto the road angle


Transects
Lines across a path at a vertex or at a regular interval
160 m lines every 200 m along North Road


Translate
Same easting and northing shift for every feature
Plots moved 25 m east and 15 m north


Rotate
One rotation about the layer center, the centroid, each feature, or a point
Plots turned 25 degrees about their center


Affine transform
Scale, then rotation, then translation
A probe point scaled, turned 90 degrees, then shifted


Orthogonalize
Corners already near 90 degrees move onto a right angle
Broomfield County with a 15 degree tolerance


Snap to a grid
Vertices round to a regular spacing
Soil samples on a 5 km grid


Snap to a layer
Vertices within a tolerance move onto a reference layer
Colorado counties snapped to themselves at 50 m


Build sections
A labeled rectangle grid, or a union of features that share an attribute
4 km cells on Broomfield, and states dissolved by region


Geometry attributes
Area, perimeter, length, and point coordinates
County area, North Road length, and sample coordinates


Collect geometries
Multipart group without dissolving overlaps
States collected by census region


Centroids
Center of mass, which can fall outside the feature
Island County, Washington


Point on surface
A point guaranteed to lie in the feature
The same county, with the point on land


Points displacement
Stacked points spread onto a circle
Shared street vertices around North Road


Check validity
is_valid and a reason for every feature
Colorado counties


Fix geometries
Repairs invalid geometry and copies valid geometry through
The same county layer


Remove duplicate vertices
Drops exact or near-duplicate corners
A 40 m tolerance on North Road


Delete holes
Removes interior rings, or only rings smaller than an area
Both holes in Broomfield, then only the smaller hole



Angles are degrees counterclockwise from east. Distances are in the units of the layer. These layers are in metres.
The geometry tools cover the constructions used to lay out plots and the cleanup used before an area is published. Start from a line or a set of points, build parallel rows and stations, and turn those stations into rectangles, ovals, or diamonds aligned with oriented_minimum_bounding_box(). transect(), rotate(), translate(), and affine_transform() place that layout on the ground.
On polygons, orthogonalize(), snap_points_to_grid(), and snap_geometries_to_layer() repair corners and close gaps. delete_holes() and remove_duplicate_vertices() simplify rings. check_validity() and fix_geometries() belong before add_geometry_attributes(). centroids() and point_on_surface() make label points. build_sections() and collect_geometries() group features into sections, and only the section builder unions overlapping area.
Read each shapefile with open_vectors_data(), then pass the layer to the geometry function. Project a geographic layer before using a width, spacing, or tolerance as a ground distance.

Further reading
GeoLattice

open_vectors_data() reads the shapefiles in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA.
The geometry functions in this notebook are exported from geolattice.vector and implemented in geolattice/vector/geometry_tools.py.
plot_layer(), plot_layers(), plot_pair(), and style_axes() are in geolattice.viz.

Libraries used by those functions

Shapely: geometry construction, affine transforms, offset_curve, validity, and make_valid.
GeoPandas: GeoDataFrames returned by the geometry tools, and the maps in this notebook.
pandas: attribute tables copied onto the new geometries.
Matplotlib: the figures in this notebook.

Data

State, county, soil-sample, street, and park shapefiles are in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA.
The Yellowstone National Park boundary is published by the National Park Service on Data.gov.

title: Visualizing Vector Data
text:
Overview
A map gives each feature a position from its geometry and a meaning from the way it is drawn. The same county polygons can be a plain outline, a choropleth of diabetes prevalence, or one layer on an interactive web map. This notebook maps three geometry types with geolattice.viz:

Polygons: US counties (Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/US_COUNTY.shp) joined to county diabetes attributes (Data/00_shared/tabular_data/usa_diabetes_data.csv).
Points: BGS well chemistry (Data/00_shared/tabular_data/bgs_geochemical.csv), written as a shapefile and projected to the Bangladesh boundary (Data/00_shared/vector_data/Bangladesh/Shapefiles/BD_Banladesh_BUTM.shp).
Lines: street centerlines around Onondaga County, New York (Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/Ononda_Street_PROJ.shp).

Static maps follow the GeoPandas mapping guide. Interactive maps follow the Folium gallery: GeoPandas builds a Leaflet map with GeoDataFrame.explore, and Folium adds markers, choropleths, and heatmaps on top of a tile layer.
The notebook is organized in three parts:

Polygon maps: US counties joined to diabetes attributes: single-symbol, choropleth, categorical, cartographic elements, and an interactive Folium map.
Point maps: BGS well chemistry written as a shapefile, projected to the Bangladesh boundary, then mapped by arsenic and well class.
Line maps: Onondaga County street centerlines by speed and type, overlays, a tile basemap, and an interactive line layer.

A short Mapping concepts section covers kinds of map, classification, and color so the map calls later use a shared vocabulary.

Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, applies the tutorial map style, and opens a shapefile as a GeoDataFrame. open_vectors_data is the same reader the vector tutorials use.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.

    CATEGORICAL,  # named categorical colormaps

# Helper: open one shapefile as a GeoDataFrame.
def read_layer(relative):
    # Docstring for this helper.
    """Open one shapefile and return a GeoDataFrame without the reader fid."""
    path = DATA / relative  # resolve the relative path under DATA
    # Open with the GeoLattice reader and convert the layer to a GeoDataFrame.

    if "fid" in frame.columns:
        frame = frame.drop(columns="fid")  # remove the fid column
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(frame, geometry="geometry", crs=crs)  # typed GeoDataFrame

title: Visualizing Vector Data
text:
Mapping concepts
The next three sections define the vocabulary used in the maps below: kinds of map, classification schemes, and color ramps.

Kinds of map
Single-symbol map. Every feature uses the same fill, line, or marker. This is a reference map: it shows where the features are, and it is the base layer under a choropleth or a set of sample points.
Choropleth. Each area is colored from a numeric attribute, such as the percent of adults with diabetes. An unclassed choropleth stretches one continuous colormap from the minimum to the maximum, so similar values get similar colors. A classified choropleth groups the values into classes first and then paints each class with one color from the ramp.
Categorical map. Color encodes a name or a code, such as urban or rural, rather than a quantity. The classes have no order, so a qualitative palette keeps neighbors distinct. A sequential ramp would imply a ranking that the categories do not have.
Graduated point map. The point stays a point. Color or size carries the measurement, such as arsenic concentration at a well. A point choropleth answers “how much is here”; a single-symbol point map only answers “a sample was taken here.”
Line map. Color or width carries a property of the line, such as a posted speed. Functional class and street type are categories; a speed limit can be treated as a category too, because the values are a short list of posted limits rather than a smooth surface.
Multi-layer map. Polygons, lines, and points share one axes. Layers that do not share a coordinate reference system will not line up, so reproject every layer to the CRS of the first one before drawing. Draw areas underneath and points or lines on top. A lower zorder is drawn first.
Interactive map. Folium places the same layers on a Leaflet map that can be panned and zoomed. Popups and tooltips read attributes, and a layer control turns layers on and off. Leaflet reads longitude and latitude, so geolattice.viz reprojects layers that use another CRS to EPSG:4326. Tile sets such as OpenStreetMap and OpenTopoMap supply the background, the same built-in tiles the Folium gallery uses.


Classification
An unclassed map is faithful to the numbers and hard to read when a few large values take most of the color ramp. Classification cuts the range into classes so the legend has a handful of colors a reader can match.
plot_choropleth(..., scheme=...) passes the scheme name through to mapclassify, which is what GeoPandas uses. k is the number of classes. Five is a useful start: fewer classes hide differences, and more classes are difficult to tell apart in the legend.







Scheme
What a class contains




quantiles
About the same number of features. A skewed distribution still uses the full ramp.


equal_interval
Equal steps of the attribute, (max - min) / k. Easy to explain. Outliers can leave a class empty.


natural_breaks
Jenks breaks that keep similar values together and split values that are far apart.


fisher_jenks
Another optimal-break method, close to natural breaks.


std_mean
Classes built from the mean and the standard deviation.


user_defined
Breaks you supply, for a threshold or a published standard.



GeoPandas also accepts percentiles, box_plot, headtail_breaks, maximum_breaks, jenks_caspall, and max_p_classifier. Pass extra arguments to the classifier with classification_kwds.
The scheme changes the story. Quantiles of a right-skewed rate will look more even than equal intervals of the same rate, because equal intervals give the long tail a class of its own and pack most counties into the lower classes.


Color
Match the palette to the kind of attribute. The names below are Matplotlib colormaps; the full set is in Choosing Colormaps in Matplotlib.

Sequential ramps (OrRd, YlGnBu, viridis) run from light to dark. Use one for a quantity that grows in one direction, such as a rate or a concentration.
Diverging ramps (RdBu_r, BrBG) use two hues and a light middle. Use one when the value is a difference from a midpoint, and set vmin and vmax so that midpoint sits in the middle of the ramp.
Qualitative ramps (tab10, Set2) keep neighboring classes distinct. Use one for categories.

SEQUENTIAL, DIVERGING, and CATEGORICAL in geolattice.viz hold those names. FACE and EDGE are the single-symbol fill and outline used throughout the tutorials.
A feature with a missing attribute is skipped unless missing_kwds assigns it a color, an edge, a hatch, and a legend label. That is how a county with no diabetes record stays visible instead of disappearing from the map.

title: Visualizing Vector Data
section: Part 1: Polygon maps: US counties and diabetes
text:
Part 1: Polygon maps: US counties and diabetes
US_COUNTY.shp is a county polygon layer in NAD83 Albers (meters). usa_diabetes_data.csv has one row per county. The shared key is FIPS. The shapefile stores FIPS as a number (1001.0); the table stores it as an integer (1001). Casting both to integer makes the join exact.
The table has 3,107 rows and the shapefile has 3,108 counties. Shannon County, South Dakota (FIPS 46113), has no row in the diabetes table, so its attributes stay empty after a left join. Later, missing_kwds draws that county on purpose instead of leaving a hole.


Code
# Load US counties, join diabetes/health attributes on FIPS, and preview the join.
counties = read_layer("vector_data/USA/US_COUNTY.shp")  # county polygons
diabetes = pd.read_csv(DATA / "tabular_data/usa_diabetes_data.csv")  # health CSV

counties["FIPS"] = counties["FIPS"].astype(int)  # integer FIPS for a clean join key
diabetes["FIPS"] = diabetes["FIPS"].astype(int)  # match counties FIPS dtype

# Columns to pull from the diabetes table onto the county polygons.
attributes = [
    "FIPS",  # join key
    "POP_Total",  # total population
    "Diabetes_count",  # count of adults with diabetes
    "Diabetes_per",  # diabetes prevalence percent
    "Obesity",  # obesity rate
    "Access_Excercise",  # exercise access indicator (source spelling)
    "Physical_Inactivity",  # inactivity rate
    "PCP_rate",  # primary-care physician rate
    "Food_Env_Index",  # food environment index
    "SVI",  # social vulnerability index
    "Urban_Rural",  # urban/rural class label
]  # end list
# Left join keeps every county and fills unmatched health fields with NaN.
counties = counties.merge(diabetes[attributes], on="FIPS", how="left")

print(f"Counties: {len(counties)}")  # number of county features after the join
print(f"CRS: {counties.crs.name}")  # CRS name on the county layer
print(f"Matched diabetes values: {int(counties['Diabetes_per'].notna().sum())}")  # non-null rates
display(counties.loc[counties["Diabetes_per"].isna(), ["FIPS", "STATE", "COUNTY"]])  # unmatched rows
display(counties[["STATE", "COUNTY", "FIPS", "Diabetes_per", "Obesity", "Urban_Rural", "REGION"]].head())  # preview

Single-symbol map and boundary
A single fill shows the county fabric without an attribute. plot_boundary draws GeoSeries.boundary instead, so the interior stays empty. That is clearer than facecolor="none": in Matplotlib, None means “use the default color,” while the string "none" means “draw no fill.”


Code
# Side-by-side filled county map and boundary-only outline map.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))  # two panels sharing one figure
# Draw one map layer.
plot_layer(
    counties,  # filled county polygons
    "US counties",  # left-panel title
    ax=axes[0],  # draw into the left axes
    facecolor=FACE,  # shared face color from geolattice.viz
    edgecolor="white",  # light edges between counties
    linewidth=0.15,  # thin county borders
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
)  # close this call
# Draw polygon outlines only.
plot_boundary(
    counties,  # outline-only rendering of the same layer
    "County boundaries",  # right-panel title
    ax=axes[1],  # draw into the right axes
    edgecolor=EDGE,  # shared edge color from geolattice.viz
    linewidth=0.2,  # slightly thicker boundary lines
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
)  # close this call
fig.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # display the figure in the notebook











Unclassed choropleth
column="Diabetes_per" paints each county by the percent of adults with diabetes. OrRd is a sequential ramp: low rates are light, high rates are dark. With no scheme, every distinct value gets its own step along that ramp, and the legend is a continuous colorbar.


Code
# Continuous (unclassed) choropleth of diabetes prevalence with an OrRd ramp.
plot_choropleth(
    counties,  # county polygons with Diabetes_per
    "Diabetes_per",  # attribute column to color by
    "Diabetes prevalence, unclassed",  # map title
    cmap="OrRd",  # sequential orange-red colormap
    legend_kwds={"label": "Percent of adults", "shrink": 0.6},  # colorbar label/size
    linewidth=0.1,  # thin county borders
    figsize=(9, 6),  # figure size in inches
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
)  # close this call











What the classes contain
The same Diabetes_per values, cut five ways. The printed breaks are the upper edge of each class. Quantiles keep the counts almost equal. Equal interval spaces the breaks evenly from the minimum to the maximum, so the upper classes hold fewer counties. Natural breaks and Fisher-Jenks place the breaks where the values cluster. Standard-deviation classes are centered on the mean rather than on a requested k.


Code
# Compare common classification schemes on diabetes prevalence with mapclassify.
import mapclassify  # choropleth classification algorithms

values = counties["Diabetes_per"].dropna()  # drop NaNs before classifying
# Build one classifier per named scheme (most use k=5 classes).
classifiers = {
    "Quantiles": mapclassify.Quantiles(values, k=5),  # equal-count classes
    "Equal interval": mapclassify.EqualInterval(values, k=5),  # equal-width classes
    "Natural breaks": mapclassify.NaturalBreaks(values, k=5),  # Jenks-style breaks
    "Fisher-Jenks": mapclassify.FisherJenks(values, k=5),  # optimal Fisher-Jenks
    "Mean and standard deviation": mapclassify.StdMean(values),  # mean +/- std classes
}  # end mapping
# Print break edges and class counts for each scheme.
for name, classifier in classifiers.items():
    breaks = ", ".join(f"{edge:.2f}" for edge in classifier.bins)  # formatted break edges
    counts = ", ".join(str(count) for count in classifier.counts)  # features per class
    print(f"{name}")  # scheme name header
    print(f"  breaks: {breaks}")  # class upper edges
    print(f"  counts: {counts}")  # class membership counts

Classified choropleths
The four maps below use one colormap and five classes. Only the scheme changes. Quantiles spread the counties across the ramp. Equal interval reserves the darkest class for the high tail, so most of the country stays in the lighter classes. Natural breaks and Fisher-Jenks sit between those two: the classes follow clumps in the data rather than equal counts or equal width.


Code
# Four-panel choropleth comparing quantiles, equal interval, natural breaks, Fisher-Jenks.
schemes = [
    ("quantiles", "Quantiles"),  # equal-count classes
    ("equal_interval", "Equal interval"),  # equal-width classes
    ("natural_breaks", "Natural breaks"),  # Jenks-style breaks
    ("fisher_jenks", "Fisher-Jenks"),  # Fisher-Jenks optimal breaks
]  # end list
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 9))  # 2x2 grid of map panels
# Draw one classified choropleth into each axes panel.
for ax, (scheme, title) in zip(axes.ravel(), schemes):
    # Draw a choropleth map.
    plot_choropleth(
        counties,  # county polygons
        "Diabetes_per",  # attribute to classify
        title,  # panel title from the schemes list
        cmap="OrRd",  # shared sequential colormap
        scheme=scheme,  # mapclassify scheme name
        k=5,  # number of classes
        ax=ax,  # target axes in the 2x2 grid
        linewidth=0.08,  # thin borders for dense national map
        axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
        show=False,  # defer plt.show until all panels are drawn
    )  # close this call
fig.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing among the four panels
plt.show()  # display the finished figure











Breaks you choose
scheme="user_defined" keeps the class edges fixed when you compare places or years. The bins below are round cuts in percentage points, passed through classification_kwds. They are a cartographic choice, not a clinical threshold. A county above the last bin falls in the top class.


Code
# Choropleth with user-defined class breaks at 6, 8, 10, and 12 percent.
plot_choropleth(
    counties,  # county polygons
    "Diabetes_per",  # attribute column
    "Diabetes prevalence, chosen breaks",  # map title
    cmap="YlOrRd",  # yellow-orange-red sequential ramp
    scheme="user_defined",  # use explicit bins instead of an algorithm
    classification_kwds={"bins": [6, 8, 10, 12]},  # upper edges of custom classes
    linewidth=0.1,  # thin county borders
    legend_kwds={"title": "Percent", "fmt": "{:.0f}"},  # legend title and integer format
    figsize=(9, 6),  # figure size in inches
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
)  # close this call











A diverging ramp
A sequential ramp is the wrong tool when the question is “above or below a reference.” Subtracting the national median puts that reference at zero. RdBu_r paints counties below the median blue and counties above it red. vmin and vmax are symmetric, so zero stays in the middle of the ramp. Counties farther out than that span share the end color.


Code
# Diverging map of diabetes prevalence relative to the national median.
median_rate = counties["Diabetes_per"].median()  # national median prevalence
counties["Diabetes_vs_median"] = counties["Diabetes_per"] - median_rate  # signed deviation
span = counties["Diabetes_vs_median"].abs().max()  # symmetric color limit
print(f"National median: {median_rate:.2f}%    color span: ±{span:.2f} points")  # summary

# Draw a choropleth map.
plot_choropleth(
    counties,  # county polygons with Diabetes_vs_median
    "Diabetes_vs_median",  # signed deviation from the median
    "Diabetes prevalence relative to the national median",  # map title
    cmap="RdBu_r",  # diverging red-blue (reversed so high=red)
    vmin=-span,  # lower color limit (symmetric)
    vmax=span,  # upper color limit (symmetric)
    linewidth=0.1,  # thin county borders
    legend_kwds={"label": "Percentage points from the median", "shrink": 0.6},  # colorbar
    figsize=(9, 6),  # figure size in inches
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
)  # close this call


National median: 8.28%    color span: ±8.68 points











Categorical map
Urban_Rural is a category, not a rate. plot_categorical sets categorical=True and uses a qualitative colormap (tab10). A sequential ramp would suggest that one class is “more” than the other.


Code
# Categorical map of urban vs rural counties with a legend and missing style.
print(counties["Urban_Rural"].value_counts(dropna=False).to_string())  # class counts
# Draw a categorical attribute map.
plot_categorical(
    counties,  # county polygons
    "Urban_Rural",  # categorical attribute
    "Urban and rural counties",  # map title
    cmap="Set2",  # qualitative colormap
    linewidth=0.08,  # thin borders
    figsize=(9, 6),  # figure size in inches
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
    missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey", "label": "No record"},  # style for nulls
    legend_kwds={"loc": "lower left", "frameon": True},  # legend placement
)  # close this call


Urban_Rural
Urban    1797
Rural    1310
NaN         1











Missing values
Shannon County is still in the layer, with an empty Diabetes_per. The default choropleth omits that polygon. missing_kwds draws it in grey, with a red outline and a hatch, and adds it to the legend. The reader can see the gap in the table instead of mistaking it for a low rate.


Code
# Quantile choropleth that highlights counties with missing diabetes values.
plot_choropleth(
    counties,  # county polygons
    "Diabetes_per",  # attribute column
    "Diabetes prevalence, with the missing county marked",  # map title
    cmap="OrRd",  # sequential colormap for non-missing values
    scheme="quantiles",  # equal-count classes
    k=5,  # five quantile classes
    linewidth=0.1,  # thin borders
    figsize=(9, 6),  # figure size in inches
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
    missing_kwds={  # distinctive style for null Diabetes_per
        "color": "lightgrey",  # fill for missing counties
        "edgecolor": "red",  # red outline to draw the eye
        "hatch": "///",  # hatch pattern for missing polygons
        "label": "Missing values",  # legend label for missing
    },  # end this layer dict
)  # close this call











The attribute beside the map
A choropleth is easier to read after a look at the distribution. The histogram shows the spread of Diabetes_per. The bars are the mean rate in each census region (one row per region, so the chart does not add the rates together). The scatter compares obesity with diabetes prevalence and colors each county by the social vulnerability index (SVI).


Code
# Supporting charts: diabetes histogram, regional mean bar chart, and scatter.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))  # histogram + bar chart panels
# Draw an attribute histogram.
plot_histogram(
    counties,  # source table
    "Diabetes_per",  # column to bin
    title="Diabetes prevalence",  # histogram title
    bins=25,  # number of histogram bins
    ax=axes[0],  # left panel
    show=False,  # defer show until both panels are ready
)  # close this call
# Mean diabetes prevalence grouped by census REGION.
region_mean = counties.groupby("REGION")["Diabetes_per"].mean().to_frame()
# Draw a bar chart.
plot_bar(
    region_mean,  # one row per REGION
    "Diabetes_per",  # bar height column
    title="Mean prevalence by census region",  # bar chart title
    ax=axes[1],  # right panel
    show=False,  # defer show
)  # close this call
fig.tight_layout()  # tighten the two chart panels
plt.show()  # display histogram + bar chart

# Draw a scatter plot of two attributes.
plot_scatter(
    counties,  # county attribute table
    "Obesity",  # x-axis attribute
    "Diabetes_per",  # y-axis attribute
    column="SVI",  # color points by social vulnerability
    cmap="viridis",  # continuous colormap for SVI
    title="Obesity, diabetes, and social vulnerability",  # scatter title
    figsize=(6.5, 5),  # figure size in inches
)  # close this call


















Labels, a north arrow, and a scale bar
Labels on all 3,108 counties would cover the map. The New York counties are a readable extent: a quantile choropleth, a north arrow, and a scale bar. Names are drawn for the highest-rate counties that are large enough to hold a label. Bronx and Queens are in that top eight, and they are listed in the table under the map; a name drawn on either borough would cover it. The axes are padded so a name on the state border is not clipped. The layer is in an equal-area projection whose unit is the meter. cartographic_elements reads that unit from the CRS and labels the bar in kilometres once the distance reaches 1 km.


Code
# Zoom to New York, label high-prevalence counties, and add cartographic elements.
new_york = counties.loc[counties["STATE"] == "New York"].copy()  # NY subset
highest = new_york.nlargest(8, "Diabetes_per").copy()  # top 8 prevalence counties
# Label only larger counties so small polygons are not overcrowded.
labeled = highest.loc[highest.geometry.area > 500 * 1e6].copy()
labeled["Name"] = labeled["COUNTY"].str.replace(" County", "", regex=False)  # short labels

# Assign ax.
ax = plot_choropleth(
    new_york,  # New York counties only
    "Diabetes_per",  # attribute for coloring
    "Diabetes prevalence in New York",  # map title
    cmap="YlGnBu",  # yellow-green-blue sequential ramp
    scheme="quantiles",  # equal-count classes
    k=5,  # five classes
    figsize=(8, 8),  # square-ish figure for the state
    linewidth=0.4,  # clearer county borders at state scale
    edgecolor="white",  # white borders between counties
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
    show=False,  # return axes for further decoration
)  # close this call
xmin, xmax = ax.get_xlim()  # current x extent
ymin, ymax = ax.get_ylim()  # current y extent
pad_x = (xmax - xmin) * 0.12  # 12% horizontal padding
pad_y = (ymax - ymin) * 0.1  # 10% vertical padding
ax.set_xlim(xmin - pad_x, xmax + pad_x)  # expand x limits
ax.set_ylim(ymin - pad_y, ymax + pad_y)  # expand y limits
add_labels(ax, labeled, "Name", fontsize=8)  # place county name labels
cartographic_elements(ax, new_york)  # north arrow / scale bar
fig = ax.figure  # parent figure for layout
fig.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # display the finished New York map
display(highest[["COUNTY", "Diabetes_per", "Urban_Rural"]].sort_values("Diabetes_per", ascending=False))  # table

interactive_map calls GeoDataFrame.explore and returns a Folium map. The quantile scheme and the tooltip fields are the same choices as the static map. OpenStreetMap tiles sit underneath, as in the Folium gallery. Hover a county for its name and rate. The New York subset keeps the notebook responsive; the same call accepts the full county layer.

center = new_york.to_crs(4326).geometry.union_all().centroid  # map center in lon/lat

title: Visualizing Vector Data
section: Part 2: Point maps: BGS well chemistry in Bangladesh
text:
Part 2: Point maps: BGS well chemistry in Bangladesh
BD_Banladesh_BUTM.shp is the Bangladesh boundary in the Bangladesh Transverse Mercator projection (BUTM). The attribute table does not carry place names, so the layer is a location frame.
bgs_geochemical.csv is a table, not a vector file. LONG_DEG and LAT_DEG are longitude and latitude in degrees. The next cell turns those columns into point geometry in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326), writes a shapefile, projects the points to the CRS of the boundary, and writes that projected shapefile. Both files go in Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder/bangladesh. The maps below read the projected shapefile, so they use what was written to disk.
As is arsenic in µg/L. The distribution is skewed: many wells are near the low end, and a long tail is far above it. WELL_TYPE has many spellings of the same kind of well, so Well_class keeps four groups, STW, HTW, DTW, and TARA, and puts the remaining names in Other.


Code
# Build BGS well points from CSV, write GCS and BUTM shapefiles, and summarize.
bangladesh = read_layer("vector_data/Bangladesh/Shapefiles/BD_Banladesh_BUTM.shp")  # boundary
chemistry = pd.read_csv(DATA / "tabular_data/bgs_geochemical.csv")  # well chemistry CSV


# Helper: collapse WELL_TYPE spellings into map classes.
def well_class(value):
    # Docstring for this helper.
    """Collapse the many WELL_TYPE spellings into five map classes."""
    # Null well types become the catch-all Other class.
    if pd.isna(value):
        return "Other"  # missing WELL_TYPE
    text = str(value).strip().upper()  # normalize spelling for matching
    # Keep the three common tube-well abbreviations as their own classes.
    if text in {"STW", "HTW", "DTW"}:
        return text  # STW / HTW / DTW
    # Any TARA spelling collapses to TARA.
    if "TARA" in text:
        return "TARA"  # Tara pump family
    return "Other"  # everything else


chemistry["Well_class"] = chemistry["WELL_TYPE"].map(well_class)  # add map classes
# Assign keep.
keep = [
    "SAMPLE_ID",  # sample identifier
    "LONG_DEG",  # longitude in degrees
    "LAT_DEG",  # latitude in degrees
    "Well_class",  # simplified well class
    "WELL_DEPTH",  # well depth
    "DIVISION",  # admin division
    "DISTRICT",  # admin district
    "As",  # arsenic concentration
]  # end list
# Build a GeoDataFrame of well points in EPSG:4326 from lon/lat columns.
wells_gcs = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    chemistry[keep].copy(),  # attribute columns to keep
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(chemistry["LONG_DEG"], chemistry["LAT_DEG"]),  # point geoms
    crs="EPSG:4326",  # geographic CRS for lon/lat
)  # close this call

point_dir = DATA / "vector_data" / "output_folder" / "bangladesh"  # output folder
point_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create folder if needed
gcs_path = point_dir / "bgs_geochemical_gcs.shp"  # GCS shapefile path
butm_path = point_dir / "bgs_geochemical_butm.shp"  # projected shapefile path

write_shapefile(gcs_path, wells_gcs, overwrite=True)  # write lon/lat points
wells_butm = read_layer("vector_data/output_folder/bangladesh/bgs_geochemical_gcs.shp")  # reload GCS
wells_butm = wells_butm.to_crs(bangladesh.crs)  # reproject into the boundary CRS
write_shapefile(butm_path, wells_butm, overwrite=True)  # write projected points
wells_butm = read_layer("vector_data/output_folder/bangladesh/bgs_geochemical_butm.shp")  # reload BUTM

inside = int(wells_butm.within(bangladesh.union_all()).sum())  # wells inside the boundary
print(f"Boundary features: {len(bangladesh)}")  # boundary polygon count
print(f"Boundary CRS: {bangladesh.crs.name}")  # boundary CRS name
print(f"Wrote {gcs_path.name} in EPSG:4326")  # confirm GCS write
print(f"Wrote {butm_path.name} in the boundary CRS")  # confirm BUTM write
print(f"Wells: {len(wells_butm)}    inside the boundary: {inside}")  # counts
print(wells_butm["Well_class"].value_counts().to_string())  # class frequencies
display(wells_butm[["SAMPLE_ID", "Well_class", "DIVISION", "DISTRICT", "As", "WELL_DEPTH"]].head())  # preview

Wells on the boundary
The boundary is drawn first. The wells go on top with a higher zorder. Both layers are in the BUTM CRS, because the points were projected to the boundary before they were drawn. One color means “a well was sampled here.” Of the 3,534 wells, 3,497 fall inside the boundary. The other 37 sit just outside the polygon and stay on the map.

# Static map of Bangladesh boundary with BGS well points overlaid.
plot_layers(
    # List of layer style dictionaries.
    [
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": bangladesh,  # country boundary polygons
            "facecolor": "#E8F1F5",  # light blue-gray fill
            "edgecolor": EDGE,  # shared edge color
            "linewidth": 0.3,  # thin boundary stroke
            "label": "Bangladesh",  # legend label
            "zorder": 1,  # draw under the wells
        },  # end this layer dict
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": wells_butm,  # well point layer
            "facecolor": "#BC4749",  # red point fill
            "markersize": 4,  # small markers for dense wells
            "linewidth": 0,  # no marker edge stroke
            "label": "BGS well",  # legend label
            "zorder": 2,  # draw above the boundary
        },  # end this layer dict
    ],  # end layer list
    title="BGS well locations",  # map title
    figsize=(7, 8),  # portrait figure for Bangladesh
    axis_off=True,  # hide axis ticks and spines
)  # close this call











Graduated color by arsenic
Arsenic is a concentration, so the points use a sequential ramp. The first map is five quantiles: each class holds about the same number of wells, which spreads a skewed distribution across the ramp. The second map uses fixed breaks at 10, 50, and 200 µg/L. Ten is the WHO guideline and 50 is the Bangladesh drinking-water standard; 200 separates the upper tail. A well above the last break stays in the top class. The first quantile is the single value 0.25 µg/L, because that many wells share the low end of the table. Quantiles cannot split a tie. The fixed breaks do not have that problem.


Code
# Two arsenic point maps: quantile classes vs user-defined breaks.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 7))  # side-by-side arsenic maps
# Draw the Bangladesh boundary under each arsenic panel.
for ax, title in zip(axes, ["Arsenic, quantiles", "Arsenic, chosen breaks"]):
    # Draw one map layer.
    plot_layer(
        bangladesh,  # boundary underlay
        title,  # panel title
        ax=ax,  # target axes
        facecolor="#E8F1F5",  # light fill
        edgecolor=EDGE,  # boundary stroke color
        linewidth=0.25,  # thin boundary line
        axis_off=True,  # hide axes
        show=False,  # defer show
    )  # close this call
# Draw one map layer.
plot_layer(
    wells_butm,  # well points colored by arsenic
    column="As",  # arsenic concentration
    cmap="YlOrRd",  # sequential colormap
    scheme="quantiles",  # equal-count classes
    k=5,  # five quantile classes
    markersize=8,  # point size
    ax=axes[0],  # left panel
    legend=True,  # show class legend
    legend_kwds={"title": "µg/L", "loc": "lower left"},  # legend title/placement
    show=False,  # defer show
)  # close this call
# Draw one map layer.
plot_layer(
    wells_butm,  # well points again with custom breaks
    column="As",  # arsenic concentration
    cmap="YlOrRd",  # same colormap for comparison
    scheme="user_defined",  # explicit bins
    classification_kwds={"bins": [10, 50, 200]},  # WHO-style break points
    markersize=8,  # point size
    ax=axes[1],  # right panel
    legend=True,  # show class legend
    legend_kwds={"title": "µg/L", "loc": "lower left"},  # legend title/placement
    show=False,  # defer show
)  # close this call
fig.tight_layout()  # tighten the two panels
plt.show()  # display both arsenic maps











Category: well class
Well_class is a code, so the point map is categorical. tab10 keeps the classes distinct. A yellow-to-red ramp would imply that one well type is a larger amount of the same thing. The histogram shows why quantiles and fixed breaks tell different stories: most of the mass is at low concentrations, and a few wells are much higher.


Code
# Categorical well-class map plus arsenic histogram and class-count bar chart.
ax = plot_layer(
    bangladesh,  # boundary underlay
    "Well class",  # map title
    facecolor="#E8F1F5",  # light fill
    edgecolor=EDGE,  # boundary stroke
    linewidth=0.25,  # thin boundary
    figsize=(7, 8),  # portrait figure
    axis_off=True,  # hide axes
    show=False,  # return axes for overlay
)  # close this call
# Draw a categorical attribute map.
plot_categorical(
    wells_butm,  # well points
    "Well_class",  # categorical column
    cmap="tab10",  # qualitative colormap
    ax=ax,  # draw on the boundary axes
    markersize=8,  # point size
    legend_kwds={"title": "Well class", "loc": "lower left"},  # legend
    show=False,  # defer show
)  # close this call
ax.figure.tight_layout()  # tighten the categorical map
plt.show()  # display the well-class map

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))  # histogram + bar chart
plot_histogram(wells_butm, "As", title="Arsenic", bins=40, ax=axes[0], show=False)  # As histogram
class_counts = wells_butm.groupby("Well_class").size().rename("wells").to_frame()  # counts by class
plot_bar(class_counts, "wells", title="Wells by class", ax=axes[1], show=False)  # class bar chart
fig.tight_layout()  # tighten chart panels
plt.show()  # display the charts


















Interactive maps
There are 3,534 wells, so the web maps use GeoDataFrame.explore through interactive_map rather than one CircleMarker per well. The first map colors wells by Well_class. The boundary is simplified by 500 m before it is sent to the browser: the shapefile has on the order of 140,000 vertices, and Leaflet does not need that density. The static maps above still use the original boundary.
Hover a well for its sample id, class, district, and arsenic. The layer control turns the boundary and the wells on and off.


Code
# Interactive map of well class with a simplified Bangladesh outline overlay.
well_center = [wells_butm["LAT_DEG"].mean(), wells_butm["LONG_DEG"].mean()]  # [lat, lon]
outline = bangladesh[["geometry"]].copy()  # geometry-only copy for overlay
outline["geometry"] = outline.geometry.simplify(500)  # simplify for lighter GeoJSON
# Assign class_map.
class_map = interactive_map(
    wells_butm,  # well points
    column="Well_class",  # categorical attribute
    categorical=True,  # treat values as categories
    cmap="tab10",  # qualitative colormap
    tooltip=["SAMPLE_ID", "Well_class", "DISTRICT", "As"],  # hover fields
    tiles="OpenStreetMap",  # basemap
    location=well_center,  # initial map center
    zoom_start=7,  # country-scale zoom
    height="520px",  # iframe height
    name="Well class",  # layer name
)  # close this call
# Add a GeoJSON overlay to the Folium map.
add_geojson(
    class_map,  # target Folium map
    outline,  # simplified boundary
    name="Bangladesh",  # overlay layer name
    color=EDGE,  # stroke color
    weight=1.2,  # stroke width
    fill_opacity=0.05,  # nearly transparent fill
)  # close this call
add_layer_control(class_map)  # enable layer toggles
class_map  # display the Folium map as the cell result

Interactive choropleth and a heatmap
The arsenic map uses the same 10, 50, and 200 µg/L breaks as the static map. The heatmap is the density view from the Folium gallery: folium.plugins.HeatMap takes [latitude, longitude] and shows where the samples cluster. It is not a map of the arsenic values. OpenTopoMap is the other built-in tile set used in that gallery.


Code
# Interactive arsenic map with the same Bangladesh outline overlay.
arsenic_map = interactive_map(
    wells_butm,  # well points
    column="As",  # arsenic concentration
    cmap="YlOrRd",  # sequential colormap
    scheme="user_defined",  # explicit class breaks
    classification_kwds={"bins": [10, 50, 200]},  # custom arsenic bins
    tooltip=["SAMPLE_ID", "Well_class", "DISTRICT", "As"],  # hover fields
    tiles="OpenStreetMap",  # basemap
    location=well_center,  # reuse the well-center location
    zoom_start=7,  # country-scale zoom
    height="520px",  # iframe height
    name="Arsenic",  # layer name
)  # close this call
# Add a GeoJSON overlay to the Folium map.
add_geojson(
    arsenic_map,  # target Folium map
    outline,  # simplified boundary
    name="Bangladesh",  # overlay layer name
    color=EDGE,  # stroke color
    weight=1.2,  # stroke width
    fill_opacity=0.05,  # nearly transparent fill
)  # close this call
add_layer_control(arsenic_map)  # enable layer toggles
arsenic_map  # display the Folium map as the cell result

Code
# Folium heatmap of well sample density on an OpenTopoMap basemap.
from folium.plugins import HeatMap  # heatmap overlay plugin

# Assign heatmap.
heatmap = interactive_map(
    location=well_center,  # center on the well cluster
    zoom_start=7,  # country-scale zoom
    tiles="OpenTopoMap",  # topographic basemap
    height="520px",  # iframe height
)  # close this call
# Add a Folium heatmap overlay.
HeatMap(
    wells_butm[["LAT_DEG", "LONG_DEG"]].to_numpy().tolist(),  # [lat, lon] pairs
    name="Sample density",  # layer name
    radius=12,  # heatmap kernel radius in pixels
).add_to(heatmap)  # attach the heatmap to the Folium map
add_layer_control(heatmap)  # enable layer toggles
heatmap  # display the heatmap map

title: Visualizing Vector Data
section: Part 3: Line maps: Onondaga County streets
text:
Part 3: Line maps: Onondaga County streets
Ononda_Street_PROJ.shp holds 999 street centerlines. The CRS is the same NAD83 Albers projection as the county layer, so the streets overlay the counties without a reprojection. SPEED is the posted speed limit (5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, or 65). Those are a short list of limits, so the map treats them as categories. PostType is the street suffix (Rd, St, Ln, …). Rare suffixes are grouped into Other so the legend stays readable.


Code
# Load Onondaga street centerlines and simplify road-type labels for mapping.
streets = read_layer("vector_data/USA/Ononda_Street_PROJ.shp")  # street centerlines
keep_types = {"Rd", "St", "Ln", "Dr"}  # common post types to keep as-is
# Map uncommon PostType values to the catch-all Other class.
streets["Road_type"] = streets["PostType"].where(streets["PostType"].isin(keep_types), "Other")

print(f"Segments: {len(streets)}")  # number of street segments
print(f"CRS: {streets.crs.name}")  # projected CRS name
print("Speed limits:")  # header for SPEED value counts
print(streets["SPEED"].value_counts().sort_index().to_string())  # mph frequencies
print("Road type:")  # header for Road_type value counts
print(streets["Road_type"].value_counts().to_string())  # type frequencies
display(streets[["StreetName", "PostType", "Road_type", "SPEED", "Label"]].head())  # preview

One symbol, then color by speed
The first map is the network alone. The second colors each segment by its posted speed. categorical=True gives each limit its own color. A continuous ramp would imply speeds between the posted values.


Code
# Side-by-side street centerlines and categorical posted-speed map.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6))  # two street-map panels
# Draw one map layer.
plot_layer(
    streets,  # all centerlines in one style
    "Street centerlines",  # left title
    ax=axes[0],  # left panel
    facecolor=EDGE,  # line color (facecolor used for lines here)
    linewidth=0.6,  # centerline stroke width
    axis_off=True,  # hide axes
)  # close this call
# Draw one map layer.
plot_layer(
    streets,  # same streets colored by SPEED
    "Posted speed",  # right title
    ax=axes[1],  # right panel
    column="SPEED",  # posted speed limit
    categorical=True,  # treat mph values as categories
    cmap="plasma",  # categorical/continuous-looking ramp
    linewidth=0.8,  # slightly thicker for class colors
    legend=True,  # show mph legend
    axis_off=True,  # hide axes
    legend_kwds={"title": "mph", "loc": "upper left", "bbox_to_anchor": (1.02, 1)},  # outside legend
)  # close this call
fig.tight_layout()  # tighten the two panels
plt.show()  # display the street maps











Street type
Road_type is a category derived from PostType. Roads dominate the file, and the other classes are the remaining suffixes a reader can still see in the legend.


Code
# Categorical map of simplified street types (Rd, St, Ln, Dr, Other).
plot_categorical(
    streets,  # street centerlines
    "Road_type",  # simplified type column
    "Street type",  # map title
    cmap="Dark2",  # qualitative colormap
    linewidth=0.8,  # line stroke width
    figsize=(8, 7),  # figure size
    axis_off=True,  # hide axes
    legend_kwds={"title": "Type", "loc": "upper left"},  # legend placement
)  # close this call











Streets on the counties they cross
The segments intersect Onondaga County and Cortland County. Both layers already share NAD83 Albers. The county fill is drawn at zorder 1 and the streets at zorder 2, so the lines stay visible. This is the same overlay pattern as the GeoPandas guide: create the axes with the area layer, then draw the next layer onto that axes.


Code
# Overlay posted speed on Onondaga and Cortland county polygons.
crossed = counties.loc[
    counties["STATE"].eq("New York")  # New York only
    & counties["COUNTY"].isin(["Onondaga County", "Cortland County"])  # two counties
].copy()  # local copy for plotting

# Compose multiple map layers.
plot_layers(
    # List of layer style dictionaries.
    [
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": crossed,  # county underlay
            "facecolor": "#F2F4F7",  # light gray fill
            "edgecolor": EDGE,  # county outline
            "linewidth": 0.8,  # outline width
            "zorder": 1,  # under the streets
        },  # end this layer dict
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": streets,  # street overlay
            "column": "SPEED",  # color by posted speed
            "categorical": True,  # categorical mph classes
            "cmap": "plasma",  # colormap for SPEED
            "linewidth": 0.7,  # street stroke width
            "legend": True,  # show mph legend
            "legend_kwds": {"title": "mph", "loc": "upper left"},  # legend options
            "zorder": 2,  # above the counties
        },  # end this layer dict
    ],  # end layer list
    title="Posted speed on Onondaga and Cortland streets",  # map title
    figsize=(8, 8),  # square figure
    legend=False,  # layer-level legend handles SPEED instead
    axis_off=True,  # hide axes
)  # close this call









County names and a scale bar finish the static line map. The labels use the county layer; the streets stay unlabeled because several hundred names will not fit.


Code
# County underlay with street overlay, county labels, and cartographic elements.
ax = plot_layers(
    # List of layer style dictionaries.
    [
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": crossed,  # Onondaga + Cortland polygons
            "facecolor": "#F2F4F7",  # light fill
            "edgecolor": EDGE,  # county outline
            "linewidth": 0.8,  # outline width
            "zorder": 1,  # under streets
        },  # end this layer dict
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": streets,  # street centerlines
            "facecolor": "#C2410C",  # orange-red line color
            "linewidth": 0.5,  # thin streets for label clarity
            "zorder": 2,  # above counties
        },  # end this layer dict
    ],  # end layer list
    title="Onondaga and Cortland",  # map title
    figsize=(8, 8),  # square figure
    legend=False,  # no legend needed for this composition
    axis_off=True,  # hide axes
    show=False,  # return axes for labels/elements
)  # close this call
add_labels(ax, crossed, "COUNTY", fontsize=9)  # label each county
cartographic_elements(ax, crossed)  # north arrow / scale bar
ax.figure.tight_layout()  # tighten layout
plt.show()  # display the labeled map











Tile basemap
Web tiles are drawn in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857). plot_layers(..., basemap=True) reprojects the layers to that CRS and then calls contextily, which is the same tile mechanism GeoPandas uses for plot(tiles=...). OpenStreetMap.HOT is a provider from that catalog and does not need an API key. CartoDB.Positron is another common name; some Carto endpoints now return a key warning instead of a map. The cell needs a network connection to the tile service. Reprojecting first keeps the tiles sharp; asking contextily to warp the image into Albers softens it.


Code
# Streets and county outlines drawn over an OpenStreetMap.HOT tile basemap.
plot_layers(
    # List of layer style dictionaries.
    [
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": crossed,  # county outlines only
            "facecolor": "none",  # no fill so tiles show through
            "edgecolor": "#101828",  # dark outline
            "linewidth": 1.0,  # stronger outline on tiles
            "zorder": 2,  # above the basemap
        },  # end this layer dict
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": streets,  # street overlay
            "facecolor": "#C2410C",  # orange-red streets
            "linewidth": 0.7,  # street stroke width
            "zorder": 3,  # above county outlines
        },  # end this layer dict
    ],  # end layer list
    basemap=True,  # enable a contextily/tile basemap
    basemap_source="OpenStreetMap.HOT",  # Humanitarian OSM tiles
    title="Streets on a tile basemap",  # map title
    figsize=(8, 8),  # square figure
    legend=False,  # no legend for this basemap view
)  # close this call











Interactive line layer
The county outline and the speed-limit lines share one Folium map. Passing a list of layers to interactive_map adds a layer control. Hover a segment for its street label and speed. The map opens near the center of the street layer.
explore writes every attribute into the web layer. The street file has dozens of address fields the tooltip does not use, so the interactive layer keeps Label, SPEED, and Road_type only.


Code
# Interactive Folium map with county outlines and streets colored by SPEED.
street_center = streets.to_crs(4326).geometry.union_all().centroid  # center in lon/lat
street_web = streets[["Label", "SPEED", "Road_type", "geometry"]].copy()  # slim web layer
# Build an interactive Folium map.
interactive_map(
    # List of layer style dictionaries.
    [
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": crossed[["COUNTY", "geometry"]],  # county polygons for outline
            "name": "Counties",  # Folium layer name
            "color": EDGE,  # outline color
            "tooltip": ["COUNTY"],  # hover field
            "style_kwds": {"fillOpacity": 0.05, "weight": 1.5, "color": EDGE},  # light fill
        },  # end this layer dict
        # One layer style dictionary.
        {
            "data": street_web,  # street segments for the web map
            "name": "Posted speed",  # Folium layer name
            "column": "SPEED",  # color by mph
            "categorical": True,  # categorical SPEED classes
            "cmap": "plasma",  # colormap
            "tooltip": ["Label", "SPEED", "Road_type"],  # hover fields
        },  # end this layer dict
    ],  # end layer list
    tiles="OpenStreetMap",  # basemap tiles
    location=[street_center.y, street_center.x],  # Folium [lat, lon]
    zoom_start=11,  # city/county-scale zoom
    height="520px",  # iframe height
)  # close this call

title: Visualizing Vector Data
text:
Summary
Use a single symbol when the question is location. Use a choropleth when the question is a quantity attached to an area, and choose the classification for the distribution you have: quantiles when each class should contain a similar number of places, equal interval when the legend must be even steps of the attribute, and natural breaks when the classes should follow clusters in the data. Use a qualitative palette for names and codes. Mark missing values explicitly. Put every layer in one CRS before you overlay them, and use Folium when the reader needs to zoom, inspect a feature, or switch a layer off.

title: Reading and Writing Vector Data
text:
Overview
Vector data is a type of geospatial data representation used in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and computer graphics. It represents spatial information using points, lines, and polygons, which are defined by their geometric coordinates. These coordinates consist of x and y (and sometimes z) values that describe the location of each point, the vertices of lines, or the corners of polygons.
Here’s a breakdown of the main elements of vector data:

Points: A single data point that represents a specific location in space, defined by its x and y coordinates (and potentially z for 3D data). Points are often used to represent features like cities, landmarks, or sampling locations.
Lines (Polylines): A series of connected points, which can be straight or curved, used to represent linear features such as roads, rivers, or boundaries. Lines are composed of multiple vertices that define their shape.
Polygons: Closed shapes formed by connecting a series of lines to enclose an area. Polygons are used to represent features like countries, lakes, forests, and other spatially bounded regions.

Vector data provides a more detailed and accurate representation of geographic features compared to raster data, which is another common data format used in GIS. One of the significant advantages of vector data is that it allows for precise measurements, editing, and analysis of geographic features. It is also more scalable and efficient for storing data with well-defined boundaries and discrete features.
Some common vector data formats include Shapefile (.shp), GeoJSON (.geojson), and Keyhole Markup Language (.kml). These formats can store various attributes along with the spatial coordinates, making it possible to attach additional information (e.g., population data for cities or elevation data for terrain) to each feature represented in the vector dataset.
This tutorial covers the full vector I/O loop: open common desktop and cloud-native formats, inspect layers and geometries, then write features back out with the same GDAL/OGR stack.
Reading. open_vectors_data opens the file formats used by desktop GIS and GPS tools and returns a VectorDataset. open_cloud_native_vector_data opens cloud-native files, lakehouse tables, and GeoParquet profiles and returns a CloudNativeDataset. In both cases the active layer exposes the CRS, extent, fields, and feature count. to_dataframe() returns a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame when GeoPandas is installed. Close either dataset with a with block so the file handle is released.
Writing. write_vector_data uses the same drivers. The file extension selects the driver. write_shapefile, write_geopackage, write_geojson, and write_csv call that function with the driver fixed.
The notebook is organized in three parts:

Reading desktop formats: walk through the GDAL samples in data/data_gdal.
Reading cloud-native layouts: open small local examples of GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf range reads, PMTiles, and related layouts.
Writing vector data: write New York counties to every creatable desktop format, convert the sample files to shapefiles, and read the outputs back for a map check.

The desktop-format files live in data/data_gdal. They are the GDAL sample files shipped with this repository. The cloud-native section writes small local examples, because those layouts are usually published as large objects on object storage. Written files land in Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder. The tables below are where the same formats usually come from when you download real data.







Format
Good sources




Shapefile
Natural Earth (naturalearthdata.com), US Census TIGER/Line, NYS GIS Clearinghouse (gis.ny.gov)


GeoJSON / GeoJSONSeq
USGS Earthquake feeds (earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed), city open-data portals (Socrata/ArcGIS Hub “Download → GeoJSON”); GeoJSONSeq usually needs to be made with ogr2ogr -f GeoJSONSeq


KML / KMZ
USGS Earthquake feeds, Google’s KML samples (developers.google.com/kml), NOAA/NWS storm and warning products


GML
Ordnance Survey (UK) OpenData, EU INSPIRE portals, WFS services (any WFS GetFeature returns GML)


GPX
OpenStreetMap public GPS traces (openstreetmap.org/traces), Garmin/Strava exports, topografix.com sample files


CSV with X/Y or WKT
USGS Earthquake CSV, NOAA station lists, EPA facility data (FRS), most data.gov tabular files


MapInfo TAB, MIF/MID
data.gov.au and Geoscience Australia (still widely published there), GDAL autotest


DXF / DWG
GDAL autotest, LibreDWG test files on GitHub, Autodesk sample files, municipal engineering/CAD portals


DGN
GDAL autotest, state DOT CADD downloads (many DOTs use MicroStation), Bentley sample datasets


File Geodatabase (.gdb)
USGS National Map (NHD, Watershed Boundary Dataset), TIGER/Line geodatabases, Esri sample data


SpatiaLite / SQLite
Natural Earth (SQLite download), gaia-gis.it SpatiaLite sample DBs


FlatGeobuf
flatgeobuf GitHub repo test/data (e.g., countries.fgb, UScounties.fgb)


OSM (.osm, .pbf)
Geofabrik (download.geofabrik.de) for country and state .osm.pbf extracts, BBBike city extracts, the “Export” button on openstreetmap.org or the Overpass API for small .osm XML



Cloud-native files, lakehouse tables, and related layouts use open_cloud_native_vector_data. GeoParquet is the better choice for analytics on selected columns. FlatGeobuf is the better choice for a spatial lookup that returns whole features. PMTiles holds tiles for web display, not analysis-ready features. COPC is the point-cloud equivalent of those layouts.







Layout
Good sources




GeoParquet
Overture Maps releases, Microsoft Planetary Computer, national field-boundary datasets published as fiboa


GeoArrow
In-memory exchange between GeoPandas, DuckDB, Sedona, and other Arrow tools; on disk as Feather or Arrow IPC


FlatGeobuf
Source Cooperative and other static HTTP hosts; the client range-requests the features inside a bounding box


PMTiles
Protomaps and Source Cooperative; one file replaces MBTiles and a tile server


GeoPackage
QGIS exchange files and Natural Earth; not cloud-native, though GDAL can read a remote .gpkg


COPC
USGS 3DEP and other LAZ octrees published for range-request access


Apache Iceberg
Lakehouse tables; v3 adds native geometry and geography types on top of Parquet


Delta Lake
Databricks and Sedona tables; geometry is stored as WKB


H3 / S2
Aggregated point tables that store a cell id instead of, or beside, a geometry

title: Reading and Writing Vector Data
text:
Setup
The next cell puts the repository root on the import path, points DATA at the sample directory, prepares the write output folders, and defines the helpers used later:

list_layers prints one row per layer.
read_vector opens a desktop format with open_vectors_data, prints layer properties, shows a short attribute table, and draws the geometries with plot_layers() from geolattice.viz.
read_cloud does the same for a cloud-native layout, and also prints the schema profile, reader, and spatial index.

County outputs go in Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder/ny_county. Shapefiles converted from the GDAL samples go in gdal_as_shapefile.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Import standard library and GIS dependencies used throughout this notebook
%matplotlib inline  

import sys  # Adjust PYTHONPATH to import local geolattice
import tempfile  # Temporary folders for KMZ and cloud-native demos
import zipfile  # Build KMZ (zipped KML) archives
from pathlib import Path  # Portable filesystem paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # Static maps and figures
import pandas as pd  # Tabular previews and catalogs
import pyproj  # CRS definitions and transforms
from IPython.display import display  # Rich notebook display for tables
from osgeo import gdal, ogr, osr  # GDAL/OGR vector I/O and spatial references
from shapely import wkb as shapely_wkb  # Load geometries from WKB bytes
from shapely.geometry.base import BaseGeometry  # Base type checks for plottable geoms
from shapely.ops import transform  # Reproject Shapely geometries with a callback




Code

# ===================================================================
# Setup and helpers for reading, writing, and visualizing vector data.
# ===================================================================

# This code block sets everything up so you can read, write, and view vector geospatial data.
# 1. Figure out where our data and code live.
# Walk up from the working directory until Data/00_shared/vector_data is found.
ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve()
while not (ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data").is_dir():
    if ROOT.parent == ROOT:
        raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find Data/00_shared/vector_data from the working directory.")
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

# 2. Bring in the tools we want from geolattice. These let us read, write, and plot geospatial data.
from geolattice.vector import (
    open_cloud_native_vector_data,  # Open fancy 'cloud' formats (remote, fast access)
    open_vectors_data,              # Open ordinary vector files (like shapefiles, GeoJSON)
    read_vector_data,               # Extra helpers for reading
    supported_cloud_native_formats, # List which 'cloud' formats are available
    supported_formats,              # List which regular formats are available
    supported_write_formats,        # List which formats we can write (save) to
    write_shapefile,                # Save data as a Shapefile
    write_vector_data,              # Save data to other formats
)
# Call read_vector_data import()
from geolattice.vector.read_vector_data import (
    GEOM_POSSIBLE_NAMES,            # List of possible geometry column names in tables
    X_POSSIBLE_NAMES,               # List of possible X column names
    Y_POSSIBLE_NAMES,               # List of possible Y column names
)
from geolattice.viz import EDGE, FACE, apply_map_style, plot_layers  # For map coloring & drawing

# 3. Set up key folders and files:
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "data_gdal"  # All our example files live here
assert DATA.is_dir(), DATA          # Make sure the DATA folder actually exists!

SOURCE = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA" / "NY_County_PROJ.shp"      # Example shapefile
OUTPUT = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "output_folder"                   # Where to put results
COUNTY_DIR = OUTPUT / "ny_county"                                          # Subfolder for counties
SAMPLE_DIR = OUTPUT / "gdal_as_shapefile"                                  # Subfolder for more samples
COUNTY_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)                              # Make folders if they don't exist
SAMPLE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# 4. Make GDAL (the software handling GIS data) not print annoying error messages.
gdal.PushErrorHandler("CPLQuietErrorHandler")

# 5. Make pandas printouts of tables look nicer.
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 12)
# Limit displayed column width
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 48)
# Widen pandas text display
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)

# 6. Set the style (colors, lines, etc) for our map plots.
apply_map_style()

# 7. Define what types of geometries we can plot: shapes, lines, points.
_PLOT_TYPES = {
    # Include Polygon
    "Polygon",
    # Include MultiPolygon
    "MultiPolygon",
    # Include LineString
    "LineString",
    # Include MultiLineString
    "MultiLineString",
    # Include LinearRing
    "LinearRing",
    # Include Point
    "Point",
    # Include MultiPoint
    "MultiPoint",
# Close mapping or set
}

# 8. Keep a running list of what we've done (for summary later)
RESULTS = []

# ---- Helper functions ----

# Define _resolve()
def _resolve(relative):
    # Try to find a file. Look first at the full path, then inside DATA.
    path = Path(relative)
    # If path.exists()
    if path.exists():
        # Return result
        return path
    # Return result
    return DATA / relative

# Define _file_label()
def _file_label(path):
    # Return a nice, short label for a file, relative to DATA if possible.
    path = Path(path)
    # Try block
    try:
        # Return result
        return str(path.resolve().relative_to(DATA.resolve()))
    # Handle error
    except ValueError:
        # Return result
        return str(path)

# Define preview_table()
def preview_table(frame, limit=5):
    # Show the first few rows of a table, with a column for geometry type (like 'Polygon')
    view = frame.head(limit).copy()
    # Call insert()
    view.insert(
        # Statement
        1,
        # Include geom_type
        "geom_type",
        # Call map()
        view["geometry"].map(lambda geom: getattr(geom, "geom_type", None)),
    # Close multi-line expression
    )
    # Set keep
    keep = ["fid", "geom_type"]
    # Set extras
    extras = [name for name in view.columns if name not in keep and name != "geometry"]
    # Return result
    return view[keep + extras[:6]]

# Define plot_frame()
def plot_frame(frame, title):
    # Include 
    """
    # Statement
    Draw a map: shows the shapes in the data as polygons, lines, or points.
    # Statement
    Uses pretty colors and groups things by type.
    # Include 
    """
    # Define plottable()
    def plottable(geom):
        # Only plot real geometry types (not empty/missing stuff)
        return isinstance(geom, BaseGeometry) and not geom.is_empty and geom.geom_type in _PLOT_TYPES

    # Set mask
    mask = frame["geometry"].map(plottable)
    # Set plot_df
    plot_df = frame.loc[mask].copy()
    # If plot_df.empty
    if plot_df.empty:
        # Call print()
        print(f"No point, line, or polygon geometries to draw for {title}.")
        # Return result
        return 0

    # Set kinds
    kinds = plot_df["geometry"].map(lambda geom: geom.geom_type)
    # Set groups
    groups = [
        # Call function()
        (
            # Include polygon
            "polygon",
            # Statement
            ["Polygon", "MultiPolygon"],
            # Statement
            {"facecolor": FACE, "edgecolor": EDGE, "linewidth": 0.6, "alpha": 0.88, "zorder": 1},
        # Close multi-line expression
        ),
        # Call function()
        (
            # Include line
            "line",
            # Statement
            ["LineString", "MultiLineString", "LinearRing"],
            {"color": "#E36414", "linewidth": 1.6, "zorder": 2},
        ),
        # Call function()
        (
            # Include point
            "point",
            # Statement
            ["Point", "MultiPoint"],
            {"color": "#F4A261", "markersize": 42, "edgecolor": "#7A3E00", "linewidth": 0.4, "zorder": 3},
        ),
    # Close multi-line expression
    ]
    # Set layers
    layers = []
    # Loop: label, types, style in groups
    for label, types, style in groups:
        # Set part
        part = plot_df.loc[kinds.isin(types)]
        # If len(part)
        if len(part):
            # Call append()
            layers.append({"data": part, "label": label, **style})
    # Set ax
    ax = plot_layers(layers, title=title, figsize=(7.6, 5.4), legend=len(layers) > 1, show=False)

    # Make sure map has a little space around the data
    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = geometry_bounds(plot_df)
    # Set span_x
    span_x = maxx - minx
    # Set span_y
    span_y = maxy - miny
    # Set pad_x
    pad_x = span_x * 0.08 if span_x else max(abs(minx) * 0.02, 1.0)
    # Set pad_y
    pad_y = span_y * 0.08 if span_y else max(abs(miny) * 0.02, 1.0)
    # Call set_xlim()
    ax.set_xlim(minx - pad_x, maxx + pad_x)
    # Call set_ylim()
    ax.set_ylim(miny - pad_y, maxy + pad_y)
    # Call tight_layout()
    ax.figure.tight_layout()
    # Call show()
    plt.show()
    # Return result
    return len(plot_df)

# Define geometry_bounds()
def geometry_bounds(frame):
    # Find the smallest box that includes all the shapes in the table.
    boxes = []
    # Loop: geom in frame["geometry"]
    for geom in frame["geometry"]:
        # If isinstance(geom, BaseGeometry) and not geom.is_empty
        if isinstance(geom, BaseGeometry) and not geom.is_empty:
            # Call append()
            boxes.append(geom.bounds)
    # If not boxes
    if not boxes:
        # Return result
        return None
    # Return result
    return (
        # Call min()
        min(box[0] for box in boxes),
        # Call min()
        min(box[1] for box in boxes),
        # Call max()
        max(box[2] for box in boxes),
        # Call max()
        max(box[3] for box in boxes),
    # Close multi-line expression
    )

# Define list_layers()
def list_layers(relative):
    # Show info about each 'layer' in a vector dataset/file (like "roads", "buildings" in a file)
    path = _resolve(relative)
    # With open_vectors_data(path) as dataset
    with open_vectors_data(path) as dataset:
        # Call print()
        print(f"{dataset.format_name}  |  driver {dataset.driver}  |  {_file_label(dataset.path)}")
        # Set rows
        rows = []
        # Loop: layer in dataset.layers
        for layer in dataset.layers:
            # Call append()
            rows.append(
                # Statement
                {
                    # Statement
                    "layer": layer.name,
                    # Statement
                    "geometry_type": layer.geometry_type,
                    # Statement
                    "features": layer.feature_count,
                    # Call crs is None else str()
                    "crs": None if layer.crs is None else str(layer.crs),
                    # Call "fields": len()
                    "fields": len(layer.fields),
                # Close mapping or set
                }
            # Close multi-line expression
            )
        # Call display()
        display(pd.DataFrame(rows))

# Define read_vector()
def read_vector(relative, layer=None, title=None, plot=True, limit=None):
    # Open a normal vector file, show all its details, and plot it.
    path = _resolve(relative)
    # Set label
    label = title or path.name
    # With open_vectors_data(path, layer=layer) as dataset
    with open_vectors_data(path, layer=layer) as dataset:
        # Set active
        active = dataset.layer
        # Set frame
        frame = active.to_dataframe(limit=limit)
        # Set read_bounds
        read_bounds = geometry_bounds(frame)
        # Call print()
        print(f"File:             {_file_label(dataset.path)}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Format:           {dataset.format_name}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Driver:           {dataset.driver}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Layer count:      {dataset.layer_count}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Layer names:      {dataset.layer_names}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Active layer:     {active.name}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Geometry type:    {active.geometry_type}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Geometry source:  {active.geometry_source}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Feature count:    {active.feature_count}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Features read:    {len(frame)}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"CRS:              {active.crs}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Bounds:           {read_bounds if read_bounds is not None else active.bounds}")
        # Call print()
        print("Fields:")
        # Loop: field in active.fields
        for field in active.fields:
            # Set width
            width = f", width={field.width}" if field.width else ""
            # Call print()
            print(f"  - {field.name} ({field.type_name}{width})")
        # If dataset.warnings
        if dataset.warnings:
            # Call print()
            print("Sidecar notes:")
            # Loop: note in dataset.warnings
            for note in dataset.warnings:
                # Call print()
                print(f"  - {note}")
        # Call display()
        display(preview_table(frame))
        # If plot
        if plot:
            # Call plot_frame()
            plot_frame(frame, label)
        # Set feature_count
        feature_count = active.feature_count if active.feature_count is not None else len(frame)
        # Call append()
        RESULTS.append(
            # Statement
            {
                # Call "file": _file_label()
                "file": _file_label(dataset.path),
                # Statement
                "format": dataset.format_name,
                # Statement
                "driver": dataset.driver,
                # Statement
                "layer": active.name,
                # Statement
                "features": feature_count,
                # Call crs is None else str()
                "crs": None if active.crs is None else str(active.crs),
                # Include status": "opened
                "status": "opened",
            # Close mapping or set
            }
        # Close multi-line expression
        )
        # Return result
        return None

# Define read_cloud()
def read_cloud(
    # Statement
    relative,
    # Set layer
    layer=None,
    # Set title
    title=None,
    # Set plot
    plot=True,
    # Set limit
    limit=None,
    # Set bbox
    bbox=None,
    # Set columns
    columns=None,
    # Set where
    where=None,
# Statement
):
    # Include 
    """
    # Call Open a 'cloud-native'()
    Open a 'cloud-native' (modern!) vector file, print LOTS of details about it, and plot it.
    # Statement
    Cloud-native just means things like Parquet or GeoParquet: fast, chunked, and can be remote.
    # Statement
    You can even show only part of the data using bbox/columns/where arguments.
    # Include 
    """
    # Set path
    path = _resolve(relative)
    # Set label
    label = title or path.name
    # Set print(f"\n{'
    print(f"\n{'=' * 72}\n{label}\n{'=' * 72}")
    # With open_cloud_native_vector_data(path, layer=layer) as dat
    with open_cloud_native_vector_data(path, layer=layer) as dataset:
        # Set active
        active = dataset.layer
        # Set frame
        frame = active.to_dataframe()
        # If limit is not None
        if limit is not None:
            # Set frame
            frame = frame.head(limit)
        # Call print()
        print(f"File:              {_file_label(dataset.path)}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Format:            {dataset.format_name} ({dataset.format_id})")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Schema:            {dataset.schema_name or 'n/a'}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Reader:            {dataset.reader}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Spatial access:    {dataset.spatial_access}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Spatial index:     {dataset.spatial_index or 'n/a'}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Geometry encoding: {dataset.geometry_encoding or 'n/a'}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Layers:            {dataset.layer_count}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Active layer:      {active.name}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"Features:          {active.feature_count}")
        # Call print()
        print(f"CRS:               {active.crs}")
        # Set extent
        extent = active.bounds if active.bounds is not None else active.compute_bounds()
        # Call print()
        print(f"Extent:            {None if extent is None else extent.to_tuple()}")
        # Call print()
        print("Fields:")
        # Loop: field in active.fields
        for field in active.fields:
            # Call print()
            print(f"  - {field.name} ({field.type_name})")
        # If dataset.warnings
        if dataset.warnings:
            # Call print()
            print("Notes:")
            # Loop: note in dataset.warnings
            for note in dataset.warnings:
                # Call print()
                print(f"  - {note}")
        # Set shown
        shown = frame
        # If bbox is not None or columns is not None or where is not
        if bbox is not None or columns is not None or where is not None:
            # Set shown
            shown = active.to_dataframe(bbox=bbox, columns=columns, where=where, limit=limit)
            # Call print()
            print(f"Filtered rows:     {len(shown)}")
        # Call display()
        display(preview_table(shown))
        # If plot
        if plot:
            # Call plot_frame()
            plot_frame(shown, label)
        # Set feature_count
        feature_count = active.feature_count if active.feature_count is not None else len(frame)
        # Call append()
        RESULTS.append(
            # Statement
            {
                # Call "file": _file_label()
                "file": _file_label(dataset.path),
                # Statement
                "format": dataset.format_name,
                # Statement
                "driver": dataset.reader,
                # Statement
                "layer": active.name,
                # Statement
                "features": feature_count,
                # Call crs is None else str()
                "crs": None if active.crs is None else str(active.crs),
                # Include status": "opened
                "status": "opened",
            # Close mapping or set
            }
        # Close multi-line expression
        )
    # Return result
    return None

# 9. Print out the main folders/files so people can see where things are.
print(f"Sample directory: {DATA}")
# Call print()
print(f"County source:    {SOURCE}")
# Call print()
print(f"Write output:     {OUTPUT}")
# Call print()
print(f"GDAL:             {gdal.VersionInfo('--version')}")

Part 1: Reading desktop formats
supported_formats() lists every file type the desktop reader knows about and whether this GDAL build includes a driver for it. The walkthrough below follows the table in the introduction. The cloud-native section later uses supported_cloud_native_formats(), which reports a reader rather than a GDAL driver.
