Shapefile
A shapefile is a small group of files that share one basename. .shp holds geometry, .shx is the index, and .dbf holds attributes. .prj stores the CRS and .cpg stores the DBF encoding. Natural Earth, TIGER/Line, and the NYS GIS Clearinghouse still publish this format.
poly.shp is the classic GDAL polygon sample. It is in British National Grid (EPSG:27700) and carries AREA, EAS_ID, and PRFEDEA.

GeoJSON is a single JSON document: a Feature, a FeatureCollection, or a bare geometry. City open-data portals and the USGS earthquake feeds offer it as a download. Coordinates in a GeoJSON file are longitude, latitude (EPSG:4326) unless the file says otherwise.

Part 3: Writing vector data
write_vector_data uses the same GDAL/OGR drivers as open_vectors_data. The file extension selects the driver. write_shapefile, write_geopackage, write_geojson, and write_csv call that function with the driver fixed.
This part makes two conversions. Both land in Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder.

Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/NY_County_PROJ.shp, the New York county layer in a custom Albers projection, is written to each format this GDAL build can create.
Each desktop format opened in Part 1 is taken from data/data_gdal and written as a shapefile. A shapefile holds one geometry type, so a layer that mixes points, lines, and polygons is split into one shapefile per type.

The last sections open several of those written files with read_vector_data and draw them.

Write the counties to each desktop format
Most formats keep the Albers coordinates and the full attribute table. A few drivers impose their own rules, so those files are prepared before the write:







Output
What is written




Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, GeoJSON Sequence, GML, CSV, MapInfo TAB, MapInfo MIF, SpatiaLite, FlatGeobuf
County polygons and attributes, in the source CRS


KML and KMZ
The same polygons and attributes, reprojected to EPSG:4326. KML and KMZ are defined in WGS 84


GPX
One waypoint per county, at the polygon’s representative point, in EPSG:4326. GPX stores waypoints, routes, and tracks, and it checks that coordinates are longitude and latitude


DXF and DGN
County outlines only. Those drivers do not accept the county attribute fields


File Geodatabase
County polygons and attributes. OBJECTID is renamed to OID_SRC because OpenFileGDB reserves OBJECTID for an integer identifier, and the shapefile stores that column as text



This GDAL build can read DWG, OpenStreetMap (.osm and .pbf), GeoParquet, and GeoArrow, and it cannot create them. Personal geodatabase (.mdb) and legacy Excel (.xls) are read-only here as well. The XLSX and ODS drivers report that they can create a file, but assigning a geometry raises an OGR error in GDAL 3.8.4, so those spreadsheets are left out.


Code
# CRS helpers: build OSR refs, reproject features, and write county formats
def spatial_ref(crs):
    # Include Build an OSR spatial reference from a geolattice CRS, EPSG code, or CRS string.
    """Build an OSR spatial reference from a geolattice CRS, EPSG code, or CRS string."""
    # Set srs
    srs = osr.SpatialReference()
    # If hasattr(crs, "to_wkt")
    if hasattr(crs, "to_wkt"):
        # Call ImportFromWkt()
        srs.ImportFromWkt(crs.to_wkt())
    # Else if isinstance(crs, int)
    elif isinstance(crs, int):
        # Call ImportFromEPSG()
        srs.ImportFromEPSG(int(crs))
    # Otherwise
    else:
        # Call SetFromUserInput()
        srs.SetFromUserInput(str(crs))
    # Call SetAxisMappingStrategy()
    srs.SetAxisMappingStrategy(osr.OAMS_TRADITIONAL_GIS_ORDER)
    # Return result
    return srs


# Define transform_geometry()
def transform_geometry(geometry, coord_transform):
    # Include Transform a Shapely geometry with an ``osr.CoordinateTransformation``.
    """Transform a Shapely geometry with an ``osr.CoordinateTransformation``."""
    # Set geom
    geom = ogr.CreateGeometryFromWkb(geometry.wkb)
    # Call Transform()
    geom.Transform(coord_transform)
    # Return result
    return shapely_wkb.loads(bytes(geom.ExportToWkb()))


# Define reproject()
def reproject(features, source_crs, target_crs="EPSG:4326"):
    # Include Return feature mappings with geometries transformed to ``target_crs`` via GDAL/OSR.
    """Return feature mappings with geometries transformed to ``target_crs`` via GDAL/OSR."""
    # Set coord_transform
    coord_transform = osr.CoordinateTransformation(
        # Call spatial_ref()
        spatial_ref(source_crs), spatial_ref(target_crs)
    # Close multi-line expression
    )
    # Set rows
    rows = []
    # Loop: feature in features
    for feature in features:
        # Call append()
        rows.append(
            # Statement
            {
                # Call "geometry": transform_geometry()
                "geometry": transform_geometry(feature.geometry, coord_transform),
                # Statement
                **feature.properties,
            # Close mapping or set
            }
        # Close multi-line expression
        )
    # Return result
    return rows


# Define county_waypoints()
def county_waypoints(features, source_crs):
    # Include One GPX waypoint per county, using the GPX name, comment, and description fields.
    """One GPX waypoint per county, using the GPX name, comment, and description fields."""
    # Set coord_transform
    coord_transform = osr.CoordinateTransformation(
        # Call spatial_ref()
        spatial_ref(source_crs), spatial_ref("EPSG:4326")
    # Close multi-line expression
    )
    # Set rows
    rows = []
    # Loop: feature in features
    for feature in features:
        # Set point
        point = feature.geometry.representative_point()
        # Call append()
        rows.append(
            # Statement
            {
                # Call "geometry": transform_geometry()
                "geometry": transform_geometry(point, coord_transform),
                # Call get()
                "name": feature.properties.get("COUNTY"),
                # Call get()
                "cmt": feature.properties.get("FIPS"),
                # Call get()
                "desc": feature.properties.get("STATE"),
            # Close mapping or set
            }
        # Close multi-line expression
        )
    # Return result
    return rows


# Define rename_objectid()
def rename_objectid(features):
    # Set rows
    rows = []
    # Loop: feature in features
    for feature in features:
        # Set properties
        properties = {
            # Set ("OID_SRC" if key.upper()
            ("OID_SRC" if key.upper() == "OBJECTID" else key): value
            # Loop: key, value in feature.properties.items()
            for key, value in feature.properties.items()
        # Close mapping or set
        }
        # Call append()
        rows.append({"geometry": feature.geometry, **properties})
    # Return result
    return rows


# Define count_features()
def count_features(path):
    # With read_vector_data(path) as dataset
    with read_vector_data(path) as dataset:
        # Set layers
        layers = []
        # Set total
        total = 0
        # Loop: item in dataset.layers
        for item in dataset.layers:
            # Set count
            count = len(item.read())
            # If count
            if count:
                # Call append()
                layers.append(f"{item.name} ({count})")
                # Set total +
                total += count
        # Return result
        return total, ", ".join(layers)


# Set WGS84
WGS84 = reproject(COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS)
# Set JOBS
JOBS = [
    # Call function()
    ("ESRI Shapefile", "NY_County_PROJ.shp", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("GeoPackage", "NY_County_PROJ.gpkg", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("GeoJSON", "NY_County_PROJ.geojson", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("GeoJSON Sequence", "NY_County_PROJ.geojsonl", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("KML", "NY_County_PROJ.kml", WGS84, 4326, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("KMZ", "NY_County_PROJ.kmz", WGS84, 4326, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("GML", "NY_County_PROJ.gml", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("GPX", "NY_County_PROJ.gpx", county_waypoints(COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS), 4326, "waypoints"),
    # Call function()
    ("CSV", "NY_County_PROJ.csv", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("MapInfo TAB", "NY_County_PROJ.tab", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("MapInfo MIF", "NY_County_PROJ.mif", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("DXF", "NY_County_PROJ.dxf", [{"geometry": item.geometry} for item in COUNTY_FEATURES], COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("DGN", "NY_County_PROJ.dgn", [{"geometry": item.geometry} for item in COUNTY_FEATURES], COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("File Geodatabase", "NY_County_PROJ.gdb", rename_objectid(COUNTY_FEATURES), COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("SpatiaLite", "NY_County_PROJ.sqlite", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
    # Call function()
    ("FlatGeobuf", "NY_County_PROJ.fgb", COUNTY_FEATURES, COUNTY_CRS, "NY_County"),
# Close multi-line expression
]

# Set county_rows
county_rows = []
# Loop: format_name, filename, data, crs, layer_name in JOBS
for format_name, filename, data, crs, layer_name in JOBS:
    # Set path
    path = COUNTY_DIR / filename
    # Set write_vector_data(path, data, layer
    write_vector_data(path, data, layer=layer_name, crs=crs, overwrite=True)
    # Set written, layers
    written, layers = count_features(path)
    # Call append()
    county_rows.append(
        # Statement
        {
            # Statement
            "format": format_name,
            # Call "file": str()
            "file": str(path.relative_to(OUTPUT)),
            # Statement
            "features": written,
            # Statement
            "layers": layers,
        # Close mapping or set
        }
    # Close multi-line expression
    )

# Set county_report
county_report = pd.DataFrame(county_rows)
# Call display()

title: Reading and Writing Vector Data
text:
Read a written file back
The GeoPackage is opened with read_vector_data, the same function used for reading earlier. The map is the county layer that was just written, so the file can be opened again and drawn.


Code
# Re-open the written GeoPackage and plot New York counties
geopackage = COUNTY_DIR / "NY_County_PROJ.gpkg"  # Path written earlier in this notebook
with read_vector_data(geopackage) as dataset:  # Open the GeoPackage
    print(f"Driver:   {dataset.driver}")  # GDAL driver name
    print(f"Layer:    {dataset.layer.name}")  # Active layer name
    print(f"Features: {dataset.layer.feature_count}")  # Feature count
    print(f"CRS:      {dataset.layer.crs.name}")  # CRS name
    frame = dataset.layer.to_dataframe()  # Load as GeoDataFrame for plotting

# Call plot_layers()
plot_layers(
    [{"data": frame, "facecolor": FACE, "edgecolor": EDGE, "linewidth": 0.4, "label": "NY counties"}],  # Single style layer
    title="New York counties written to GeoPackage",  # Map title
    figsize=(8, 7),  # Figure size
    legend=False,  # No legend needed for one layer
)

Write every sample format as a shapefile
These are the files Part 1 opens from data/data_gdal. Each non-empty layer is written with write_shapefile. data/data_gdal also contains GDAL autotest files that are truncated, empty, or invalid on purpose. Those files are not among the samples opened in Part 1, so they are not converted here.
A shapefile can store points, lines, or polygons, and only one of those families in a single file. Where a sample layer mixes types, or stores a geometry collection, each part is written to its own shapefile. The KMZ is built the same way as in Part 1: kml/placemark.kml is zipped as doc.kml.


Code
# Split mixed-geometry GDAL samples into one shapefile per geometry type
SHAPE_TYPES = {
    # Include Point
    "Point",
    # Include MultiPoint
    "MultiPoint",
    # Include LineString
    "LineString",
    # Include MultiLineString
    "MultiLineString",
    # Include LinearRing
    "LinearRing",
    # Include Polygon
    "Polygon",
    # Include MultiPolygon
    "MultiPolygon",
# Close mapping or set
}


# Define geometry_parts()
def geometry_parts(geometry):
    # If geometry is None or geometry.is_empty
    if geometry is None or geometry.is_empty:
        # Return result
        return []
    # If geometry.geom_type == "GeometryCollection"
    if geometry.geom_type == "GeometryCollection":
        # Set parts
        parts = []
        # Loop: child in geometry.geoms
        for child in geometry.geoms:
            # Call extend()
            parts.extend(geometry_parts(child))
        # Return result
        return parts
    # If geometry.geom_type in SHAPE_TYPES
    if geometry.geom_type in SHAPE_TYPES:
        # Return result
        return [geometry]
    # Return result
    return []


# Define safe_name()
def safe_name(text):
    # Set cleaned
    cleaned = "".join(character if character.isalnum() or character in "-_" else "_" for character in str(text))
    # Return result
    return cleaned.strip("_") or "layer"


# Define write_sample_as_shapefiles()
def write_sample_as_shapefiles(tag, source):
    # Include Write each layer of ``source`` to one shapefile per geometry type.
    """Write each layer of ``source`` to one shapefile per geometry type."""
    # Set rows
    rows = []
    # With open_vectors_data(source) as dataset
    with open_vectors_data(source) as dataset:
        # Try block
        try:
            # Set relative
            relative = str(Path(source).resolve().relative_to(DATA.resolve()))
        # Handle error
        except ValueError:
            # Set relative
            relative = Path(source).name
        # Loop: layer in dataset.layers
        for layer in dataset.layers:
            # Set grouped
            grouped = {}
            # Loop: feature in layer.read()
            for feature in layer.read():
                # Loop: part in geometry_parts(feature.geometry)
                for part in geometry_parts(feature.geometry):
                    # Call setdefault()
                    grouped.setdefault(part.geom_type, []).append(
                        # Statement
                        {"geometry": part, **feature.properties}
                    # Close multi-line expression
                    )
            # If not grouped
            if not grouped:
                # Call append()
                rows.append(
                    # Statement
                    {
                        # Statement
                        "format": tag,
                        # Statement
                        "source": relative,
                        # Statement
                        "layer": layer.name,
                        # Include geometry": 
                        "geometry": "",
                        # Statement
                        "features": 0,
                        # Include shapefile": 
                        "shapefile": "",
                        # Include status": "no geometry
                        "status": "no geometry",
                    # Close mapping or set
                    }
                # Close multi-line expression
                )
                # Statement
                continue
            # Set several
            several = len(grouped) > 1
            # Loop: geom_type, records in grouped.items()
            for geom_type, records in grouped.items():
                # Set stem
                stem = f"{tag}__{safe_name(Path(source).stem)}__{safe_name(layer.name)}"
                # If several
                if several:
                    # Set stem
                    stem = f"{stem}__{geom_type}"
                # Set destination
                destination = SAMPLE_DIR / f"{stem}.shp"
                # Try block
                try:
                    # Call write_shapefile()
                    write_shapefile(
                        # Statement
                        destination,
                        # Statement
                        records,
                        # Set layer
                        layer=safe_name(layer.name),
                        # Set crs
                        crs=layer.crs,
                        # Set encoding
                        encoding="UTF-8",
                        # Set overwrite
                        overwrite=True,
                    # Close multi-line expression
                    )
                    # Set status
                    status = "written"
                # Handle error
                except Exception as exc:
                    # Set status
                    status = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
                # Call append()
                rows.append(
                    # Statement
                    {
                        # Statement
                        "format": tag,
                        # Statement
                        "source": relative,
                        # Statement
                        "layer": layer.name,
                        # Statement
                        "geometry": geom_type,
                        # Call "features": len()
                        "features": len(records),
                        # Statement
                        "shapefile": destination.name,
                        # Statement
                        "status": status,
                    # Close mapping or set
                    }
                # Close multi-line expression
                )
    # Return result
    return rows


# Set kmz_path
kmz_path = SAMPLE_DIR / "placemark.kmz"
# With zipfile.ZipFile(kmz_path, "w", compression=zipfile.ZIP_
with zipfile.ZipFile(kmz_path, "w", compression=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as archive:
    # Set archive.write(DATA / "kml" / "placemark.kml", arcname
    archive.write(DATA / "kml" / "placemark.kml", arcname="doc.kml")

# Set SAMPLES
SAMPLES = [
    # Call function()
    ("shapefile", DATA / "poly.shp"),
    # Call function()
    ("geojson", DATA / "geojson" / "grenada.geojson"),
    # Call function()
    ("geojsonseq", DATA / "geojsonseq" / "test.geojsonl"),
    # Call function()
    ("kml", DATA / "kml" / "samples.kml"),
    # Call function()
    ("kml", DATA / "kml" / "placemark.kml"),
    # Call function()
    ("kmz", kmz_path),
    # Call function()
    ("gml", DATA / "gml" / "gnis_pop_110.gml"),
    # Call function()
    ("gpx", DATA / "gpx" / "test.gpx"),
    # Call function()
    ("csv", DATA / "wkt.csv"),
    # Call function()
    ("mapinfo_tab", DATA / "mitab" / "all_geoms.tab"),
    # Call function()
    ("mapinfo_mif", DATA / "mitab" / "small.mif"),
    # Call function()
    ("mapinfo_mid", DATA / "mitab" / "small.mid"),
    # Call function()
    ("dxf", DATA / "dxf" / "assorted.dxf"),
    # Call function()
    ("dwg", DATA / "cad" / "line_r2000.dwg"),
    # Call function()
    ("dgn", DATA / "dgn" / "smalltest.dgn"),
    # Call function()
    ("filegdb", DATA / "openfilegdb" / "polygon_golden.gdb"),
    # Call function()
    ("spatialite", DATA / "sqlite" / "poly_spatialite.sqlite"),
    # Call function()
    ("flatgeobuf", DATA / "testfgb" / "poly.fgb"),
    # Call function()
    ("osm", DATA / "osm" / "test.osm"),
    # Call function()
    ("pbf", DATA / "osm" / "two_points.pbf"),
# Close multi-line expression
]

# Set sample_rows
sample_rows = []
# Loop: tag, path in SAMPLES
for tag, path in SAMPLES:
    # Call extend()
    sample_rows.extend(write_sample_as_shapefiles(tag, path))

# Set sample_report
sample_report = pd.DataFrame(sample_rows)
# Set written
written = sample_report[sample_report["status"] == "written"]
# Set display(written.reset_index(drop
display(written.reset_index(drop=True))
# Call print()
print(f"Shapefiles written: {len(written)}")
# Set skipped
skipped = sample_report[sample_report["status"] != "written"]
# If not skipped.empty
if not skipped.empty:
    # Call print()
    print("Layers with no shapefile geometry:")
    # Set display(skipped.reset_index(drop
    display(skipped.reset_index(drop=True))

text:
Visualize written files
These maps read files from Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder. They do not reuse the features still held in memory from the write step.
The first figure compares four county outputs: the shapefile and FlatGeobuf stay in the Albers projection, the KML is in EPSG:4326, and the GPX file is the county waypoints. The next map draws those waypoints on the county shapefile. plot_layers reprojects the waypoints onto the shapefile CRS. The choropleth uses SQUARE_MIL from the written shapefile. The last figure reads six shapefiles that were converted from the GDAL samples: polygons, points, and lines.


Code
# Compare written county formats side-by-side and summarize sample outputs
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
# Statement
from geolattice.viz import plot_layer

LINE = "#E36414"
POINT = "#F4A261"
POINT_EDGE = "#7A3E00"


# Define read_output()
def read_output(path, layer=None):
    # Include Open a written file and return its GeoDataFrame, driver, and CRS name.
    """Open a written file and return its GeoDataFrame, driver, and CRS name."""
    # With read_vector_data(path, layer=layer) as dataset
    with read_vector_data(path, layer=layer) as dataset:
        # Set frame
        frame = dataset.layer.to_dataframe()
        # Set crs_name
        crs_name = None if dataset.layer.crs is None else dataset.layer.crs.name
        # Return result
        return frame, dataset.driver, crs_name


# Define draw_map()
def draw_map(frame, title, ax):
    # Set kind
    kind = frame.geometry.geom_type.iloc[0]
    # If kind in ("Point", "MultiPoint")
    if kind in ("Point", "MultiPoint"):
        # Call plot_layer()
        plot_layer(

title: GeoLattice: Vector & Raster Data
text:
GIS stores the world in two ways. Vector data describes discrete features as points, lines and polygons, each with a row of attributes. Raster data describes continuous surfaces and imagery as a grid of cells, each holding a value. Almost every spatial workflow starts with one of them, and most combine the two.
These ten notebooks are the first two chapters of the GeoLattice tutorials. They cover reading and writing both data models, coordinate reference systems, mapping, and the core operations on features and grids, using geolattice.vector and geolattice.raster with real data from the United States and Bangladesh.

GeoLattice
GeoLattice is a Python library for geospatial analysis that brings vector and raster processing, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics, spatial databases, web and cloud GIS and remote sensing together under one import. It is built on GDAL, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely and xarray, so its functions take and return objects these libraries already use: GeoDataFrames, NumPy arrays and GDAL-readable files.

Vector data
A vector layer is a table in which every row is a feature and one column holds its geometry. Points mark locations such as wells or soil samples, lines trace roads and rivers, and polygons outline counties, fields and watersheds. Because each feature keeps its exact shape and its attributes, vector data suits boundaries, networks and anything you count, join or select by attribute.

title: GeoLattice: Vector & Raster Data
text:
Raster data
A raster is a grid of equal-sized cells laid over the ground. Each cell holds one value per band: elevation in a DEM, reflectance in a satellite image, a land-cover class or a modelled soil property. The cell size sets the resolution, the geotransform ties the grid to map coordinates, and a nodata value marks cells with no measurement. Rasters suit anything that varies continuously over space.

Raster functions in GeoLattice
geolattice.raster reads and writes through GDAL. Most operations take a source path and a destination path, so they work on files of any size without loading them into memory first.

title: Vector Data
text:
Overview
Vector data is one of the two fundamental spatial data models in Geographic Information Science (GIS). It represents the world as a collection of discrete objects, points, lines, and polygons, each carrying both a geometric shape (where it is) and an attribute table (what it is). Unlike raster data, which divides the world into a grid of uniform cells, vector data captures features with crisp boundaries and precise coordinates, making it the natural choice for roads, administrative boundaries, building footprints, water networks, survey points, and countless other real-world entities.
This notebook serves as the entry point for Module 01 of GeoLattice. It explains what vector data is, why it matters, and provides a structured overview of every sub-notebook available in this module.

title: Vector Data
text:
1. What is Vector Data?
Vector data represents geographic features as mathematically defined geometric objects embedded in a coordinate space. Each feature is an individual entity with:

A geometry: one or more coordinate pairs (x, y, and optionally z and m) that define its shape and location.
An attribute record: a row in a table of properties (name, population, land use class, date, etc.) associated with that geometry.


Geometry Types
The Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) Simple Features standard, implemented by virtually every GIS library, defines the following geometry types:








Geometry Type
Description
Real-world examples




Point
A single coordinate pair (x, y)
Weather station, well, tree, city centroid


MultiPoint
A collection of points treated as one feature
ATM locations for a single bank branch


LineString
An ordered sequence of coordinate pairs forming an open path
Road segment, river reach, utility line


MultiLineString
A collection of linestrings as one feature
Complete highway route with multiple segments


Polygon
A closed ring of coordinates enclosing an area, with optional interior holes
Country boundary, lake, land-use parcel


MultiPolygon
A collection of polygons as one feature
Country with islands, archipelago


GeometryCollection
A heterogeneous mix of any geometry types
Complex infrastructure asset





Attributes and the Feature Table
Beyond geometry, each feature carries attributes, tabular data stored alongside the geometry in a format like a database table. Attributes can be integers, floats, strings, dates, or booleans, and they are what make vector data analytically powerful. You can join external tables, compute new fields, filter features by attribute value, and group features to produce summary statistics, all within a GIS environment.


Comparison with Raster Data








Aspect
Vector
Raster




Representation
Discrete objects (points, lines, polygons)
Continuous grid of cells (pixels)


Storage
Coordinate lists + attribute table
Array of values


Precision
Exact boundary coordinates
Resolution-limited


Best for
Features with well-defined boundaries
Continuous phenomena (elevation, temperature)


File size
Scales with feature count
Scales with spatial extent × resolution


Editing
Easy to add, move, delete individual features
Must modify cell values


Analysis
Overlay, network, proximity, geoprocessing
Map algebra, surface analysis, image processing

title: Vector Data
text:
2. Why Vector Data Matters
Vector data underpins a vast range of real-world workflows across every discipline that relies on location:

Urban Planning & Land Use: Cadastral parcels, zoning polygons, road centrelines, and building footprints are all vector datasets that planners use for site analysis, infrastructure design, and zoning enforcement.
Environmental Science: Habitat boundaries, watershed delineations, protected-area polygons, and species-occurrence point records are collected and analysed as vector data.
Public Health: Disease case locations (points), catchment areas of clinics (polygons), and travel routes to facilities (lines) are core to health geography and epidemiology.
Transportation & Logistics: Road, rail, and shipping networks are stored as routable vector line graphs with attributes (speed limit, capacity, travel time).
Agriculture: Field boundaries and irrigation canal networks are vector datasets used in precision agriculture and farm management systems.
Disaster Management: Flood inundation extents, evacuation route lines, and affected-community polygons are produced during emergency response as vector layers.
Business Intelligence: Customer locations, store catchment areas, and territory boundaries are spatial layers that drive retail location analysis and market segmentation.

Python, through GeoPandas, Shapely, Fiona, PyProj, and Matplotlib / Folium / Plotly, has become the dominant open-source stack for vector data work. GeoLattice wraps these libraries behind a consistent, learner-friendly API organised around the workflows covered in this module.

title: Vector Data
text:
3. Core Concepts
Before diving into the notebooks, the following concepts are worth reviewing.

3.1 Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
All vector data has coordinates. Those coordinates are meaningless without a Coordinate Reference System that defines the datum, ellipsoid, and projection used to convert the curved surface of the Earth into a flat (or 3-D) coordinate space.








CRS Type
Description
When to use




Geographic (lon/lat)
Angles in degrees on a reference ellipsoid (e.g., WGS 84 / EPSG:4326)
Data storage, global mapping, GPS exchange


Projected
Metres or feet on a flat surface (e.g., UTM, BTM, US National Atlas)
Distance, area, and buffer calculations


Local / engineering
Arbitrary origin, often in feet (e.g., State Plane)
Engineering surveys, cadastral work




Key rule: Always reproject to a suitable projected CRS before computing distances, areas, or buffers. Using longitude/latitude for these operations gives wrong results because degrees are not a constant unit of distance.



3.2 Common Vector File Formats








Format
Extension
Notes




Shapefile
.shp + sidecar files
Legacy Esri standard; ubiquitous but limited (255-char field names, 2 GB cap, no NULL)


GeoJSON
.geojson
Human-readable, web-native; always uses WGS 84 by spec; not ideal for large datasets


GeoPackage
.gpkg
Modern, single-file SQLite container; supports multiple layers, raster tiles, extensions


FlatGeobuf
.fgb
Cloud-optimised, streamable; ideal for large datasets served over HTTP


GeoParquet
.parquet
Columnar analytics format; best for large-scale joins and aggregations


KML / KMZ
.kml, .kmz
Google Earth format; stores style information alongside geometry


File GDB
.gdb
Esri proprietary geodatabase; readable via GDAL with limitations


CSV + WKT/XY
.csv
Tabular data with coordinates; geometry must be parsed from a column





3.3 The GDAL/OGR Stack
Almost every Python vector library reads and writes data via GDAL/OGR under the hood:
Your code (GeoPandas / Fiona / GeoLattice)
        ↓
    GDAL / OGR
        ↓
  File / database / remote source
  (Shapefile, GeoPackage, PostGIS, S3 GeoParquet, ...)
GeoLattice exposes a higher-level API on top of this stack while keeping the full power of GDAL drivers available.


3.4 The GeoDataFrame
In the Python ecosystem, the central data structure for vector data is the GeoDataFrame (GeoPandas). It extends a Pandas DataFrame with:

A geometry column (Shapely geometry objects).
A .crs attribute storing the Coordinate Reference System.
Spatial methods: .to_crs(), .buffer(), .sjoin(), .dissolve(), .plot(), and more.

All GeoLattice vector functions accept and return GeoDataFrames, making them fully interoperable with the broader GeoPandas/Pandas ecosystem.

title: Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
text:
Overview
This tutorial covers coordinate reference systems (CRS) for vector data: what a geographic and a projected CRS are, how common projections are defined, and how to assign and reproject layers with geolattice.vector.vector_CRS.
Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS) are used in cartography, geography, and GIS (Geographic Information Systems) to define the positions of points, lines, and areas on the Earth’s surface. A CRS provides a framework for translating geographic locations, which are expressed as latitude and longitude or other coordinate values, into a specific location on a map or a two-dimensional plane.
There are two main types of Coordinate Reference Systems:

Geographic Coordinate Systems (GCS): Geographic Coordinate Systems use latitude and longitude to define locations on the Earth’s surface. Latitude measures the north-south position, while longitude measures the east-west position. The coordinates are expressed in degrees, minutes, and seconds or decimal degrees. Common GCS examples include WGS 84 (World Geodetic System 1984) and NAD83 (North American Datum 1983).
Projected Coordinate Systems (PCS): Projected Coordinate Systems use Cartesian coordinates (X, Y) to represent locations on a flat, two-dimensional map. The projection converts the three-dimensional geographic coordinates (latitude, longitude, and often elevation) into these two-dimensional coordinates. Different map projections, such as Mercator, Robinson, or UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator), create projected coordinate systems.

Source: Esri, Coordinate systems and projections

The equidistant lines that run east and west each have a constant latitude value called parallels. The equator is the largest circle and divides the earth in half. It is equal in distance from each of the poles, and the value of this latitude line is zero. Locations north of the equator have positive latitudes that range from 0 to +90 degrees, while locations south of the equator have negative latitudes that range from 0 to -90 degrees.

The lines that run through north and south each have a constant longitude value and form circles of the same size around the earth known as meridians. The prime meridian is the line of longitude that defines the origin (zero degrees) for longitude coordinates. One of the most commonly used prime meridian locations is the line that passes through Greenwich, England. Locations east of the prime meridian up to its antipodal meridian (the continuation of the prime meridian on the other side of the globe) have positive longitudes ranging from 0 to +180 degrees. Locations west of the prime meridian have negative longitudes ranging from 0 to -180 degrees.

The latitude and longitude lines cover the globe to form a grid known as a graticule. The point of origin of the graticule is (0, 0), where the equator and the prime meridian intersect. The equator is the only place on the graticule where the linear distance corresponding to one degree of latitude is approximately equal to the distance corresponding to one degree of longitude. Because the longitude lines converge at the poles, the distance between two meridians is different at every parallel.
To maintain accuracy in GIS and cartographic applications, it is essential to use the appropriate coordinate reference system and datum for the specific region or project. Choosing the wrong CRS can lead to distortions and inaccuracies when transforming between geographic locations and map coordinates.
CRS is a fundamental aspect of spatial data management, as they allow for the integration of different data sources, analysis, and visualization of geographic information consistently and meaningfully. Understanding CRS is crucial for cartographers, GIS analysts, and anyone working with geographic data to ensure accurate spatial representation and analysis.
The notebook is organized in three parts:

CRS concepts: map projections, WGS 84, UTM, PROJ strings, and Albers Equal Area Conic.
Bangladesh districts: assign WGS 84 to a shapefile with no .prj, then project to Bangladesh Transverse Mercator.
New York counties: reproject a WGS 84 county layer to North America Albers (ESRI:102008).

Sample shapefiles live in Data/00_shared/vector_data/Bangladesh/Shapefiles and Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA. Written outputs land in Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder under bangladesh and ny_county.

title: Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
text:
Part 1: Coordinate reference systems
The cells below define common geographic and projected CRS values with define_crs, print their parameters, and show the PROJ strings used later when layers are assigned or reprojected.

Map projection
Map projection is a method used to represent the three-dimensional surface of the Earth on a two-dimensional map. Since the Earth is a spherical object, it is challenging to depict its curved surface accurately on a flat surface. This problem arises because representing the entire curved surface of the Earth on a flat map results in distortions in shape, size, distance, or direction.

Various map projections are available, each designed to address different needs and minimize certain types of distortion. Here are some common types of map projections:
Mercator projection. Developed by Gerardus Mercator in the 16th century, this projection preserves straight lines, making it useful for marine navigation. However, it distorts the sizes of landmasses, with areas near the poles appearing significantly larger than they are.
Robinson projection. This compromise projection attempts to balance size, shape, and distance distortions across the entire map. It is commonly used for world maps.
Conic projection. This projection involves projecting the Earth’s surface onto a cone and then unrolling the cone to form a flat map. It preserves shapes and distances well within the cone area but can have significant distortions as one moves away from that central area.
Cylindrical projection. This projection wraps the Earth’s surface around a cylinder. Examples include the Mercator projection mentioned earlier and the Miller projection, which preserves relative size but distorts shapes.
Azimuthal projection. These projections project the Earth’s surface onto a plane from a specific point on the Earth’s surface. They preserve directionality but can have considerable distortions in other aspects.
Goode’s Homolosine projection. This projection combines the sinusoidal and Mollweide projections to reduce landmass size distortion, although it sacrifices shape accuracy.
The choice of map projection depends on the intended use of the map, the area being represented, and the extent to which certain distortions are acceptable. No single projection can perfectly represent the entire Earth without any distortions, and mapmakers must make trade-offs based on their specific needs.
It is important to understand that map projections are just one aspect of cartography, and producing accurate and valuable maps often involves other techniques, such as generalization, symbolization, and labeling.
Map projections (LizardTech University)


The World Geodetic System 84
The World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS 84) is a global geodetic reference system developed and maintained by the United States Department of Defense (DoD). It is widely used as the standard coordinate reference system for the Earth’s surface in various applications, including mapping, navigation, surveying, and GPS (Global Positioning System).
WGS 84 is an Earth-centered, Earth-fixed coordinate system known as a geocentric coordinate system. It defines a three-dimensional model of the Earth, where the center of the Earth serves as the origin, and the X, Y, and Z axes are oriented with respect to the Earth’s rotation and equator.
The key features of WGS 84 include:

Ellipsoid: WGS 84 uses the WGS 84 ellipsoid, a mathematically defined surface approximating the shape of the Earth. It is an oblate spheroid, slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator.
Datum: WGS 84 defines a specific datum, which includes the ellipsoid’s size, shape, and orientation in relation to the Earth’s center. The datum is a reference frame for measuring positions on the Earth’s surface.
Coordinate units: WGS 84 uses degrees of latitude and longitude to express geographic positions. Latitude measures the north-south position, and longitude measures the east-west position.
GPS reference frame: WGS 84 is the coordinate system used by the Global Positioning System (GPS). GPS receivers use WGS 84 to accurately determine the user’s position on the Earth’s surface.
Constantly updated: The WGS 84 reference frame is continuously refined and updated to account for crustal movements, which can affect the Earth’s shape and position. As such, newer versions of WGS 84 have been released, with slight adjustments to improve accuracy.

The adoption of WGS 84 as a global standard has been instrumental in enabling accurate navigation, mapping, and geospatial data exchange across the world. It ensures consistency and interoperability among different mapping and navigation systems, making it possible to integrate data from various sources into a coherent spatial framework.


The parameters of WGS 84
WGS 84 is EPSG:4326. define_crs(4326) (from vector_CRS) loads and validates that definition. spatial_reference.pretty_wkt writes the same WKT the notes list: the WGS 84 datum, the WGS 84 spheroid (semi-major axis 6378137 m, inverse flattening 298.257223563), the Greenwich prime meridian, and the degree unit.


Code
# Define WGS 84 from EPSG:4326 and print a short summary plus pretty WKT.
wgs84 = define_crs(4326)  # EPSG:4326 = WGS 84 geographic lon/lat
show_crs(wgs84)  # print name, EPSG, PROJ, and area of use
print()  # blank line before the WKT block
print(wgs84.spatial_reference.pretty_wkt)  # indented WKT from the GDAL spatial ref

Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM)
The Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) is a widely used map projection and coordinate reference system that divides the Earth’s surface into a series of zones, each with its own unique coordinate system. It is designed to minimize distortion within each zone, making it suitable for accurate mapping and navigation in relatively small areas.
The UTM projection is a type of cylindrical projection that projects the Earth’s surface onto a cylinder. The cylinder is then unwrapped to create a flat map. The key features of the UTM system include:

Zone system: The Earth is divided into 60 longitudinal zones, each spanning 6 degrees of longitude. Each zone is 6 degrees wide, except for zones 1 and 60 around the poles, which are narrower to account for the convergence of meridians. Zones are numbered from 1 to 60, starting at the 180° meridian and progressing eastward.
Transverse projection: Unlike the Mercator projection, which is based on a standard parallel, the UTM projection is transverse, meaning that the cylinder is oriented along the meridians rather than the equator. This results in better accuracy for regions closer to the equator.
Cartesian coordinates: Each UTM zone’s positions are expressed in a Cartesian coordinate system with X and Y values. The X-coordinate represents easting (measured in meters) from the central meridian of the zone, and the Y-coordinate represents northing (also measured in meters) from the equator. The origin of each zone is set at the equator and the central meridian of the zone, providing a local reference system.
False easting and northing: To ensure that all coordinates within a zone are positive, a false easting value (500,000 meters) is added to all X-coordinates, and a false northing value is added to all Y-coordinates. This creates a smooth coordinate system without negative values, simplifying calculations.
Scale factor: UTM uses a varying scale factor along the central meridian of each zone to further minimize distortion. The scale factor is set to 0.9996, meaning that distances measured on the map are slightly shorter than the actual distances on the Earth’s surface.


Bangladesh falls in zone 45N (EPSG:32645) and zone 46N (EPSG:32646) on WGS 84.
The UTM grid that covers the conterminous 48 United States comprises 10 zones, from Zone 10 on the west coast through Zone 19 in New England (USGS, 2001). New York State falls in zones 17N (EPSG:26917) and 18N (EPSG:26918) on the North American Datum 1983 (NAD83). Part 2 uses the Bangladesh Transverse Mercator for the district layer. Part 3 reprojects the New York county layer to Albers Equal Area Conic.

UTM is widely used in various applications, including topographic mapping, GPS navigation, military operations, and geospatial data analysis. It is particularly useful for local mapping tasks, covering areas up to a few thousand kilometers in extent, where the distortion is generally kept within acceptable limits. However, it may not be suitable for global maps or large-scale mapping that requires extremely precise measurements over very large areas.

Projection format
The PROJ string (often called PROJ.4) is a widely used way of defining the projection and coordinate system parameters for geospatial data. It is employed in many geospatial software libraries and applications to specify how to transform coordinates from one coordinate system to another, or to perform various geospatial operations accurately.
The format consists of a set of parameters, where each parameter represents a specific aspect of the coordinate system or projection. It is typically represented as a single string with key-value pairs:

+proj=<projection> +datum=<datum> +units=<units> +<other_parameters>


+proj: the projection method or algorithm used to transform coordinates. For example, +proj=utm for Universal Transverse Mercator, or +proj=longlat for the WGS 84 geographic coordinate system.
+datum: the geodetic datum used for the coordinate system. It determines the position of the coordinate system relative to the Earth’s ellipsoid. Examples include +datum=WGS84 or +datum=NAD83. In general +datum= is preferred to +ellps=, because the datum always fixes the ellipsoid, but the ellipsoid never fixes the datum.
+units: the units of measurement used in the coordinate system. Common examples include +units=m or degrees for a geographic CRS.
Other parameters: false eastings and northings, the central meridian, the scale factor, and similar values that the projection needs.

The notes give these PROJ strings for WGS 84 Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) and for UTM zones 45 and 46:

+proj=merc +datum=WGS84 +units=meters +no_defs


+proj=utm +zone=45 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs +type=crs


+proj=utm +zone=46 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs +type=crs

CRS.proj prints the string stored in the PROJ database for each of those codes. define_crs builds a CRS from a string of this form.

    print(f"  {crs.proj}")  # indented PROJ definition string

Albers Equal Area Conic
Albers Equal Area Conic uses two standard parallels to reduce the distortion of shape in the region between those parallels. This projection is best suited for an area that extends east to west, such as the conterminous United States. Used for the conterminous United States, the two standard parallels are normally 29.5°N and 45.5°N. For this projection, the maximum scale distortion for the 48 states is 1.25 percent.

The contiguous-USA definition is ESRI:102003. Its PROJ string is:

+proj=aea +lat_1=29.5 +lat_2=45.5 +lat_0=37.5 +lon_0=-96 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs

Part 3 uses the North America Albers definition stored in NY_County_PROJ.prj, ESRI:102008. The standard parallels are 20°N and 60°N, the latitude of origin is 40°N, and the central meridian is 96°W:

+proj=aea +lat_1=20 +lat_2=60 +lat_0=40 +lon_0=-96 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs

Part 2: Bangladesh
This exercise checks, defines, and changes the CRS of vector data. That step matters whenever layers from different sources do not share a projection.

This part uses the district polygons of Bangladesh, bd_district.shp, in Data/00_shared/vector_data/Bangladesh/Shapefiles. That shapefile has no .prj.
Part 3 uses the New York State county polygons, NY_County_GCS.shp, in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA. That shapefile already carries a WGS 84 .prj, and the task is to reproject it. NY_County_PROJ.shp in the same folder is the counties already stored in North America Albers.

read_vector_data opens bd_district.shp and returns a dataset. The active layer reports the feature count, geometry type, extent, and CRS. to_dataframe() returns a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame.


Code
# Open Bangladesh districts, inspect CRS metadata, and preview attributes.
district_path = BD_SHP / "bd_district.shp"  # path to the district polygon shapefile
print(f"shapefile:  {district_path.name}")  # basename only for a short print
print(f".prj file:  {district_path.with_suffix('.prj').exists()}")  # True if .prj exists

# Open with the GeoLattice reader context manager (closes the dataset on exit).
with read_vector_data(district_path) as dataset:
    print(f"driver:     {dataset.driver}")  # OGR driver name (usually ESRI Shapefile)
    print(f"features:   {dataset.feature_count}")  # number of district polygons
    print(f"geometry:   {dataset.layer.geometry_type}")  # geometry type string
    print(f"bounds:     {dataset.bounds}")  # layer extent (minx, miny, maxx, maxy)
    show_crs(dataset.crs)  # CRS summary from the layer
    districts = dataset.to_dataframe()  # GeoDataFrame of all district features

# Preview admin names for the first few districts.
display(districts[["ADM2_EN", "ADM1_EN", "ADM0_EN"]].head())

Define the CRS
define_crs / validate_crs build a CRS from an EPSG code or PROJ string. Assigning that CRS with GeoPandas set_crs records which CRS the coordinates are already in: it leaves the coordinate numbers unchanged. Either definition below is WGS 84. define_crs(4326) is the authority code. define_crs("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84") is the PROJ string. +datum=WGS84 is used here so the datum, and therefore the ellipsoid, is stored with the layer.


Code
# Assign a validated WGS 84 CRS to the districts table and verify equality.
wgs84 = validate_crs(4326)  # normalize EPSG:4326 into the shared CRS type
# wgs84 = define_crs("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84")  # alternate PROJ-string form

# Attach EPSG:4326 to the GeoDataFrame (coordinates are already lon/lat).
districts_gcs = districts.set_crs(wgs84.to_epsg())
show_crs(wgs84)  # print the validated WGS 84 summary
print()  # blank line before the frame CRS print
print(districts_gcs.crs)  # CRS now stored on the GeoDataFrame
# Confirm the frame CRS matches EPSG:4326 via crs_equal().
print("crs_equal(layer, EPSG:4326):", crs_equal(districts_gcs.crs, 4326))

Projection
reproject_vector transforms coordinates from the CRS on the layer to another CRS. That is the conversion between projections (reprojection). For a simple projection, when no datum change is required, the coordinates are projected on the same datum. When a datum transformation is required, both the source CRS and the target CRS need a datum. Pass datum_operation= to pick a named path from choose_datum_transformation when several paths exist.
The target in the notes is the Bangladesh Transverse Mercator. The notes cite EPSG:9677. This PROJ database publishes Gulshan 303 / Bangladesh Transverse Mercator as EPSG:9678, on the Everest 1830 ellipsoid. The exercise uses the PROJ string from the notes, which keeps the WGS 84 datum:

+proj=tmerc +lat_0=0 +lon_0=90 +k=0.9996 +x_0=500000 +y_0=-2000000 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs

define_crs builds that CRS. reproject_vector then converts the district polygons from degrees to meters. The projected layer reports projected: True.


Code
# Build Bangladesh Transverse Mercator from a PROJ string, compare to EPSG:9678,
# reproject the GCS districts, and print extent changes in degrees vs meters.
btm = define_crs(
    # Custom BTM PROJ string from the tutorial notes (transverse Mercator).
    "+proj=tmerc +lat_0=0 +lon_0=90 +k=0.9996 "
    # Assign "+x_0.
    "+x_0=500000 +y_0=-2000000 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs"
)  # close this call
print("Target CRS from the notes")  # label for the custom BTM definition
show_crs(btm)  # summarize the PROJ-string BTM
print()  # blank line before the EPSG:9678 comparison
print("EPSG:9678  Gulshan 303 / Bangladesh Transverse Mercator")  # official name
show_crs(define_crs(9678))  # summarize the EPSG registry entry

# Reproject district polygons from WGS 84 lon/lat into BTM meters.
districts_btm = reproject_vector(districts_gcs, btm)
print()  # blank line before bounds comparison
print("WGS 84 bounds (degrees):", districts_gcs.total_bounds)  # lon/lat extent
print("BTM bounds (meters):    ", districts_btm.total_bounds)  # projected extent
print()  # blank line before CRS summary
show_crs(districts_btm.crs)  # CRS attached to the reprojected frame

title: Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
text:
Summary
A coordinate reference system locates features on the Earth. A geographic CRS, such as WGS 84 (EPSG:4326), records longitude and latitude in degrees. A projected CRS records easting and northing in meters on a flat map. UTM does that inside 6-degree zones: Bangladesh falls in zones 45N and 46N (EPSG:32645 and EPSG:32646), and New York falls in zones 17N and 18N (EPSG:26917 and EPSG:26918). Albers Equal Area Conic is the east-west alternative used for the United States, as ESRI:102003 for the conterminous states and ESRI:102008 for North America.
geolattice.crs holds the shared CRS catalog. geolattice.vector.vector_CRS is the vector side: define_crs / validate_crs load a definition, is_geographic / crs_equal inspect it, and reproject_vector calculates new coordinates in a target CRS. Assigning a CRS without moving coordinates (for a layer that already uses those values) still uses GeoPandas set_crs after define_crs.
The two exercises use those steps on layers that arrive in different states.

Part 2. bd_district.shp has no .prj, so the 64 district polygons open with an undefined CRS. The coordinates are degrees, about 88.01°E-92.68°E and 20.59°N-26.63°N. Assigning EPSG:4326 names that geographic CRS, and writing bd_district_GCS.shp stores it in a .prj. Projecting to the Bangladesh Transverse Mercator (+proj=tmerc +lat_0=0 +lon_0=90 +k=0.9996 +x_0=500000 +y_0=-2000000 +datum=WGS84 +units=m) converts those degrees to meters. The current authority name for Gulshan 303 / Bangladesh Transverse Mercator is EPSG:9678, on the Everest 1830 ellipsoid. The exercise keeps the WGS 84 form of the same projection parameters. The projected copy is Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder/bangladesh/bd_district_BTM.shp.
Part 3. NY_County_GCS.shp already carries a WGS 84 .prj. The 83 counties span about -79.76° to -71.86° and 40.50° to 45.01°, and projected is false because the coordinates are still degrees. Reprojecting to North America Albers (ESRI:102008) puts them in meters. That definition matches Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/NY_County_PROJ.prj. The new copy is Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder/ny_county/NY_County_PROJ.shp.

The side-by-side maps show the same boundaries before and after projection: degrees on the left, meters on the right. The shape of each map changes with the projection, and the coordinate numbers change units. Check the CRS before measuring distance or area, before overlaying layers, and before writing a file that other software will read. A missing .prj leaves the CRS undefined. A geographic CRS is the right record for longitude and latitude. A projected CRS such as UTM, the Bangladesh Transverse Mercator, or Albers is the right record when the map needs meters.

Further reading

Using map projections
Map projections in R
Variations on map projections in R
PROJ and pyproj, which supply the definitions geolattice.crs and vector_CRS use
SpatialReference.org for the WKT, PROJ, and PROJJSON forms of an authority code
geolattice.vector.vector_CRS for define / validate / reproject on vector layers, and geolattice.raster.raster_CRS for GDAL warp on rasters

title: Geoprocessing
text:
Overview
Geo-processing is a GIS operation used to manipulate spatial data. This tutorial covers the common desktop geoprocessing tools for vector layers with GeoLattice, which uses GeoPandas and Shapely.
Shapefiles are opened with open_vectors_data(). Maps use plot_layer(), plot_pair(), and style_axes() from geolattice.viz. The geoprocessing tools are:







Operation
Function




Select features from the attribute table
filter the GeoDataFrame


Clip
clip()


Intersect
intersect()


Union
union(), or a row bind when many files share one attribute table


Dissolve
dissolve()


Erase
erase()


Convex hull
convex_hull()


Buffer
buffer()



The notebook is organized in three parts:

Load and inspect data: US states, counties, soil samples, streets, and the Yellowstone boundary.
Overlay tools: clip, union, dissolve, intersect, and erase.
Geometry construction: convex hull and buffer on polygons, lines, and points.

Sample files live in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA. Written outputs land in Data/00_shared/vector_data/output_folder.

text:
Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, applies the tutorial map style, and defines read_layer for shapefiles under Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA.
Geoprocessing calls use clip, union, dissolve, intersect, erase, convex_hull, and buffer from geolattice.vector. Maps use plot_layer, plot_pair, and style_axes from geolattice.viz.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library: path search on sys.path and temporary output folders.
import sys  # mutate sys.path so geolattice can be imported from the repo root
import tempfile  # create a throwaway folder for written shapefiles
import warnings  # available if a cell needs to silence noisy library warnings
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for data and image folders

# Third-party GIS / data / plotting stack used throughout the notebook.
import geopandas as gpd  # GeoDataFrame constructors and CRS handling
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for custom maps
import numpy as np  # numeric arrays for hull coordinates
import pandas as pd  # tabular display options and concat for row-binding layers
from IPython.display import display  # rich table previews in the notebook
from scipy.spatial import ConvexHull  # vertex order for a convex envelope of points





Code
# ===================================================================
# Setup and helpers for geoprocessing and maps.
# Walk up from the working directory to the repo root, import GeoLattice tools,
# point DATA/IMAGES at the sample folders, and define read_layer().
# ===================================================================

# Resolve the current working directory to an absolute Path.
ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve()
while not (ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data").is_dir():
    if ROOT.parent == ROOT:
        raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find Data/00_shared/vector_data from the working directory.")
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

# Geoprocessing helpers exported from geolattice.vector.
from geolattice.vector import (
    buffer,  # distance buffer around features
    clip,  # cookie-cut overlay that keeps attributes of the input layer
    convex_hull,  # smallest convex polygon containing points
    dissolve,  # aggregate geometries that share a group key
    erase,  # remove the part of a layer that falls inside another polygon
    intersect,  # keep overlapping pairs and attributes from both layers
    open_vectors_data,  # open a shapefile (or other vector source) as a dataset
    union,  # overlay union of two layers
)
# Shared map styling helpers from geolattice.viz.
from geolattice.viz import EDGE, FACE, apply_map_style, plot_layer, plot_pair, style_axes

# Sample vector data for this tutorial (US states, counties, etc.).
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA"
# Banner and figure assets under the repository Images folder.
IMAGES = ROOT / "Images"
# Fail early if the expected folders are missing.
assert DATA.is_dir(), DATA
assert IMAGES.is_dir(), IMAGES  # assert this folder exists

# Keep printed attribute tables readable in the notebook.
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 12)  # show up to 12 columns
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 48)  # truncate long string cells
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)  # wider console wrapping for tables

# Apply the shared GeoLattice map style (fonts, colors, spines).
apply_map_style()


# helper: open one shapefile under DATA as a GeoDataFrame
def read_layer(relative):
    # short description of what read_layer returns
    """Open one shapefile and return a GeoDataFrame without the reader fid."""
    # Build an absolute path under DATA from a relative shapefile path.
    path = DATA / relative
    # Open the vector dataset and convert it to a pandas/GeoPandas table.
    with open_vectors_data(path) as dataset:
        frame = dataset.to_dataframe()  # attribute table plus geometry column
        crs = frame.crs  # coordinate reference system of the layer
    # Drop the driver-added fid column when present so demos stay tidy.
    if "fid" in frame.columns:
        frame = frame.drop(columns="fid")  # remove the driver-added fid column
    # Rebuild an explicit GeoDataFrame with the preserved CRS.
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(frame, geometry="geometry", crs=crs)

Part 2: Overlay tools

Clipping
Clipping spatial data is a basic GIS task. For vector data, it involves removing unwanted features outside of an area of interest. For example, you might want to do some geospatial modeling covering an area in New York state, but we may have data for the USA. In this case you need to apply a clipping function to remove the area outside of New York State. It acts like a cookie cutter to cut out a piece of one feature class using one or more of the features in another feature class.




Clipping

You can do this several ways. In this exercise, we will clip out other states or counties from the US State and County polygon shape files, except our area of interest (for example New York).
The most direct way to select an area of interest from the attribute table is a filter on the STATE field.

Union
Union combines two or more spatial objects and creates new features where the geometry and attributes of the input features are retained.




Union

We will use the state boundaries of Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wyoming. The shapefiles of these states are in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/GP_STATE.

Shared field names get _1 and _2 suffixes. These four states meet along borders rather than overlapping, so each state comes back as its own polygon. A shared border is a line, and keep_geom_type=True drops that line.

Dissolve
Dissolve aggregates features based on an attribute. It is a tool used regularly in spatial data processing.




Dissolve

One way to dissolve every polygon is to give them the same group. Cutting the centroid x coordinate across its full range makes a single bin, so every state is dissolved together.
dissolve() aggregates by one or more fields and unions the geometries in each group. With no by argument it dissolves the whole layer.


Code
# Dissolve all four states by putting every feature into one centroid-x bin.
centroids = gp_state.geometry.centroid  # one centroid point per state polygon
gp_binned = gp_state.copy()  # work on a copy so the original layer stays intact
# Cut centroid eastings into a single bin spanning min..max x.
gp_binned["bin"] = pd.cut(
    centroids.x,  # values to bin: centroid X coordinates
    bins=[centroids.x.min(), centroids.x.max()],  # one interval covering the range
    include_lowest=True,  # include the left edge so the min falls in the bin
)
# Dissolve geometries that share the same bin label.
gp_dissolve_01 = dissolve(gp_binned, by="bin")
print(f"Groups: {len(gp_dissolve_01)}")  # print a short status line
# Map the single dissolved outline.
plot_layer(gp_dissolve_01, "Dissolved state boundary")

# Dissolve the whole layer with no group key (one output feature).

# Map the fully dissolved boundary.
plot_layer(gp_dissolve_02, "Dissolved state boundary - dissolve()")

title: Geoprocessing
text:
Part 3: Geometry construction

Convex hull
The convex hull, also called the convex envelope or convex closure, is the smallest convex polygon that contains a set of points.
Read the point shapefile, take the coordinates, and close the hull by repeating the first vertex. scipy.spatial.ConvexHull returns that vertex list. convex_hull(..., as_one=True) builds the same polygon from the whole point layer.


Code
# Build a convex hull around Colorado soil-sample points two ways.
points = read_layer("CO_SOC_data.shp")  # soil sample point locations
print(f"Soil sample points: {len(points)}")
# Preview a few attribute columns.
display(points[["ID", "STATE", "COUNTY", "SOC"]].head())

# Stack X/Y coordinates into an (n, 2) array for SciPy.
xy = np.column_stack([points.geometry.x, points.geometry.y])
# Vertex indices of the convex hull in counterclockwise order.
hull_index = ConvexHull(xy).vertices
# Close the ring by appending the first hull vertex again for plotting.
coords = xy[np.append(hull_index, hull_index[0])]
# Same hull as a one-feature GeoDataFrame via geolattice.vector.convex_hull.
hull_layer = convex_hull(points, as_one=True)  # one polygon for the whole layer
# Report the hull area in square metres (CRS units).
print(f"Hull area from convex_hull(): {hull_layer.geometry.iloc[0].area:,.0f} square metres")

Buffer
Buffering creates an envelope of space around selected features in vector data. It is sometimes called a zone of a specified distance around a polygon, line, or point feature. Buffering is often used for proximity analysis. In this section we create a 100 m buffer around a piece of the Onondaga County road network and a 20 km buffer around the Colorado soil-sample points. Distance is in the units of the layer coordinates. These layers are in a metre-based Albers projection, so 100 means 100 metres.

title: Geoprocessing
text:
Summary
This exercise applied the main vector geoprocessing operations to US states and counties, the Yellowstone boundary, Colorado soil-sample points, and a piece of the Onondaga County road network.








Operation
What it does
Example in this notebook




Attribute filter
Keeps features whose attributes match a condition, with geometry and attributes unchanged
Counties whose STATE is New York


Clip
Cuts features to a mask, like a cookie cutter, and keeps the attribute table of the layer being cut
US counties cut to the New York boundary


Intersect
Keeps each overlapping pair and the attributes of both layers. Shared field names receive _1 and _2
States that overlap Yellowstone National Park


Union
Builds the overlay of two layers: the overlap, plus the part unique to each input
Colorado joined with Kansas


Row bind
Stacks layers that share one attribute table into a single layer
pandas.concat of the four state shapefiles


Dissolve
Unions geometries that share a group. With no by argument, the whole layer becomes one feature
The four states dissolved into one polygon


Erase
Removes the part of a layer that falls inside another polygon
Kansas removed from the four-state layer


Convex hull
Builds the smallest convex polygon that contains a set of points
Hull around the Colorado soil-sample points


Buffer
Builds a zone of a given distance around each feature. dissolve=True merges those zones
100 m around streets and 20 km around sample points



keep_geom_type=True drops points and lines created where polygons only touch along a border. Buffer distance is in the units of the layer coordinates. These layers use a metre-based Albers projection, so 100 is 100 metres and 20 * 1000 is 20 kilometres.
Clipping, union, dissolve, intersect, erase, convex hull, and buffer cover the usual questions asked of vector data: which features fall in an area, how layers combine, which features share an attribute, where two layers overlap, what remains after one area is removed, what polygon encloses a set of points, and what lies within a set distance.
The same functions work on polygons, lines, and points. Read each shapefile with open_vectors_data(), then pass the resulting layer to clip(), union(), dissolve(), intersect(), erase(), convex_hull(), or buffer(). Check that both layers share a projected coordinate reference system before measuring a buffer or comparing areas, because the distance and the area are expressed in the units of that system.

Further reading
GeoLattice

open_vectors_data() reads the shapefiles in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA.
clip(), union(), dissolve(), intersect(), erase(), convex_hull(), and buffer() are in geolattice.vector.

Libraries used by those functions

GeoPandas: GeoDataFrames, plotting, and overlay operations. See the set-operations guide.
Shapely: geometry predicates and constructors (intersection, union, difference, buffer, convex_hull).
pandas: attribute filters and concat for binding layers that share one table.
SciPy ConvexHull: vertex order of the convex hull drawn around the soil-sample points.
Matplotlib: the maps in this notebook.

Data

State, county, park, point, and street shapefiles are in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA. The four state boundaries are in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/GP_STATE.
The Yellowstone National Park boundary is published by the National Park Service on Data.gov.

title: Raster Data
text:
What is Raster Data?
Raster data divides a geographic area into a regular grid of equal-sized rectangular cells. Every cell (also called a pixel) stores one numeric value per band. The position of a cell in space is defined by:

The origin of the grid (the top-left or bottom-left corner coordinate).
The cell size (spatial resolution): how many metres, degrees, or other units each cell represents on the ground.
The number of rows and columns: the grid dimensions.
A Coordinate Reference System (CRS): the coordinate frame that anchors the grid to the Earth.

Together these four properties define the geotransform that maps any cell’s row/column index to real-world coordinates.

Raster vs. Vector








Aspect
Raster
Vector




Representation
Regular grid of cells
Discrete objects (points, lines, polygons)


Best for
Continuous phenomena (elevation, temperature)
Features with crisp boundaries (roads, parcels)


Storage
Array of values; size grows with extent times resolution
Coordinate lists + attribute table; size grows with feature count


Precision
Resolution-limited
Exact boundary coordinates


Analysis
Map algebra, surface analysis, image processing
Overlay, network, proximity, geoprocessing


Editing
Modify cell values
Add, move, delete individual features





Bands
A raster can contain multiple bands: layers within the same grid extent and resolution, each storing a different variable or spectral channel. Common examples:







Dataset
Bands




Grayscale DEM
1 (elevation)


RGB image
3 (Red, Green, Blue)


Landsat 8
11 (spectral bands from Coastal Aerosol to Thermal)


Sentinel-2
12 (spectral bands, 10-60 m resolution)


MODIS daily land surface temp
2 (Day LST + Night LST)


ERA5 NetCDF
Many (temperature, precipitation, wind, and related fields across time steps)





Cell Data Types
Raster cells store values using standard numeric data types inherited from GDAL and NumPy:









GDAL type
NumPy dtype
Range
Typical use




Byte
uint8
0-255
Classified land cover, RGB imagery


UInt16
uint16
0-65 535
Satellite reflectance (scaled), population counts


Int16
int16
-32 768 to 32 767
Signed elevation (metres), temperature (scaled)


Int32
int32
about +/- 2.1e9
Large integer IDs


Float32
float32
about +/- 3.4e38
Most derived analysis products (slope, NDVI, precipitation)


Float64
float64
about +/- 1.8e308
High-precision scientific data





NoData
Raster files carry a NoData sentinel value: a special number (for example, -9999 or 255) that marks cells where data is absent (outside the study area, cloud-masked, or sensor fill). Functions in GeoLattice always mask NoData values before analysis and propagate the mask through operations.

title: Raster Data
text:
Why Raster Data Matters
Raster data is the backbone of Earth observation and environmental modelling:

Elevation Modelling: Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) are the foundational raster dataset for terrain analysis, hydrology, visibility, and engineering design. Global products include SRTM (90 m), NASADEM (30 m), CopDEM (30 m), and USGS 3DEP (1 m).
Remote Sensing and Satellite Imagery: Multispectral and hyperspectral images from Landsat, Sentinel, MODIS, and commercial satellites are rasters. They underpin land-cover mapping, vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI), water quality monitoring, and change detection.
Climate and Weather Data: Gridded products such as ERA5 reanalysis, CHIRPS rainfall, and CMIP6 projections are rasters with time, latitude, and longitude dimensions: the foundation of climate science and agriculture modelling.
Environmental Risk Mapping: Flood inundation models, wildfire risk surfaces, earthquake ground-shaking maps, and air-quality rasters are used directly in disaster management and insurance.
Urban Remote Sensing: High-resolution LiDAR point clouds (COPC rasters), building height models, and land surface temperature products feed urban heat island, solar potential, and noise modelling studies.
Precision Agriculture: Crop stress indices, yield maps, and soil moisture rasters are central to variable-rate fertilisation and irrigation management.
Public Health and Epidemiology: Population density grids (WorldPop, LandScan), malaria risk surfaces, and air-pollution rasters are used to model exposure and access to services.

Python, through GDAL, Rasterio, NumPy, xarray, and Matplotlib / Cartopy, is the dominant open-source stack for raster data processing. GeoLattice wraps these libraries behind a consistent, learner-friendly API organised around the workflows covered in this module.

title: Raster Data
text:
Core Concepts
Before diving into the notebooks, the following concepts are essential.

Spatial Resolution
Spatial resolution is the ground dimension of a single cell. A 30 m DEM means each pixel represents a 30 m by 30 m patch of ground. Choosing the right resolution involves a trade-off:









Resolution
File size
Level of detail
Typical products




< 1 m
Very large
Building-level features
LiDAR derivatives, drone imagery


10-30 m
Large
Field / block scale
Sentinel-2, Landsat, NASADEM, SRTM


90-250 m
Moderate
Catchment / district scale
SRTM 90 m, MODIS land products


0.25 deg to 1 deg
Small
Regional / continental scale
ERA5 climate, global precipitation




Rule: Always match raster resolution to your analysis scale. Resampling to a finer resolution does not add real information (it only interpolates).



Extent and Geotransform
The spatial extent (bounding box) of a raster is defined by: - xmin, xmax: left and right edges - ymin, ymax: bottom and top edges
The GDAL geotransform is a 6-element tuple (x_origin, x_pixel_size, x_rotation, y_origin, y_rotation, y_pixel_size) that fully encodes the spatial registration. For north-up rasters the rotation terms are 0 and y_pixel_size is negative.


Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS) for Rasters
Like vector data, every raster must carry a CRS. GDAL stores it internally as Well-Known Text (WKT2). Key rules:

Use a geographic CRS (lon/lat) for global datasets and data exchange.
Use a projected CRS (metres) for distance, area, slope, and any analysis where cell size must be constant.
Changing a raster’s CRS requires reprojection: resampling the pixel grid into the new coordinate space. This is computationally intensive and slightly lossy; do it once, early in the workflow.



Resampling Methods
When a raster is reprojected or resized, cell values must be redistributed into the new grid. The resampling algorithm determines how:







Method
When to use




Nearest Neighbour
Categorical / classified data (preserves original class values)


Bilinear
Continuous numeric data (smooth interpolation between 4 neighbours)


Cubic / Cubic Spline
Smooth continuous data; reduces aliasing at cost of speed


Average
Aggregating to a coarser resolution (mean of contributing cells)


Mode
Categorical downsampling (most frequent class in contributing cells)


Lanczos
High-quality downsampling of imagery





Common Raster File Formats








Format
Extension
Notes




GeoTIFF
.tif, .tiff
The universal standard; supports multiple bands, CRS, NoData, compression


Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF
.tif
GeoTIFF with internal tiling and overviews for HTTP range requests


NetCDF
.nc
Self-describing array format; used for climate, oceanographic, and time-series data


HDF5
.h5, .hdf5
Hierarchical format; used for MODIS, VIIRS, and other NASA products


Zarr
.zarr
Cloud-native chunked array store; used with xarray for large data cubes


ESRI ASCII Grid
.asc
Plain-text grid; portable but large and slow


Erdas Imagine
.img
Esri legacy format; still common in older datasets


ENVI
.img + .hdr
Common in hyperspectral remote sensing


USGS DEM
.dem
Legacy USGS elevation format


PNG / JPEG
.png, .jpg
Image formats; PNG is lossless, JPEG is lossy; georeference with world files (.pgw, .jgw)





The GDAL/Rasterio Stack
All GeoLattice raster I/O is backed by GDAL: the Geospatial Data Abstraction Library, which supports over 160 raster formats:
Your code (GeoLattice / Rasterio / xarray)
        |
    GDAL / OGR
        |
  File / object storage / remote source
  (GeoTIFF, NetCDF, COG on S3, HDF5, ...)
Rasterio provides a Pythonic wrapper around GDAL for file I/O and coordinate transforms. NumPy handles the pixel arrays. xarray adds labelled dimensions and time-series support on top of NumPy arrays.

Visualisation is provided by geolattice.viz:

Key Design Principles







Principle
What it means in practice




GDAL-backed I/O
Every format GDAL can read or write is accessible via open_raster_data


NumPy arrays
All pixel data is returned as numpy.ndarray; standard array operations apply


CRS-aware
All operations preserve or explicitly transform the CRS


NoData-safe
Sentinel values are masked before analysis and restored on write


Path-based outputs
Every operation that produces a new file accepts an output path argument


Learner-friendly
Verbose metadata printing, sensible defaults, and clear error messages
